MASTERS IN BUSINESS Rich Steinmeier, CEO, LPL Financial Bloomberg Radio · Host: Barry Ritholtz · Transcript

00:00:07 BARRY RITHOLTZ: This week on the podcast, yet another banger. Rich Steinmeier is my extra special guest. He’s CEO at LPL. They run $2.6 trillion — with a T — trillion dollars. Really a fascinating conversation if you’re interested in how a giant firm like that interacts with 32,000 advisors, plus a staff of 10,000 people in-house, and then another 30-plus thousand people working outside; how they provide a variety of options and tools and a giant tech stack for their clients, as well as all sorts of really interesting insights about what’s going on in this marketplace. I found this conversation fascinating, and I think you will also. With no further ado, my conversation with LPL’s Rich Steinmeier.
Rich Steinmeier, welcome to Bloomberg.
00:01:14 RICH STEINMEIER: Thanks, Barry. It’s great to be here.
00:01:15 BARRY RITHOLTZ: It’s great to have you. My data, more or less correct?
00:01:19 RICH STEINMEIER: I think you got it.
00:01:19 BARRY RITHOLTZ: I research it. My research assistant researches it. We run it through AI, which you always have to double-check.

We’re gonna talk a lot about what you guys have been doing with AI and science, but before we do that, I have to delve into your background. You get a BS in economics from Wharton at University of Pennsylvania and then an MBA from Stanford. What was the original career plan? That looks like banking, consulting, a lot of different finance-related spaces.

00:01:48 RICH STEINMEIER: You know, I think the original career plan was to challenge myself. So when I got to Wharton, I did finance, though I don’t know that finance was my life’s passion, and ended up as a consultant at McKinsey. And in a pivot, I was trying to think about — I really wanted to be an entrepreneur. And so for me, at some point I thought about owning auto dealerships. And when I came to the conclusion that probably wasn’t going to be my pathway, I went back to business school at Stanford to really try to hone my leadership craft and how to lead people, because it felt like that was something that I seemed reasonably good at. And it really filled me.

00:02:25 BARRY RITHOLTZ: It’s funny you say auto dealerships. I just finished The Everywhere Millionaire [author names unclear in recording], and they talk about how it’s not the CEOs of public companies, it’s people who own auto dealers, HVAC outfits, medical practices, things like that. And they’re everywhere. And they outnumber the public wealth like a thousand to one. The numbers are shocking. We’ll talk about that in a bit.
You meet your wife at Stanford. She also becomes a management consultant.
00:03:00 RICH STEINMEIER: We met at McKinsey.
00:03:00 BARRY RITHOLTZ: Oh, you did meet at McKinsey?

00:03:00 RICH STEINMEIER: Yeah. There were four business analysts in the Cleveland office. There were three young men and one young female — that was my wife. And so there was a battle of the fittest to try to woo her. I was successful in wooing her, and then we went to business school together.

But yeah, the discussions are oftentimes problem-solving oriented. And so it’s a little bit odd when we try to get into, like, emotional discussions about the kids — we’re putting frameworks in place and decision trees. It’s not super interesting.

00:03:33 BARRY RITHOLTZ: You spend time at McKinsey, you get the MBA, you spent some time at Ford. So you have a pretty broad background before going into financial services. Started at Merrill Lynch — was that the first financial services company?
00:03:33 RICH STEINMEIER: Yes.
00:03:47 BARRY RITHOLTZ: What did those outside experiences teach you about running a financial company?

00:03:52 RICH STEINMEIER: Well, I never intended to go into wealth management. I was a person that was really into tangible products. I worked on factory floors, I did lean manufacturing work, worked with automotives as well as Caterpillar, et cetera. And believe it or not, that pivot came because I liked solving problems.

And for me, the problem is the fun of pulling information, putting it together, discerning what a right strategy and pathway might be. And I got a call from a headhunter about an opportunity to take the Merrill Lynch brand to the mass affluent market, or to the mass market. And I thought, this is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity and I probably shouldn’t look past it just because it doesn’t have, kind of, hard wood and isn’t a finished product.

00:04:37 BARRY RITHOLTZ: It’s a service, not a good. So your timing is auspicious. You joined Merrill in ’06, just as the financial crisis is starting to gather a little bit of momentum. The market peaked October ’07, and then everybody knows what happened in ’08, ’09. What was that experience like? What did that teach you about risk, about leadership, and especially — given your current seat — about the relationship between a client and an advisor?

00:05:07 RICH STEINMEIER: Yeah, so I learned a lot about leadership. Look, Merrill Lynch was in a bad way, as so many of the financial services firms were. And we had a change in leadership to where there was more transparency provided to the rank and file — and I would count myself as a rank-and-file employee at that point. And learning from the leadership and seeing how to be, even in times that are very difficult, as transparent as possible. Let the people who are there, who are doing the hard work, know: okay, either we have control of this situation or we don’t have control of this situation. Here are the risks as we see them, here’s how we’re mitigating risks. And actually, in spite of a bad outcome or a challenged outcome, I thought that the firm was well managed during that time.

How does that kind of relate back into every day? I can tell you that from my upbringing, one of the things that I didn’t have the good benefit of was sound financial advice. And I grew up kind of lower middle class.
00:06:05 BARRY RITHOLTZ: Single mom running the household. That’s always a challenge.

00:06:09 RICH STEINMEIER: Yeah. And we struggled. I mean, she’s amazing, and she was able to figure it out with me, but even to get through college was, you know, sometimes a real struggle monetarily. And so understanding the value of advice — her first advisor I can remember was an Edward Jones advisor who was actually helping her on her 401(k). And I remember when she was so proud that she had earned the right into advice.

And I think for me it was about, can I work somewhere where we can make advice more available to everyday families? Can we get the quality delivery of advice to more American families? It’s actually why I went into automotive. I wanted to be in an industry that I thought benefited Americans. And at the time, in the early eighties, you could imagine that that could be automotive. And I think I’ve realized I found my way in wealth management because it’s about helping families actually create better outcomes for themselves and for their kids and their future generations.
00:07:04 BARRY RITHOLTZ: What was the role at Merrill Lynch?

00:07:06 RICH STEINMEIER: So I started — I moved into a business called the Financial Advisory Center, which was a call-center-based advisor model that ultimately became Merrill Edge, in time, after Merrill was bought by Bank of America. And so I was running the Merrill Edge Advisory Center, or call it the remote advice channel, for Merrill Lynch. And I really came to a realization that I loved financial advisors, I loved what they did, and I wanted to get actually out into the field. I liked a lot of what Merrill Edge did, but I loved the Merrill Lynch advisors. And so for me, that charted my path: how can I be more directly involved with financial advisors and help make the road easier for them?
00:07:45 BARRY RITHOLTZ: And how did you go from Merrill to UBS?

00:07:49 RICH STEINMEIER: Yeah, I had gotten to a point in my career — and I think there are points where people come into inflection points in their career — and I had gotten comfortable. I remember I was 38 years old, but I didn’t think I was learning anymore. I felt like this can’t be the capstone. I can’t be the head of this business and feel like, okay, this is just my run for the next five years, 10 years, whatever it might be. I didn’t feel like I was growing.

And so I began to put my head up, even though I really enjoyed what we were doing at Merrill Edge. I put my head up and I really wanted to move towards supporting advisors. I think of advisors as entrepreneurs, and so less structured in a corporate environment and more in support of those entrepreneurs. And, you know, people can say different things about how they think about wirehouse advisors, but I think that advisors hang their own shingle. And so for me, I wanted to get to what I thought at the time was the most advisor-centric firm that was a wire. And so I ended up at UBS.

00:08:49 BARRY RITHOLTZ: And I don’t know what you started doing there, but eventually you lead the development of all of their digital advice capabilities. That sounds fascinating. Tell us a bit about that.

00:08:59 RICH STEINMEIER: Yeah, I started there doing the call-center advice model, but part of where my energy is found is in strategy. And so as we began to progress that business, and it began to look like there were solutions that were more digitally oriented — we’re talking about the robo environment — I then realized, and just kind of raised my hand, to play a role that was more active in crafting the strategy. How do these technological components not just become a Frankenstein environment, where it’s just one appendage after another appendage, but how can we have a cohesive strategy for how we’re going to use technology to advance how advisors deliver advice to their clients? How do we broaden advice?

And so in just raising my hand, I started crafting the digital strategy for the firm. And then when that got recognized, I became the chief digital officer, which was more about: okay, you may have the strategy; take the pieces and assemble not only the strategy, but assemble the implementation of our technological footprint to be able to better serve advisors.
00:10:00 BARRY RITHOLTZ: So that’s in the mid-2010s, somewhere along those lines?
00:10:03 RICH STEINMEIER: Yeah, that’s right.

00:10:04 BARRY RITHOLTZ: It’s kind of fascinating, ’cause I am just at the edge of the generation, and the younger people in my office grew up always digital first, always internet first. It seems amazing that it took that long — and it wasn’t just UBS, it’s the whole industry — to come around and say, hey, this internet thingy looks like it’s gonna stick around for a while. Is it just the conservative nature of these big shops? Why is it that it just seems that — and we’re certainly making up for lost time with AI — but on the digital platform side, it seems like most of the big shops were very late to the party?

00:10:44 RICH STEINMEIER: Yeah, I don’t know that it’s conservative. I think that it is honoring the role of the advisor. What you’ll see — and I would say even at LPL — one of the things that we certainly don’t wanna do is get in front of the advisor. We want the advisor to be at the front of the relationship. And I would say at UBS, in the same way, I think the answer was that you moved more trepidatiously at that time into technology because it was clear who was meant to deliver the advice, who was meant to have the relationship, and the technology was meant — and is meant — to support the advisor.

And so sometimes I think when you see a little bit slower movement, it can often have to do with the principle of the firm and how the firm was founded. Not necessarily that the firm is slow; it may just be that that’s in the principle, and it’s slower to adjust. And so I would say that’s probably more what I would say: the advisor leads, the firm follows. And certainly I feel that way at LPL. But when the firm follows, that means that you need to make sure that the technology is lifting the advisor versus displacing.

00:11:52 BARRY RITHOLTZ: So do you think investors want something very different from their technology than they want from the advisors? How do you divide that? ‘Cause I remember back to the mid-2010s, a number of the big ETF firms and some other shops were kind of terrified the robo-advisors were gonna take over everything. And that turned out to be very misplaced fear, because it looks like high-net-worth investors wanna be able to pick up the phone and get a human being on the end of the line.

00:12:23 RICH STEINMEIER: I think the robo — I would say even broader than the ETF shops. I can tell you that we were quite scared about what it meant and what was the role of robo. And I’ll speak for myself; I don’t want to speak broadly for UBS, ’cause that’s where I was at the time. But I think it was this question, which is like, oh my goodness, is the role of the advisor set to be disintermediated? And what is it that we’re going to do?

And I think that was a big learning because, you know, it was: this is gonna wash in and wash all the advisors away. And what happened was it washed in, and there was a lot to be learned there, and there were a lot of capabilities. And quite honestly, there was some price transparency there that was helpful. There was performance transparency that was helpful to clients, to end investors. And I think you start to realize that there is this combination of technology and human that can be better than either one of them individually. And I think that’s the course that I saw kind of charted after that inflection point.

00:13:21 BARRY RITHOLTZ: Let me bounce something off of you, ’cause my shop was launched by four really middle-class guys that didn’t come from money, didn’t come from wealth, and were reluctant to put — as so many firms do — a $1 million, $5 million, $10 million minimum on accounts. We found that working with either a robo we built or a robo like Betterment that we worked with, we could get rid of minimums, ’cause the cost of onboarding went to next to nothing as opposed to lots of hours, lots of people. To bring a household on with $25,000 doesn’t make sense if it’s gonna cost you $1,200 by the time you’re done. But if it costs you 11 bucks, well then, why not?

00:14:08 RICH STEINMEIER: Yeah. I think that’s what you’re seeing. I think the access point into advice is being lowered pretty dramatically. And I think that is where technology plays an incredibly important role, especially when you think about account maintenance, account opening, I think rebalancing, and even personalized investing and elements of direct indexing that are enabled to get to personalized solutions and derivations of portfolios that are appropriate for individuals. I think that is the pathway that we’re on, which is: can you raise the level of advice delivered to different household levels than would’ve historically been profitable?

00:14:47 BARRY RITHOLTZ: You’re dancing around one of my favorite topics, which is: everybody spent the eighties and nineties chasing market alpha. What we’ve been seeing over the past, I don’t know, 10, 20 years is software driving, for lack of a better word, organizational alpha — the ability to deliver solutions that used to be limited to only the wealthiest households, because there was such a high cost of throwing, here’s three accountants, here’s a couple of tax attorneys and the estate attorney, we’re gonna clean this up. That’s now software today. What does that mean for the future of advice? How do you think that’s gonna change the interactions with firms such as LPL and all their advisors and clients?

00:15:30 RICH STEINMEIER: This is where we think about — and you can go back even further and say, okay, it was first about the traders, and first it was about capital market access. Then it was about, okay, can I get a balanced portfolio? Can I then update that portfolio? And so much of it, as you say, evolved away from “can I outperform the markets?” It’s about, can I actually understand goals?

Financial planning is really at the core of, I think, where the great advisors are and will continue to be, which is actually contextualizing a family’s experience, contextualizing what they’re trying to achieve, and then putting decisions in place and making trade-offs relative to those outcomes, and then tracking those outcomes. And where you get into that is, there’s a lot more involved in that engagement than just picking a portfolio, updating the portfolio, and then quarterly telling you what’s going on with the contagion in Europe or whatever it might be. It is about understanding the discrete actions that are taken. There’s a lot more complexity in it. And the tools will allow us to manage that complexity.

So what does it mean in time? It means that I think the quality of advice delivered will continue to rise. Also, I think the great part about this is consumer expectations. And that’s where I don’t find this huge conflict between the automated solutions. The automated solutions are going to raise the expectations of consumers, right? When you have a [unclear] come out and everyone says, oh my gosh, this is the end of the advisor — it’s not. It is the expectation that we will continue to deliver value at a higher level, and it will put questions in place to the viability of advisors who are simplistic in the delivery of advice. But it’s a raising of the game. I’m excited about the future of advice, ’cause I think more families are going to get better advice and make better decisions.
00:17:09 BARRY RITHOLTZ: Huh. That’s really fascinating.

Coming up, we continue our conversation with Rich Steinmeier, chief executive officer of LPL Financial, discussing how he helped build out the firm to a $2.6 trillion wealth manager. I’m Barry Ritholtz. You’re listening to Masters in Business on Bloomberg Radio.

00:17:31 BARRY RITHOLTZ: I’m Barry Ritholtz. You’re listening to Masters in Business on Bloomberg Radio. My extra special guest today is Rich Steinmeier. He’s chief executive at LPL Financial. The firm manages $2.6 trillion in client assets — one of the largest firms, and the largest independent firm, in the United States.

So I have so many questions about your leadership at LPL. You join in 2018 for business development, and this is before AI was a household word. What did the firm look like in 2018, and what was biz dev like back then?

00:18:10 RICH STEINMEIER: I say when I joined the firm, it looked like a big small firm. What that meant was that we were substantial, we were sizable, but we were immature: our processes, our talent evaluation, our strategy and go-to-market. And that’s not meant to be demeaning; it’s just meant to be a reflection that I had been at a couple of other larger, more mature firms, and it felt like we had some things to do to grow up into.

But the thing that I would say is it had a culture that had been built over three decades of knowing that we served financial advisors. When you come to work and you have a clarity as to who your client is and what success means for the firm — and ours is that we make financial advisors and institutions successful — it makes your job easier, because you don’t have to figure out all these markets. You go, okay, are our advisors and our institutions made better off today than they were yesterday? And I love that about the culture of the firm.
8139955d4dd2f2f9: PETALING JAYA: Seorang pemimpin Parti Rakyat India Malaysia (MIPP) menolak tanggapan bahawa keputusan tidak bertanding pada PRN Melaka sebagai satu tindakan boikot selepas gagal mencapai persetujuan dengan kepimpinan Perikatan Nasional (PN).

647a6bf1ef08b0bc: PETALING JAYA: The Seremban High Court today rejected an application by Dewan Keadilan dan Undang (DKU) secretary Raja Norazli Raja Nordin to intervene in an originating summons filed by 10 former Negeri Sembilan executive council members over the interpretation of the state constitution.
Justice Roz Mawar Rozain said during an online hearing that the DKU secretary had no personal interest in the case, Sinar Harian reported.
However, she allowed the DKU itself to intervene and named the institution as the third defendant, with its involvement limited to relevant issues to be determined later.
The originating summons filed by the 10 assemblymen names the Negeri Sembilan state secretary and the state government as the first two defendants.
Roz Mawar said the interest raised in the application was that of the DKU as an institution, rather than that of its secretary in his individual capacity.

She said the DKU’s involvement was important to ensure that a decision could be made effectively and comprehensively, including on the issue of the “ruler” raised by the plaintiffs under Article 28(1) of the state constitution.
She agreed with the plaintiffs’ argument that the DKU had no function in the appointment or removal of exco members.

The court recorded the plaintiffs’ confirmation that the proceedings would continue without asking the court to determine the validity of the proclamation dated April 19, 2026, or who held the office of the Yang Dipertuan Besar.
The plaintiffs also applied for the proceedings to be adjourned pending the Federal Court’s decision on the constitutional issue.
The defendants sought time to respond to the application.
The court directed that affidavits be filed by Nov 6 and submissions by Nov 11, with the hearing set for Nov 16.

4429a0075221de17: PETALING JAYA: Kementerian Kesihatan (KKM) menaik taraf skim perkhidmatan pemandu bagi memperkukuh keupayaan operasi logistik kesihatan termasuk perkhidmatan ambulans.
Menteri Kesihatan Dzulkefly Ahmad, berkata langkah itu membabitkan penstrukturan skim pemandu kenderaan kepada perkhidmatan kemahiran (H) di bawah Sistem Saraan Perkhidmatan Awam (SSPA).

“Langkah penstrukturan ini amat penting bagi memastikan pemandu ambulans kita bukan sahaja mahir, malah dilengkapi kemahiran pelbagai yang mematuhi standard kecemasan tertinggi demi keselamatan nyawa pesakit,” katanya dalam hantaran Facebook.
Beliau berkata, pembantu khidmat am sedia ada yang melepasi saringan kompetensi juga dibenarkan menjalankan tugas pemanduan di fasiliti berkaitan bagi memastikan operasi perkhidmatan tidak terjejas.

“Ujian kompetensi pemanduan (UKP) bagi pengambilan baharu selesai dijalankan pada 27 Okt, manakala pengambilan dan penempatan pemandu berkemahiran akan dilaksanakan secara berperingkat mulai April 2027 dengan kerjasama Suruhanjaya Perkhidmatan Awam (SPA),” katanya.

Sebelum ini, KKM berkata perubahan skim itu memerlukan penelitian lebih rapi terhadap kelayakan calon bagi memastikan mereka benar-benar sesuai dan kompeten menjalankan tugas pemanduan, khususnya ambulans.
Kementerian turut memberi jaminan perkhidmatan logistik kesihatan termasuk ambulans terus beroperasi dengan kapasiti yang optimum, sementara proses pengambilan baharu dilaksanakan.
Dalam pada itu, KKM mempunyai 8,863 jawatan pemandu di seluruh negara, dengan 7,687 daripadanya telah diisi setakat 30 Sept, bersamaan kadar pengisian 86.7%.
Ini bermakna terdapat 1,176 kekosongan jawatan pemandu, termasuk bagi mengendalikan ambulans dan kenderaan lain milik fasiliti kesihatan awam.
Kekosongan itu dijangka berlarutan sehingga April 2027 susulan penangguhan pengambilan pada 2024 bagi memberi laluan kepada pelaksanaan skim baharu di bawah SSPA.
f6394d6b9e1a8b3a: KUALA LUMPUR: The government is finalising the draft Children (Amendment) Bill 2026 for submission to the cabinet for consideration, said Deputy Minister in the Prime Minister's Department (Law and Institutional Reform) M Kulasegaran.
He said the proposed amendments aimed to improve Section 97 of the Child Act following the abolition of mandatory death sentences and life imprisonment in 2023.
He said the changes would introduce a more proportionate sentencing framework and prevent juvenile offenders from being imprisoned indefinitely without a specified detention period.

Under the existing Section 97(2) of the Act, courts must order child offenders to be detained in prison at the pleasure of the Yang di-Pertuan Agong or the Ruler of the relevant state, without specifying a maximum detention period.

"The Madani Government is committed to improving this legal framework to ensure a clearer and more proportionate sentencing approach that takes into account the principles of justice for children as well as public safety," he said when winding up the debate on the Supply Bill 2027 at the committee stage in the Dewan Rakyat.

He said a Special Committee to Review and Amend Section 97 of the Act had been established to examine proposed improvements to the provision, taking into account the principles of the best interests of the child, rehabilitation and reintegration, as well as international best practices.
Kulasegaran said the findings of the review had led to the cabinet's agreement on Sept 30 to four policy decisions concerning the proposed amendments.
He said the proposed policy decisions were then presented to the Conference of Rulers on Oct 14 for consideration and deliberation.

"This matter merits consideration within the framework of implementing the Parliamentary Services Act 2025, subject to deliberation by the Parliamentary Service Council and the relevant staffing and legal requirements," he said.

6d692b84c715efcf: KUALA LUMPUR: A chicken slaughterhouse suspected of operating without local authority permits was not listed in the Department of Islamic Development (Jakim)'s monitoring records because it did not have halal certification.

Minister in the Prime Minister's Department (Religious Affairs) Dr Zulkifli Hasan said preliminary inspections found that the premises in Puchong was also processing and distributing fresh chicken without the necessary approvals.
"Jakim views this issue seriously as it involves Syariah compliance, hygiene, and public confidence in the halal status of chicken in the market.

"All operational and sales records of this premises are not in the halal certification monitoring records of Jakim or the respective State Islamic Religious Departments," he said when winding up the debate on the Supply Bill 2027 at the committee stage in the Dewan Rakyat today.
He said halal certification authority in Malaysia is governed under the Trade Descriptions Act 2011 through the Trade Descriptions (Certification and Marking of Halal) Order 2011.

In addition, a slaughterhouse scheme was introduced to enable operators to apply for the halal certification ensuring slaughtering and animal handling comply with Syariah principles and halal certification requirements.

Zulkifli said Jakim, together with State Islamic Religious Departments and State Islamic Religious Councils, enforces oversight through halal certification, audits, and monitoring of premises that hold the halal certification.
He said audits cover animal sources, qualifications of slaughterers and halal supervisors, stunning methods, slaughtering processes, hygiene, product handling, and halal management systems.

However, as halal certification in Malaysia is voluntary, he noted that regulating all slaughterhouses requires cross-agency cooperation with local authorities, the Department of Veterinary Services (DVS), the Domestic Trade and Cost of Living Ministry, and other enforcement agencies according to their respective jurisdictions.

Meanwhile, Zulkifli said Jakim continues to intensify joint inspections, intelligence sharing, and investigations into complaints to protect consumer interests and preserve the integrity of the halal poultry supply chain.

For products or premises suspected of using misleading halal logos or statements, Jakim collaborates with the domestic trade and cost of living ministry and relevant agencies to conduct verification and investigations.
"Stationing halal supervisors at abattoirs is a mandatory condition for any slaughterhouse applying for the Malaysian Halal Certification," he said.
Zulkifli said Jakim had taken action in several past cases, including issuing compounds totalling RM40,000 against three companies for regulatory non-compliance.

On Oct 30, more than 6.5 tonnes of raw chicken, which was processed without complying with Syariah slaughtering regulations and halal requirements, were seized during a raid on a warehouse in Puchong, Selangor.
Twelve Bangladeshi and Pakistani men, believed to be involved in slaughtering and processing chicken at the premises, were also detained during the operation, codenamed Ops Taring Chiller.

79bf5a97a89f09a6: BRUSSELS: Belgian prime minister Bart De Wever tendered his resignation to King Philippe on Monday over deadlocked budget talks, but the monarch deferred his decision until after a new meeting Friday.

The Flemish conservative has been locked in protracted coalition talks to agree a federal budget for next year, with the government seeking €10 billion (US$11.6 billion) in savings by 2029 to reduce the country's high deficit.
The latest talks broke down hours before De Wever put forward his resignation.

"The king is withholding his decision and will launch discussions tomorrow with the different party leaders of the governing coalition," said a royal statement, adding that De Wever would be received again on Friday.
Belgium "cannot afford a prolonged political crisis," the palace warned. "The king regrets the lack of agreement to give the country a credible budget that meets the current challenges".
"The king therefore calls on everyone to show a sense of responsibility and urges all parties involved to put the general interest and the spirit of compromise first," it added.
De Wever has led a five-party centre-right coalition since February 2025.
A similar budget impasse occurred a year ago, when De Wever nearly tendered his resignation to the king.
The government is seeking billions in savings and new revenue to reduce Belgium's budget deficit, which exceeds five percent of GDP.
Its plan relies mainly on cuts in public spending, including healthcare spending, but also includes a VAT increase that has been strongly opposed by one coalition partner.
That party, the French-speaking liberal MR party, is firmly against further tax hikes, which it says would fuel inflation.
The talks are taking place under pressure from trade unions, which have been mobilising for months against austerity measures.
Rolling protests have brought tens of thousands of people into the streets.
530b7a6e011da290: PETALING JAYA: Mahkamah Tinggi Seremban membenarkan Dewan Keadilan dan Undang Negeri Sembilan (DKU) dimasukkan sebagai defendan ketiga dalam saman pemula difailkan berhubung isu pembatalan pelantikan 10 bekas exco.

Mahkamah mengambil maklum bahawa walaupun DKU tidak mempunyai sebarang peranan berkaitan pelantikan atau pembatalan jawatan Exco, kepentingannya terletak pada tafsiran dan pemakaian istilah 'Raja Pemerintah' dalam Perkara 28(1) UUTKNS, sebagaimana dibangkitkan pihak terlibat.

Susulan keputusan itu, Roz Mawar merekodkan pengesahan daripada peguam plaintif bahawa saman pemula berkenaan akan diteruskan tanpa meminta mahkamah menentukan kesahihan pemasyhuran bertarikh 19 April ataupun menentukan pihak yang memegang jawatan Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan.

Terdahulu, peguam Syed Faisal Al-Edros Syed Abdullah, yang mewakili semua plaintif, berhujah permohonan mencelah itu hendaklah ditolak atas alasan mereka gagal membuktikan sebarang hak atau kepentingan undang-undang secara langsung berkaitan perkara yang menjadi subjek saman pemula berkenaan.

Beliau berkata, saman pemula itu hanya menyentuh isu Perlembagaan, iaitu kesahihan pembatalan pelantikan semua plaintif sebagai exco di bawah Perkara 28, Perkara 38 dan Perkara 40 UUTKNS yang sama sekali berbeza daripada dakwaan penghinaan mahkamah yang dibangkitkan dalam satu lagi saman pemula.

Peguam Steven Thiru, yang mewakili DKU dan Raja Norazli, pula membantah hujah itu atas alasan pihak yang berdepan permohonan bagi kebenaran memulakan prosiding komital perlu terlebih dahulu mematuhi perintah mahkamah sebelum memohon remedi perlembagaan substantif di mahkamah lain.

Beliau juga berhujah bahawa DKU, sebagai badan perlembagaan negeri yang penting terdiri daripada para Undang di bawah Perkara 28(1) UUTKNS, memiliki kepentingan undang-undang yang jelas untuk turut serta dalam prosiding itu.
DKU turut diwakili peguam-peguam David Mathew, Shafrin Halim, dan Gurjeevan Singh.

Roz Mawar kemudian menetapkan 16 Nov untuk mendengar bantahan awal defendan yang mencabar penggunaan saman pemula bagi memulakan prosiding itu atas alasan perkara tersebut sepatutnya dibawa ke mahkamah melalui permohonan semakan kehakiman.

23b7a50fd8101d6e: Microsoft has discovered once again that few things strike fear into the heart of a software engineer quite like a government deciding to fiddle with the clocks.

Parts of Canada stopped observing seasonal clock changes on November 1, leaving affected areas of British Columbia, Alberta, and Manitoba permanently on UTC-07:00, UTC-06:00 and UTC-05:00 respectively. Unfortunately, Microsoft's sprawling software empire hasn't entirely caught up.
The company has confirmed problems across a chunk of its software estate, leaving some customers facing incorrect times, broken schedules and a collection of workarounds while Redmond catches up.

Outlook users have been left with the most homework. Switching to the new Canadian time zones won't automatically update existing calendar entries, meaning that meetings scheduled after November 1 are potentially an hour out of whack.
Microsoft advises users to change their Outlook calendar time zone, then update upcoming events and meetings to use it. For meetings involving other people, only the organizer can make the change.

Recurring meetings come with an additional treat: changing the time zone resets any previously moved occurrences, which then have to be recreated. Anyone with a calendar full of recurring meetings may wish to put the kettle on first.

Microsoft is working on an Exchange Online PowerShell cmdlet to remediate non-recurring meetings, but according to its guidance, that's not due until later this week. A fix for recurring meetings remains "in development," with an ETA yet to be confirmed.

Things get stranger with Power Automate and Fabric, where Microsoft's temporary fix involves pretending you're somewhere else entirely. Depending on the product and province, that could mean Saskatchewan, Arizona or, for Manitobans, Bogota. Because apparently time zones weren't confusing enough already.

SharePoint On-Prem customers, meanwhile, have to wait until November 10 for the correct time zones to arrive, while Power Pages users could see server-formatted dates appear an hour out until a service fix lands. Microsoft's current milestone for that is December 12.

Admins dealing with the fallout aren't exactly delighted. One sysadmin on Reddit said Microsoft's guidance had been "terrible" and claimed to have written roughly 900 lines of PowerShell to change users' Outlook settings and manually adjust calendar events. Others described switching systems to Saskatchewan time while waiting for Microsoft's new zones to settle in.

Microsoft published its guidance on October 26, less than a week before the change took effect, and was still adding affected products and workarounds four days later. Meanwhile, admins were urged to test calendars, recurring meetings, and schedules before the November 1 switch, leaving little time to find out what might break.

If any of this sounds familiar, it's because time has caused trouble for Microsoft before. In 2022, Chile delayed its switch to daylight saving time by a week. Microsoft responded by warning that Windows clocks could be wrong, scheduled tasks could run at unexpected times, and timestamps on files, transactions, and logs could end up an hour out.
Four years later, governments are still messing with time and software is still apparently objecting. ®

7b309aaa72eb95f2: PETALING JAYA: Google memperuntukkan USD160 juta (RM651 juta) membiayai pembangunan infrastruktur bekalan air guna sama baharu di Negeri Sembilan bagi memenuhi keperluan masyarakat setempat serta menyokong operasi pusat datanya yang bakal beroperasi di Springhill Industrial Park, Port Dickson.

Syarikat teknologi multinasional Amerika Syarikat itu dalam kenyataan, berkata projek itu melibatkan pembinaan sebuah takungan simpanan air luar sungai serta loji rawatan air yang mampu menghasilkan 65 juta liter air terawat sehari apabila mula beroperasi.

“Setelah siap, kemudahan berkenaan akan dimiliki oleh Menteri Besar Negeri Sembilan (Pemerbadanan) (MBINS), sebuah badan berkanun di bawah kerajaan negeri yang bertanggungjawab menguruskan aset negeri,” menurut kenyataan dipetik Bernama.

Terletak di sepanjang Sungai Linggi, takungan simpanan air luar sungai itu direka bentuk untuk menakung lebihan aliran sungai dan air hujan, khususnya ketika kadar aliran air tinggi bagi membantu mengurangkan risiko banjir di kawasan sekitar yang mudah dilanda bencana alam berkenaan.
Air mentah yang disimpan itu kemudiannya akan disalurkan ke loji rawatan untuk dirawat, sebelum dibekalkan bagi kegunaan domestik dan komersial.

Ketika aliran air berkurangan, loji berkenaan boleh menggunakan bekalan air daripada simpanan takungan itu secara langsung bagi memastikan bekalan air kepada masyarakat setempat kekal terjamin tanpa menjejaskan aliran semula jadi sungai.

Google memberitahu, pembangunan infrastruktur digitalnya di Negeri Sembilan akan merangkumi kampus pusat data yang dirancang, infrastruktur bekalan air guna sama serta program pendidikan dan pembangunan tenaga kerja yang disasarkan.

Syarikat itu juga akan menanggung sepenuhnya kos elektrik yang digunakan oleh kampus pusat datanya serta kos infrastruktur secara langsung yang diperlukan untuk menghubungkan kemudahan berkenaan kepada grid elektrik selain mematuhi semua peraturan tempatan yang berkuat kuasa.
Komitmen syarikat itu terhadap Negeri Sembilan akan meliputi fasa pembinaan serta keseluruhan tempoh operasi kampus pusat data itu yang dijangka merentasi selama beberapa dekad.
Kampus pusat data yang dirancang di Port Dickson tersebut direka khusus untuk menjadi antara pusat data paling cekap tenaga di dunia.

Apabila mula beroperasi nanti, keupayaan pengkomputeran canggihnya akan menyokong perkhidmatan Google termasuk Search, Maps dan Chrome yang digunakan setiap hari oleh jutaan individu dan organisasi di seluruh Malaysia.

Sementara itu, Pengarah dan Ketua Infrastruktur Global dan Tenaga Google bagi Asia Pasifik Drew Byrnes berkata pembiayaan bagi pembangunan infrastruktur bekalan air guna sama itu mencerminkan aspirasi global syarikat untuk mengembalikan 120% daripada jumlah air tawar digunakannya.

Beliau memberitahu, meskipun penilaian risiko air Google menunjukkan bahawa sumber air tempatan tidak berisiko tinggi untuk mengalami kekurangan atau penyusutan, syarikat itu kekal komited untuk berkembang secara lestari menerusi usaha pengisian semula sumber air, penambahbaikan infrastruktur bekalan elektrik serta pembangunan kemahiran.
6783cdf1ccaf76df: PETALING JAYA: Google will spend US$160 million (RM651 million) on new shared water infrastructure in Negeri Sembilan to support the needs of the local community and its upcoming data centre at Springhill Industrial Park in Port Dickson.

The US multinational technology corporation said the project would involve the construction of an off-river storage reservoir and a water treatment plant capable of producing 65 million litres of potable water daily once operational.
It said the project would be carried out by Gamuda Bhd in partnership with the Negeri Sembilan government and Syarikat Air Negeri Sembilan Sdn Bhd.

“Upon completion, the facilities will be owned by Menteri Besar Negeri Sembilan (Incorporated), a statutory body under the state government responsible for managing state assets,” the corporation was quoted as saying by Bernama today.

Located along Sungai Linggi, the off-river storage reservoir is designed to capture excess river flow and rainfall, particularly during periods of high water yield, to help mitigate flood risks in surrounding flood-prone areas.
The stored raw water will be channelled to the treatment plant for purification before being supplied for domestic and commercial use.
During periods of lower water yield, the plant can draw directly from the reservoir's reserves to maintain a reliable water supply for the community without disrupting the river’s natural flow.

Google said its digital infrastructure development in Negeri Sembilan would feature shared water infrastructure, a planned data centre campus, and targeted education and workforce development programmes.
It said it would also bear the full cost of electricity consumed by its data centre campus, as well as the infrastructure costs of connecting the facility to the power grid.
Once operational, the planned data centre campus in Port Dickson will power Google services such as Search, Maps and Chrome.
Google’s director and head of global infrastructure and energy for Asia Pacific, Drew Byrnes, said the funding reflected the company’s ambition to replenish 120% of the freshwater volume it consumed.

He said that although Google’s water risk assessment showed local water sources were not at high risk of scarcity or depletion, the company remains committed to sustainable growth through water replenishment, power infrastructure enhancements and skills development.

Invest Negeri Sembilan CEO Najmuddin Sharif Sarimon also said the planned data centre marked a significant milestone in the state's efforts to become a competitive destination for high-value digital infrastructure investment.
7da93d242516a122: The cyberattacks on commercial refrigerators and freezers in Europe continue, as a slew of grocery stores in Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden report widespread food wastage as a result of miscreants raising the temperatures to highs of 50ºC (122°F).

Coop stores are affected by similar attacks too, with six locations in central Sweden experiencing fridge-freezer issues, according to a company spokesperson.
Likewise, at least 13 SuperValue stores in Ireland are also affected, with fresh and frozen food being thrown out, according to parent company Musgrave speaking to RTE.
The news comes less than a month after various grocery chains in France resorted to discarding bucketfuls of produce after their appliances were remotely defrosted by cybercrooks.
Carrefour, Coopérative U, Intermarché, Monoprix, and others were hit with cyberattacks in mid-October, and hundreds of stores across the chains were reportedly impacted.

At least some of the affected stores were running outdated firmware on their Danfoss refrigeration controllers, and shortly after the attacks were confirmed, CERT-FR published an alert pertaining to numerous Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controller compromises.
Other retailers, such as Coopérative U, confirmed they were not Danfoss customers.
It remains unclear if the latest attacks across Europe used the same methods as those used for the disruption in France last month.
None of the companies that spoke to The Register on Monday responded to questions about who was behind the intrusions. ®

13d2cc1b2e283f02: When a developer gives an AI agent a coding task, the agent does more than answer once. It plans, generates code, runs tests, and repeats the process to correct errors. A single task can use 10 to 50 times more tokens than a basic chat prompt. The more useful the agent becomes, the more calls it makes. With per-token pricing, the workflows creating the most value can also become the most expensive.

The financial pressure is already visible. Uber reportedly exhausted its entire 2026 AI budget by April after expanding its use of Claude Code. GitHub Copilot moved from flat-rate pricing to metered credits. Gartner predicts that AI coding token costs will surpass average developer salaries by 2028.

The natural response is rationing usage caps, seat limits, and approvals before developers launch agents. But blanket limits can restrict the workflows delivering value. They also optimize the wrong number. Cost per token measures consumption, not results. Some spending reflects waste, including retries and runaway loops. Some represents the work of shipping software. A meter cannot distinguish them, and neither can a spending cap.
Measure the software that ships

A better measure is cost per merged pull request: total AI-assisted development cost divided by the number of changes that pass review and are merged. Track rework and defects alongside it so cheaper changes do not conceal lower quality.

If that cost falls as AI usage rises, without compromising quality, developers are converting more consumption into useful software. The question is not how many tokens they use, but how much finished work the investment produces.
Improving that equation requires two changes: reserve expensive inference for tasks that need it, and lower the cost of routine work.
Match the model to the task

Agentic coding does not require the most powerful model at every step. Use a frontier model, or an on-premises flagship when policy requires it, for difficult planning and novel reasoning. Route suitable work, including code generation, test creation, and repeated refactoring, to open-weight models you operate yourself.

A gateway can route requests according to task complexity, data sensitivity, cost, and latency. This reserves premium inference for the moments that justify it rather than applying premium pricing to an entire workflow. Meter the exception, not the workload.

Open-weight models make this division increasingly practical. Software-engineering benchmarks show that leading open-weight models can approach frontier performance on some tasks. That does not establish equivalence across every repository or workflow. Evaluate candidates against your own code, tests, and acceptance criteria before assigning production work.
Change the economics of repeated use

Next, decide who owns the capacity. With rented inference, every call adds to the bill. With owned capacity, most of the cost is committed upfront, so each additional call gets cheaper as usage grows.

The economics are simple: per-token pricing makes heavy use more expensive, while owned capacity becomes more efficient as teams use it more. Ownership is not free, though. Power, operations, maintenance, and depreciation all must be considered. The number that matters is the fully loaded cost per merged pull request.

Owned capacity also delivers a type of value that never appears on an invoice: control over sensitive code. When code generation and testing run on-premises, proprietary code stays inside the enterprise. Only approved planning prompts and governed exceptions go to external models, through a gateway the organization controls. That opens the sensitive repositories where security usually stalls adoption, and where the biggest gains are waiting.
Test the operating model

At HPE, a hybrid AI platform routes routine workloads from more than 150 internal applications to open-weight models running on premises, including on HPE Private Cloud AI. The result: token costs down 30 to 50%.
That is the point of hybrid. With HPE Private Cloud AI, owning your inference does not mean giving up frontier models. Run the volume on capacity you own and let a gateway send the hardest work.

Data also shows that usage, not licensed headcount, drives spend. The top 5% of users generated most of the consumption, and the heaviest used roughly 450 times more than the lightest on the same license. If power users grow from a small minority to half the workforce, monthly spend can rise about 4.4 times with flat headcount. Your mix will differ, which is exactly why you need to measure it.

HPE tracks two metrics and recommends customers do the same. First, it tracks cost per active developer, because averaging across all licenses hides the power users driving spend. Second, it tracks cost per merged pull request, because it connects AI spending to software that ships.

Baseline both costs before changing infrastructure. Then run a complete development cycle on owned capacity. If both metrics do not improve as usage grows, your current model may still be the better choice.
Build for adoption, not rationing

Owned capacity is not for everyone. Low or unpredictable usage favors APIs, with no capital tied up in idle infrastructure. Ownership pays off when sustained demand keeps it busy. Most enterprises will run hybrid: frontier APIs for demanding or intermittent work, owned capacity for repeatable volume. A governed gateway decides what leaves the building, so you get frontier models without giving up sovereignty over your code.

As developers lean harder on coding agents, usage will keep rising. The real choice is whether that growth shows up as a bigger variable-cost bill or as more software shipped on capacity you own. The companies that lead AI-assisted development will not ration adoption to control costs. They will build an operating model where more AI use improves the economics instead of undermining them.

d51b4457514d99c5: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.
The agentic web is here

In 2001, a decade after inventing the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision: an internet navigated by autonomous software agents that address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves.

At the time, the idea seemed far-fetched. But a quarter-century on, AI agents are beginning to make it a reality. They can triage your inbox, do your grocery shopping, and even access your bank accounts.
This new era is being called the agentic web. It will inevitably transform the internet—and whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess.
Find out how AI agents are transforming the internet, and what we stand to lose in the process.
—Grace Huckins
Are we there yet? Eliminating traffic deaths

Every year, traffic crashes kill more than 1 million people worldwide. They’re also the leading cause of death for children and young adults. Cheap, proven ways to make roads safer exist, including tightening intersections with planters and lowering speed limits. But government logjams and red tape can make it difficult to roll out these changes.
Still, some cities are making impressive progress by investing in public transit, extending curbs, and using cameras to spot danger zones in need of a redesign.
Here’s how close we are to eradicating traffic deaths.
—Sara Kiley Watson

4d3744be4285318b: Does it make sense to wait until late December to wrap up, like these California shoppers did in 2023? Mel Melcon/Los Angeles Times via Getty ImagesAmazon, Costco, Target, Walmart and other retailers begin their holiday sales as early as October. But there’s no need to rush to buy wool scarves, fuzzy throw blankets and the other holiday gifts on your list the second you spot some tinsel while shopping. As a finance professor who studies how people and companies make financial decisions, I can explain why the holiday shopping season starts so early: It can help retailers attract more customers while allowing cash-strapped shoppers to stretch purchases out across multiple paychecks. And, for people with deeper pockets, buying gifts early can help them avoid the stress that goes with last-minute shopping. Why retailers get such an early start Estimates for spending on holiday gifts, decor and the like between late 2026 and January 2027 range from about US$1 trillion to $1.7 trillion in the U.S. Some 29% of Americans plan to shell out their share of those large sums in early to mid-December this holiday season, while 17% will shop on Black Friday, the day after Thanksgiving, according to the Bank of America Holiday Spending survey. But many people like to shop for holiday gifts early – meaning before Halloween. Some do this out of necessity: They can’t afford to buy all the gifts they want to give unless they spread the cost over multiple paychecks. For others, it’s more of a preference. In a 2025 survey, about 54% of early shoppers said they want to manage their budgets gradually. In addition, 41% said they buy gifts early to avoid the stress associated with last-minute shopping. Retailers are adjusting by getting an early start on holiday sales and promoting seasonal items. By offering customers deals months before gift-giving commences, they can encourage even more people to join the early birds. And by launching promotions in October, they might secure sales that otherwise would go to their competitors later in the season. A longer selling season offers other advantages to retailers. It may ease pressure on their supply chain and logistics, since they can receive seasonal orders over three months instead of one or two. This minimizes shipping difficulties and lowers warehouse overhead costs. Building more time into the calendar to move seasonal inventory gives retailers more opportunities to sell those items. However, an earlier shopping season does not necessarily increase consumer spending overall. Some purchases may simply shift from December to October. Early birds could buy these Christmas decorations at a discount on Oct. 17, 2026. Smith Collection/Gado via Getty Images Beware of some early-shopping pitfalls To make sure that buying gifts long before the holidays occur is a wise move, early shoppers should read vendors’ fine print and research their return policies. Many big retailers are making their return policies more restrictive by shortening the length of time you can return purchases and adding return/restocking fees. In some cases, the deadline you face for returning an item could fall before the holidays. For example, Best Buy’s extended policy takes effect in 2026 only for purchases made on or after Oct. 30. Target similarly restricts its holiday-season returns window to items bought on or after Nov. 1. Amazon extended its holiday return policy in 2026. If you buy an item from Nov. 1 to Dec. 31, it can be returned until Jan. 31, 2027, except for Apple products, which can be returned until Jan. 15. Anyone who bought gifts beforehand will likely be subject to a standard 30-day return policy, which will expire long before Christmas. The timing of holiday shopping varies whether you buy gifts online or in brick-and-mortar stores. Anchiy/E+ via Getty Images When buying early makes financial sense Shopping early is smart when the costs of waiting could outweigh the potential benefits of spending your money earlier than otherwise necessary. For example, if a popular wool scarf that was priced at $100 in October is out of stock on Amazon by November, the supply is gone, but demand remains high. If you want to buy it for your mom and ensure it arrives in time, you may need to get it from other retailers. Maybe you can find the scarf on a website but is selling for $150. If time has run out, you might have to pay, say, $30 more for expedited shipping, bringing the total to $180. Clearly, you would have been better off buying it early on at a lower price. But that doesn’t mean you necessarily need to rush to buy a gift weeks or months ahead of when you’ll be placing it under a tree. First make sure that the price is in line with your expectations and what you’re willing to shell out. And you should do some comparison shopping to make sure other retailers aren’t charging less for the same or similar items. Remember, waiting to do your holiday shopping until the last minute can lead to unnecessary costs, like rush shipping fees. The key is to have a budget, recognize when the price is right, and know when to stop shopping. e02e271f23361a0a: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 2 — As the sun sets over Kampung Orang Asli Sg Relang, a devouring darkness comes with the stretching shadows, swallowing almost all sight and sound.

Here and there, in the ramshackle and spartan homes, the soft glow of solar-powered lamps shines through broken window slats. Sometimes there is the flicker of a television screen, accompanied by the hum of a diesel generator.
Solar lamps are on in the home of Yati Yusof, 25, something she is grateful for. Her family had spent the last two months in darkness, broken only by candles.

“Kena pakai lilin bila malam. Sebab lampu rosak (We have to use candles at night. Because the lamps are broken),” she told a technician from SOLS Foundation earlier.The NGO had supplied the village with solar-powered lamps and battery packs funded by Google in July, and Bernama was accompanying its staff on a follow-up visit to check on the equipment.
She did not seem too bothered having to cook dinner by candlelight. Her kids don’t attend school despite the oldest being 12 years old, so they weren’t worried about doing their homework.
Like at least 116 Orang Asli villages, according to government data in 2024, Kampung Sg Relang has mostly gone without electricity throughout the years.

What is unusual about the village, however, is its lack of electricity access despite being easily accessible. Located 500 metres off KL-Karak Highway, the Temuan village is a testament to the difficulties of electrification of rural areas, despite the government’s efforts to fulfil everyone’s basic needs.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A view of Kampung Orang Asli Sungai Relang during a recent Bernama visit. — Bernama pic

In this case, the issue is not necessarily the distance but the size of the kampung, which has 12 households and about 50 residents total. It is difficult to justify the cost of laying transmission lines to the village. And while off-grid renewable energy systems are likely the villagers’ best bet for electricity, they usually require a different approach from conventional energy projects.
Electrification

Malaysia has committed to providing universal energy access to the population since independence in 1957 as a way to eradicate poverty and enhance economic growth. And for the most part, it has succeeded.

The Department of Statistics Malaysia (DoSM) reported in 2022 that 99.7 per cent of households had direct access to electricity. The figure, however, did not specify the tiers of the electrification, a system by which to grade electricity access.
The World Bank classifies electricity access into six tiers, ranging from Tier 0 to Tier 5, with Tier 5 representing at least 23 hours of electricity supply a day.

“Tier 0 means having no electricity connection at all, while Tier 5 is what we enjoy in the cities,” said SOLS Foundation Energy Access Director Nur Syaeista Khanum Mohamed Fuad in an interview with Bernama at her office in Sungai Besi.
The foundation had provided the villagers with pico solar panels connected to battery packs, which produce enough electricity to light lamps for a few hours and to charge phones and power banks.
Syaeista estimated that the villagers were currently at Tier 1, with enough power for at least four hours of use.
“Our plan is, of course, to get (the kampung) to (Tier) five, but it is a struggle,” she said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
SOLS Foundation technician Ahmad Fakhrul Azmi installs battery packs at several homes in Kampung Orang Asli Sungai Relang during a recent Bernama visit. — Bernama pic
She added that access to a stable electrical supply was necessary for the villagers’ well-being, economic and otherwise.

For example, not having access to 24-hour electricity means no refrigerators, a basic necessity in the modern age. In Kampung Sg Relang, no one owns a refrigerator or freezer, which makes foodkeeping a tricky affair.
Otok Singgah, who is in her 70s, told Bernama her son has to drive to a supermarket 30 minutes away to buy fresh meat every two days.
“Itu kalau ada duit, kalau takde duit, (makan) pucuk ubi lah (That is if we have money. If not, we’ll just eat cassava leaves),” she said.
It’s not that the government and others have not tried to get the village to Tier 2 and above. But it is not easy, as evidenced by relics of past energy projects in the kampung.
Relics
Near the centre of the kampung are relics of renewable energy projects that were installed and then fell into disuse.

Near the village community hall is a hydro-solar microgrid. It is no longer in use, a remnant of a 2012 project by Tonibung, a Sabah-based indigenous-led NGO focusing on providing community-based renewable energy options to rural communities.

Opposite the hybrid energy plant and across the muddy road, solar panels measuring about 4m by 1.7m stand atop of several tall, abandoned metal sheds in the midst of dense foliage. Located by Yati’s house, each unit bears a house number. On the side are printed the names of the Sustainable Energy Development Authority (SEDA) and the contractor Times-Lite Electrical Engineering (TLEE).
Both projects were able to provide Tier 3 energy access, capable of supporting medium-load and productive appliances like a television.

Adrian Banie Lasimbang, founder and executive director of Tonibung, told Bernama the hydro-solar project was operational until 2014 when floods destroyed the microgrid. When asked why it was never repaired, Adrian said the funds were not there.
“The cost to repair the damaged intake is beyond the community’s financial capability,” he said.

As for the off-grid solar energy system, TLEE told Bernama in an email that it did the installation from October to December 2018. The company held Operations and Maintenance Training on March 13, 2019, before handing over the project to Selangor Economic Planning Unit (UPEN), which funded the project, the following month.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Kampung Orang Asli Sungai Relang resident Rapi Aweh plays with his young child during a recent Bernama visit. — Bernama pic
“Matters relating to the system’s operation, maintenance and status after April 2019 would fall under the purview of the project owner,” wrote Haley Khou Siew Ying from TLEE.
When contacted, UPEN Sectoral Section Deputy Director Rahayu Ali said the unit was considering funding an energy project for the village once its needs had been assessed.

“Lawatan siasatan bersama-sama pihak yang berkaitan akan dilaksanakan selepas menerima laporan (A joint investigative visit involving the relevant parties will be conducted upon receipt of the report),” she wrote in an email.
Bernama sent SEDA and the Department of Orang Asli Development (Jakoa) a list of detailed questions but received no answers.
Self-reliance
Villagers told Bernama that the off-grid solar power system lasted only about a year after the handover. None knew or had the training to maintain or fix it.

“Dia orang bila dah pasang, dia orang tak pergi lagilah. Dia orang cakap pandai-pandai sendirilah. Dia orang cakap macamtu (Once they had installed it, they never came back. They just told us to manage on our own),” said Otok.
Renewable energy experts who work with Orang Asli communities told Bernama that installing the equipment is rarely the problem. The problem usually comes afterward.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Remnants of several renewable energy projects that were previously installed but have since fallen into disuse are seen during a recent Bernama visit to Kampung Orang Asli Sungai Relang. — Bernama pic

“A lot of these projects, I can say, it’s poorly planned, or they just, like, doing it to, like, tick the boxes. Like, macam ada orang sponsor, and then just, like, go to do it, then put it in, and then leave. So it’s like hit-and-run project, lah,” (Many of these projects, I would say, are poorly planned, or are carried out just to tick the boxes. It is as though someone sponsors the project, they go ahead and install it, then leave. So, it is like a hit-and-run project),”Adrian said via Google Meet.

Experts said maintenance is usually the weakest link with these projects. Orang Asli villages tend to lie in isolated, hard-to-reach areas, and repair services there are very limited. Even Kampung Sg Relang, so close to a major highway, still lacks dependable telecommunications coverage. Calling a maintenance person to fix a faulty system remains a challenge.

Centre for Orang Asli Concerns Coordinator Dr Colin Nicholas told Bernama that the approach needs to change, and that NGOs and other agencies should involve the Orang Asli in these projects from beginning to end.
“But they don’t train the Orang Asli to problem-solve certain small issues and so on,” he said.

Adrian, who is also a former senator, agreed. Due to difficulties accessing and communicating with their village, project leaders need to provide villagers with the training to be operators rather than recipients of the solar programme. Otherwise, he warned, the problem will keep repeating itself every few years.

“One day of training is not enough. Need to set up village committee, appoint community operator. Training needs to be at least four or five days to cover system management to system maintenance,” he said.
He also acknowledged that some damage and system malfunctions were beyond the community’s means to repair.

Syaeista said foundation volunteers and staff provide orientation and training on how to use their system. She added that maintaining systems was easier when they have Orang Asli trainees on their team.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Kampung Orang Asli Sungai Relang resident Yati Yusof, 25, uses her smartphone with the help of a solar-powered light during a recent Bernama visit to her home. — Bernama pic

“Because we have one key team member there, like he’s able to tell us like, “Okay, oh, ada yang rosak, how do I do this? (Because we have a key team member there who can tell us, ‘Okay, something is broken. How do I fix this?)”

For now, the NGO only has enough funds to send staff for site visits every two or three months to check on the systems, which are under 24-month warranty. Once it expires, the villagers will have to maintain the systems by themselves.
The off-grid solar energy system SOLS Foundation provided for Kampung Sg Relang, which costs thousands of ringgit, is expected to last five years with care.
Better than nothing

Back at the kampung, the SOLS technician soon gave up on trying to repair the battery pack that stores the solar energy collected by the panels. The panels were functioning, but the battery pack was no longer working.
Luckily, he had brought a spare pack with him during this visit. Yati’s wall now sports a new bright yellow battery box. A green light flashes, showing it is ready to be used.
Despite the fix, Yati told Bernama she wished they could get more continuous electricity. Still a little light is better than nothing, she added.

“Kita pun takut-takut juga (pergi toilet bila malam). Takut ularlah. Banyak ular kat sini (We’re also afraid to go to the toilet at night because we’re scared of snakes. There are a lot of snakes here).” — Bernama
520c0476b6c44eff: BEIJING, Nov 2 — Dozens of robots took on more than 3,000 steps up one of China’s most famous peaks Monday, carrying eggs and watermelons in a race organisers billed as a test of real-world machine endurance, state media showed.
For hundreds of years, Mount Tai — the tallest peak in China’s eastern Shandong province — was an important pilgrimage for Chinese emperors and features prominently in Chinese mythology.

But the rugged terrain would prove a stern test for some competitors. One humanoid robot wearing a bandana collapsed in a heap on the cobbled route before engineers rushed in to repair it, while another tumbled down a flight of stairs and came to rest beside a rubbish bin.
The Unesco World Heritage site hosted technologies of the future as part of a new World Mountain Robot Challenge, footage from state broadcaster CCTV showed.

Over a 3.9-kilometre (2.4-mile) course with more than 600 metres (1,970 feet) of ascent, robots and their engineers from around 90 teams were tasked with either completing the route as fast as possible or transporting fragile goods like fresh eggs and watermelons to the summit.
A canine robot made by Beijing Lingyi Technology — a subsidiary of industry giant Unitree — completed the course in 43 minutes, 41 seconds, to win the four-legged speed category.
Most tourists take at least two hours to complete the route, according to CCTV.
The fastest humanoid robot — belonging to Beijing-based team Zhishen Lingyue — completed a shorter race course in 27 minutes and 26 seconds.
Organisers called Mount Tai’s rocky terrain a “natural extreme testing ground” that could help train robots for real-world use, local media reported.
The race, organised by the state-run China Media Group, featured cash prizes for winners in several categories, including the fastest robots and the best load-carrying four-legged machine. — AFP
bdeadcd40c4343db: MEXICO CITY, Nov 2 — The celebrations will run long and hard in the Mercedes camp after the crowning of 20-year-old Kimi Antonelli as the youngest ever world champion, but there is one man for whom the Italian’s joy will be tinged with regret.
After all, this season was supposed to be all about George Russell.
After dominating early season testing, Russell went into the campaign as universal favourite to take the title, the heir to Lewis Hamilton at Mercedes ready to assume his place in the pantheon.

That status was reinforced by an imposing victory in the opening race in Australia. Since then, however, that early optimism has turned to ashes as he has had to watch the young pretender steal in and claim his crown.
Russell needed to win in Mexico to have any hope of stalling the young Italian but a faltering sixth place, which included a 10-second penalty for bumping Isack Hadjar, was nowhere near good enough.
But it summed up a disappointing season of mistakes and bad luck.
“I’ve probably learned more about myself this year than I would have liked to, in all honesty,” the Englishman said before the race in Mexico.
“The highs and lows you go through in sport are immense and that’s because we all care so much for what we’re doing.”
Russell has always been candid and he will undoubtedly think back to a perfect opening weekend in Melbourne and wonder how it all went so badly wrong.

He dominated qualifying, taking pole position with three-tenths of a second in hand over Antonelli, and followed up by winning the race with a three-second gap to his teammate with the rest flailing in his wake.
Was there a touch of complacency, however, behind his smile on the podium?
“After his performances in Australia and given the gap to the other teams, he already pictured himself as world champion. Maybe he got ahead of himself a bit too soon,” a paddock insider told AFP.
Fourth in the 2025 championship with twice as many points as Antonelli, who was in his rookie F1 season, the 28-year-old Englishman cannot have foreseen such a tussle with his teammate.
Not that it was much of a tussle: Antonelli has proved stronger in his head and on the track all season.
‘Struggling’
Things quickly went off the rails for Russell.
Despite a pole position and a sprint win at the second event in China, Russell then watched, powerless, as Antonelli delivered a masterclass to claim his first ever grand prix win.
It was the first of five consecutive wins for the Italian which left his teammate reeling.
After his victory in early June in Monaco, the sixth round of the season, Antonelli already held a 68-point lead over a disheartened Russell, who was running third behind Hamilton.
Hit with two penalties in Monaco, where he dropped from third to 12th place right at the end of the race, the Englishman fumed.
“I’m beyond frustrated and I’m struggling to understand how this season is unfolding,” he said.
Russell has certainly had his share of misfortune this season, as he was forced to retire in Canada and Malaysia due to technical problems, and in Belgium after being hit by Hamilton.
Antonelli, by contrast, has on several occasions benefited from safety car interventions, as in his victory in Madrid.

But Russell seemed to give in far too early. After his retirement at Spa, he said he felt “numbed by disappointment”, and as early as the summer break he considered the gap to his teammate almost impossible to close.

There were glimmers of the old Russell as he pulled out superb drives to win in Austria and Azerbaijan but by then it was all but over with the gap between the two drivers sharply illustrated by the Italian GP at Monza.
Russell qualified second while Antonelli was forced to begin in 19th. The race was Russell’s to lose, which he did.
He finished second, nearly four seconds behind the winner, Antonelli, who had picked his way through the field in one of the all-time great drives.
In Austin last week, before the US Grand Prix, a disarmingly straight Russell said what everyone has been thinking: “I haven’t been up to the task.”
No one can argue with that but ahead of Mexico, Russell hinted that his best is yet to come.
“I remind myself that I’m 28 and I see Lewis (Hamilton) still competing extremely well at 41 and Fernando (Alonso) at 45,” he said.
“And you know Lewis won the majority of his titles in his thirties so this year is absolutely not going to define my career as a whole.
“It’s not going to break me. If anything, it’s going to make me stronger.” — AFP
1ddb6e52d056bade: BAGHDAD, Nov 2 — A decade ago, the Islamic State group broadcast its crimes as it recruited radicals from around the world and imposed a brutal system of oppression across swathes of Syria and Iraq.

Years on from the group’s military defeat, accused members are again in the spotlight — this time on trial in Iraq, including French nationals, for atrocities committed against the people trapped in the so-called caliphate.
Trials began in September for 47 French citizens who were transferred from Syria last year, charged with belonging to the group that controlled large parts of both countries between 2014 and 2017.
In its first verdicts handed down last week, Baghdad’s Karkh Criminal Court sentenced nine men to jail terms of up to 20 years.
A 24-year-old defendant, taken to Syria by his mother more than 10 years ago, was given 15 years. AFP is withholding his identity for legal reasons.
When the sentence was announced, the man said in Arabic: “I went to Syria, but it was my mother who chose for me. What is my fault?”
‘Deceived’
Thousands of people travelled from Europe to join IS during the war in Syria, where it declared a caliphate in 2014.
France, while repatriating hundreds of family members of jihadists, has refused to bring back most of the men accused of involvement, leaving them to face justice abroad.
Many French recruits were from disadvantaged suburbs of major cities and faced limited opportunities. They included descendants of immigrants, as well as converts to Islam.
The group imposed an extreme interpretation of sharia, forcing women and girls into sexual slavery, and jailed or killed anyone who dared speak out against its atrocities.
Fear was the group’s instrument of domination over areas where women were hidden from view and where executions were carried out by bearded militants in public squares, for all to see.
Now, the accused are now being brought to court with shaved faces, wearing orange jumpsuits.
About 1,500 French people are believed to have joined IS.
Among them was Kamel Ben Mbarek, 42, who said he had worked as a driver for the group’s Islamic police in Raqqa, in northern Syria.
“I regret it... because I wasn’t young when the organisation deceived me,” he told the court.

Driven by “anger at the abuses of the Syrian regime”, he embraced an ideology “that retained only certain passages of the Quran” — a manipulation he only realised when he read the holy book in prison.
Fewer than half of the French defendants have appeared so far.
“I regret everything I did. I’ve lost everything,” said Adel Bouaoun, 28, accused of taking part in IS operations in Syria’s Aleppo and Palmyra.
He recounted harsh conditions in Kurdish-run prisons in Syria, saying detainees had died, and described “physical and psychological torture”.
IS was defeated in Iraq in 2017 and then in Syria in 2019 by a US-led coalition.
Thousands of jihadists, along with their families, were left in Syrian prisons and camps under Kurdish command.
Earlier this year, the new Syrian authorities that came to power after the fall of Bashar al-Assad took over the prisons holding the jihadists.
The US army then transferred more than 5,700 detainees of about 60 nationalities to Iraq, including at least five French nationals.
Rights groups have criticised the judicial process, calling it rushed and saying that confessions were extracted under duress.
“This entire procedure is a form of pressure. You have recorded statements that are not mine,” Lakhdar Sebouai, 34, said in court.
Also among those awaiting trial is Adrien Guihal, who claimed responsibility on behalf of IS for the July 2016 attack in Nice, when a truck rammed Bastille Day crowds, killing 86 people.
‘Law of the jungle’
At one hearing, three defendants were visibly moved when they saw their siblings, who had come from France, for the first time in years.
The judge allowed them to speak together for a few minutes.

In October, French lawyers Matthieu Bagard and Marie Dose, who are defending many of the 47 French nationals, said the Iraqi judiciary had barred them from entering the country to attend the hearings, after they described the detainees’ treatment as “inhumane”.
The two lawyers are calling for the defendants’ repatriation to France so they can be tried there.
Two Iraqi lawyers appointed in their absence refused to speak to AFP.
“Even if his sentence is different, he was tortured like an adult and tried like an adult,” Bagard told AFP, referring to the 24-year-old taken to Syria as a child.
Observers, representatives of the French embassy and journalists are attending the trials.
Rights groups fear death sentences will be handed out.
Before the court, Thomas Barnouin, 45, whose verdict is expected November 18, recalled travelling to Syria at the start of the conflict, convinced that he had a religious duty.
But “the organisation applied the law of the jungle, not the law of God”, he said.
“We did not know that it also wanted to carry out terrorist attacks in our own country, in France,” he added.
“I reject all its crimes.” — AFP
