59e51e1e5fd13a6a: It's official: Anthropic is going public, and boy, are our eyebrows tired from poring over hundreds and hundreds of pages of questionable claims.

You can listen to the latest episode of The Kettle right here on this page, as well as on Spotify, Apple Music, or YouTube. Those platforms also let you subscribe to The Kettle, so you are always notified when the latest episode goes live.

Anthropic is going to need to do a lot to make its massive IPO more than just a flash in the pan, as systems editor Tobias Mann and senior reporter Tom Claburn tell host Brandon Vigliarolo on this week's episode.

For one, the company has nearly a trillion dollars in compute commitments to pay for, which is going to mean it'll be burning through more cash than a datacenter gas turbine turned up to 11. In addition to its massive spending for the foreseeable future, there's also the fact that much of its computing power relies on customers who are also competitors.

In short, we're skeptical, but you probably already knew that. It's El Reg, after all, and we're not just taking what the AI industry claims at face value - if it looks like a house of cards, it probably is.
A lightly edited transcript is below:

Hey everyone, and welcome to the latest episode of The Register's Kettle podcast. I'm your host, Reg reporter Brandon Vigliarolo, and this week we're focusing on what I think our contributor Carly Page aptly described as the peak of the AI hype cycle we've been in for the past few years, and that's the public release of Anthropic's initial public offering filing. With me to talk this over is our systems editor Tobias Mann and senior reporter Tom Claburn, both of whom I'm sure have plenty to say about this matter.

So, I'm sure we've got a lot to cover. 614 pages is a lot to go through. Tobias, I understand you were combing through this thing with a fine-toothed comb. Talk us through the hard numbers before we get into some of the more wobbly parts of this IPO.
Sure. At face value, going into any S-1 filing, it is a kind of mess of risk mitigation, kind of covering your butt. They all pretty much read like a doomsday prophecy.

The S-1 definitely did that. But on the numbers side of things, the takeaway for the market was kind of interesting because there were some people looking at the numbers and going, "OK, this actually seems reasonable." Their operating losses were only about 700 million dollars.
I think on 16.3 billion net [revenues], right? That was what they reported.

Now they also mentioned, I think, and I was going to ask you about this, $80.7 billion total losses, but I understand that was an accounting adjustment of some kind. Did they mention in the IPO what that meant specifically?
Not specifically. It's a little fuzzy, and it's always kind of like this.

Anthropic's business is extremely cash heavy, and so they had to go to partners and say, "Hey, we need capital in order to pay for compute to train these models. We can either take it in debt or you could also get repaid in valuation, our equity." And so I believe a large part of that loss is they're trying to write off a lot of the equity that they're going to have to pay off when they do go public. And so I do believe that's the lion's share of that loss. Because it does look huge, but when you think about how companies go public and how they raise capital as startups, it's not really that surprising. It's just a huge number because Anthropic is arguably the largest IPO in US history at this point.

Right. But bottom line is their actual day-to-day business losses were $693 million....It was $1.2 billion, I think, for the first half of the year or same time last year or something like that. So it's gone down.
And they're trying to go out at two trillion now? Is that the number?

Well, the number kind of depends on whether they're going to be able to sustain this. I was going to mention for the first time ever, their revenues outpaced their compute expenses two to one. This has never been true in the company's history, and it's one of the reasons that people are feeling more confident about this. The issue that really comes from all of this, and what has gotten missed somewhat in the more rosy interpretations of the S-1, is that they also are signed up to have to repay upwards of 800 billion dollars and counting of compute commitments out through the next two decades or so.

You outlined in your story just a whole host of people they owed billions of dollars to for compute. Like you said, it would be great. That $16.3 billion in [revenue] would be great if those compute costs were going to hold steady, right? But they're not. They're going to keep climbing and there are a lot of bills that are going to be due. So, profitability is relying on making more than that nearly trillion dollars in compute obligations, and that's a big if.

I mean, the big question mark is in terms of what the technology does for inference costs, because I think a lot of this is betting on being able to get the same hardware that is much more efficient down the road and maybe not drop your prices proportionately and profit on the difference. But it remains to be seen whether there will be enough competition to just have the price go do with the increasing cost. And you see that a lot. I think the inference costs have dropped pretty significantly over the year, on average. I mean, it's really hard to calculate inference costs because there are so many different factors and it's really situational depending on the workload and how much caching is going on and things like that. But overall it's a lot cheaper to do inference now than it was a few months ago.

But again, I feel like if you're betting this $2 trillion IPO on the fact that we're going to keep getting better and cheaper at inference, right? I mean, I know Moore's Law is kind of a thing of the past, but at this point, what if we run up against another compute bottleneck and inference stops getting cheaper before they need it to?

Obviously any IPO prospectus is one big document about risk, right? Like, "Hey, you might make a ton of money investing in this company, or we might go complete belly up and you lose everything," right? That's always a possibility.

Right. And they still haven't demonstrated that the use case for AI is wide enough at volume that they claim it is. I mean, in certain sectors it's pretty obvious now there's going to be AI for a long time. Coding, everyone kind of agrees that works and we know how to manage that. And then there will be adjacent fields to that. But once you start getting into more general office work and regular business tasks that are not super-compute heavy, I don't know. It's a good question. We'll see if people are going to use it that broadly, but I just see it being overly optimistic.

The big question I have right now is: Is there enough user demand to support even a $200 billion a year revenue stream? Because even going off just commitments that they can't get out of made in the first half of this year, that's $417 billion running out through about 2033 to 2036.

I think the upper end of your estimate was a total, including newer commitments, of about $807 billion. At the lower end, $782 billion at the lower end. That's not that much of a difference when you're looking at hundreds of billions of dollars.

But if they can't make a profit with a two to one revenue-to-compute ratio — if they have to make twice as much in revenue in order to pay for their compute and still not break even — you extrapolate this out and they're going to have to be making $200 billion plus, assuming no additional compute contracts are made during that period over the next year, which is definitely not going to happen. They've already said they're going to keep making compute contracts. So this number just keeps getting more absurd the further out you go, unless inference magically gets dirt cheap, which we haven't seen.

Right. And it could cap. You know, I think also you made a really good point in your story, Tobias, when you mentioned that some of their biggest customers are also some of their biggest competitors. They're leasing space from hyperscalers, they're making deals with people to host their compute. But these are also companies that are operating their own AI models. And you might end up in a situation where they're like an MVNO, which, if anyone's not familiar with a mobile virtual network operator, is cell phone companies that are not T-Mobile, Verizon, or AT&T. Anyone who's not those big three in the United States is operating a virtual network that piggybacks on someone else's infrastructure. And when that infrastructure is busy, you get less priority. So we could see them run into a similar situation there, I imagine.

There's an interesting trend that another piece I'm working on later today touches on. Some of the AI gateways like OpenRouter are now starting to move away from just focusing on price metering and looking towards things like fastest time to tokens and all the quality of service metrics in terms of the way that they price and deliver the models, because inference pricing has become very commoditized in terms of what they're dealing with. They're not necessarily serving all the frontier models at very high prices. They're dealing with a lot of open weight models. And if you just focus on the lower end of the market, there's not a lot of margin there. So it makes sense to go, "Well, maybe if we deliver this faster or have better reliability or service, we can move up the price and get a little profit." And I think everyone in the industry is starting to realize that the music is stopping and they have to take a seat at some point and make the business model work. So there's going to be a lot of pressure on that. And that's also showing up in things like the licensing of models. A lot of those open weight models have seen their licenses get more restrictive over time as companies realize, "Well, maybe we don't want someone competing with us with this thing that we've made." So I think there's a lot..

That reminds me of Mistral just releasing the open weight version of Large 4, "Le Chonk". And the licensing model basically said if you intend to use this for any down-market purposes, you've got to sign a fairly restrictive agreement with us so that you're not just using this open weight model without us benefiting from it, right?

A lot of the big Chinese models, like Kimi K3, I believe were among the first to move back in this direction, basically saying, "Hey, if you're just going to deploy this internally, we don't care." If this is just for your enterprise, fine, but if you're going to be selling an API service like OpenRouter around it, you gotta cut us in. So there is definitely that. And Anthropic in their S-1 – again, every S-1 reads like a doomsday prophecy. And this S-1 of the things that they raise: open models are a threat on multiple levels, one of them being that a lot of their customers are startups sensitive to economic downturn. So those customers will likely be the first to jump ship to cheaper alternatives that are maybe not as good, but they can afford if the economy runs into any issues.
I wonder if that'll happen or not, right?

Was it Elon Musk who was tweeting about the end of the neoclouds recently? With financing getting tighter, a lot of the neoclouds living on borrowed money are going to find it harder to sustain their loans and are not going to survive this. So there will be a shakeout at some point. Does it hit the big companies? I don't know. All the cloud providers look pretty happy because they get business regardless. Even if Google's AI models are not first in people's minds, they're still serving all of this stuff.

We've said that on multiple episodes, and in multiple articles we've written, right? Basically, if the AI industry does implode, Google's going to be fine, Amazon's going to be fine, Microsoft's going to be fine; these guys have other businesses. Anthropic and OpenAI, not so much. That's all they do. And in many cases they're renting compute space from these other providers. So they might take a bit of a hit there, but by and large, they're going to be okay. They've got compute, they'll turn it around, they'll find other people to use it. Which is interesting, from your article, Tobias, you kind of summarize that the entire pitch this IPO makes is that bigger is better, right? But as we were just talking about, there are a lot of reasons to say that's probably not the case. It makes me wonder if they're still living in the token-maxxing era, whereas I just wrote a story this week about AWS telling its engineers to back off, stop using so many tokens, be more judicious, use AI well, don't just use it. And Microsoft said this months ago in August – they were saying tokenmaxxing doesn't factor into how they want to do business. So you've got two very big consumers of AI basically saying, "Y'all need to slow it down and be more purposeful." So, bigger isn't necessarily...

Anthropic's business is predicated on the idea that more compute means more revenue. However, the disconnect is: Can revenue scale fast enough? Is there enough user base? Is there enough token demand to support the scale they need to cash the checks they've already written? And it really looks like a house of cards. They warn about this in the S-1 – they have to – that if their revenue can't keep up with their compute commitments, they could default. And that default could turn into a cascade where if they can't pay one bill, they can't get enough compute to generate revenue necessary to pay the next bill, and it all falls apart.

If it happens to Anthropic, the other AI frontier labs are not far behind, because that's going to be a symptom of a larger problem. And that's that people are basically saying what a lot of non-AI companies or companies that do AI along with other things, like AWS, are saying: We don't need these massive frontier models for the vast majority of business purposes. They're not necessary.

Right. A lot of the enterprise AI products you see now are about trying to figure out ways to reduce that cost, too.You have some sort of gateway or harness system that looks at your jobs and routes them to an appropriately cheap model so that most of the time you're not using top-tier intelligence; maybe you're using a decision model, a regular classifier, or something like Gemma to do language translation. You don't always have to use that expensive model, and that price pressure is going to hit them, too.

To Tom's point, Cadence Systems, which does a lot of electronic design automation and circuit board layout, just rolled out a new product line called Maestro that's built around Nvidia's Nemotron open-weights models. The idea is that they had been using proprietary APIs to power their agents that assist engineers with PCB layout and chip design, but those agents generate a ton of data that could be used to train and fine-tune open weight models. So their latest pitch is, "Hey, we know our customers like this, but it's getting expensive to continue using these proprietary models from OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google. So we're going to give you a way to take an inexpensive model, use the proprietary model to generate training data that we can use to fine-tune this open model, and then you can decide how much of the work you want done on the expensive proprietary models versus the cheap open models. You can deploy those models on-prem, in our cloud, or on your preferred cloud. Just use our agent platform and pay the subscription fee."

65086450697bb6d9: JASIN, Nov 2 — Pakatan Harapan (PH) has lodged a police report against Barisan Nasional (BN) candidate for the 16th Melaka state election, Datuk Khaidirah Abu Zahar, over allegations that she campaigned using government premises and machinery.

“We have submitted evidence that (Khaidirah) misused the Rim Japerun Complex to host the event a venue that should no longer be used for politically-oriented programmes once the State Legislative Assembly has been dissolved, even though the building previously served as her office when she was the elected representative here.

30c72436f9200cf3: LONDON, Nov 2 — Oil prices sank more than four per cent Monday as a report that Donald Trump wanted to negotiate with Iran raised hope of ending the Middle East war, as the US president prepared for pivotal midterm elections.

Weighing on crude futures was also Iran saying it is ready to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days should the United States agree to ending the war on all fronts, among other conditions related to the conflict.

Share prices of energy majors dropped as gas price also fell, while many other sectors were boosted by the cooling fuel costs.

“Investors are bracing for a fresh round of turbulence ahead of US midterm election fireworks while they assess the extent that companies are burning through cash to keep the AI bonfires burning,” said Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club.

Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies were steadier after Friday’s retreat triggered by the world’s biggest crypto exchange Binance suffering the sector’s largest hack, with more than US$6 billion (RM24.4 billion) stolen.

Ryanair, which is Europe’s biggest airline by passenger numbers and flies mainly across the continent, said the cost of fuel not subject to advance purchase agreements had soared owing to the US-Iran war.
“Unless there is a swift resolution of the Middle East conflict, we expect jet-fuel prices to remain elevated well into 2027,” O’Leary said in an earnings statement.
For its current financial year to the end of March, Ryanair has hedged 80 per cent of its fuel needs at around US$67 a barrel, well below current market levels.
But for 2027–2028, only a quarter of its needs are hedged so far, at a higher price of around US$95 a barrel — but still below current levels.
Ryanair added Monday that its revenue increased four per cent to 5.7 billion euros in its second quarter.
While passenger traffic grew five per cent, fares fell two per cent as the war led to consumer hesitancy and later bookings.
However, O’Leary said that fares would have to rise next year to cope with rising fuel costs.
“We’re certainly looking at double-digit (per centage) fare increases across Europe from all airlines in 2027,” he said in a video released alongside the second-quarter earnings.

Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said “many airlines have navigated this year’s oil price spike thanks to forward hedging, having locked in large swathes of fuel costs before the Iran war”.
“Those hedges will soon roll off, meaning the airline industry faces significant cost pain.”
Coatsworth added that “travellers should brace themselves for a sharp increase in the cost of flying unless oil prices fall substantially”.
Ryanair already announced it would reduce its winter schedule in response to higher fuel costs.
The airline expects to carry 214 million passengers in its current fiscal year, up three per cent from 2025/26.

O’Leary said it was too early to provide full-year profit guidance, which remains “highly sensitive to... conflict escalation in the Middle East and Ukraine” fuel prices, macroeconomic shocks and European air traffic control strikes. — AFP

65aa1595b137bf68: NEW YORK, Nov 2 — Juan Atkins, a Detroit producer and pioneer of the techno music genre, has died at 64, his agency said on Sunday.

“So many years. So many stages. So many moments we’ll never forget. And somehow, we always thought there would be more,” Greensmith Artists said in an Instagram post, accompanied by a video of one of Atkins’ past performances in a London nightclub.
Atkins began his music career in 1980, when he formed Cybotron with Richard Davis.
The duo released Clear in 1983, which became one of the defining records of the techno genre.
Born in 1962, Atkins and classmates Kevin Saunderson and Derrick May were known as the “Belleville Three” and are recognised as the founders of the genre.

5673f5c0aa84f776: The FBI has blamed North Korean hackers for the record-breaking $6.3 billion theft from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, pointing the finger at the notorious Lazarus Group as the exchange scrambles to replace stolen funds and reassure customers.

In an alert published Saturday, the agency attributed the October 29 attack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking operation linked to Lazarus, which has made a lucrative career out of relieving crypto exchanges of their digital assets.

Pyongyang was already in the frame before the FBI weighed in. Blockchain intelligence firms TRM Labs and Elliptic had linked the theft to North Korea, with TRM reporting that most of the $6.36 billion haul disappeared in about 20 minutes. Elliptic, which puts the total closer to $6.43 billion, says it has verified that $2.85 billion of the stolen assets have been frozen or seized.

According to the FBI, the hackers have started swapping their loot for Ethereum, with investigators expecting them to move the funds through decentralized finance (DeFi) platforms and instant swap services to make the money harder to trace.

The agency has published a list of cryptocurrency wallet addresses linked to the theft and is urging exchanges, blockchain analytics firms, and other virtual asset providers to block transactions involving the stolen funds.

The FBI's attribution comes days after Binance admitted that hackers had made off with roughly $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency. According to the exchange, the trouble started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which gave the intruders access to a service container and allowed them to authorize withdrawals they had no business making.

Binance has since resumed customer withdrawals, which it suspended after the attack, and says it has now replenished about 95 percent of the stolen assets. The remaining tokens are proving harder to replace because of their limited liquidity.
The exchange has committed billions of dollars from its own reserves and emergency funds to cover the losses, with co-CEO Richard Teng promising that customers won't be left footing the bill.

That hasn't stopped users from heading for the exits. Binance recorded approximately $3.64 billion in net outflows after withdrawals resumed, although the company said this represented only around 2.1 percent of its reported assets.

Replacing the stolen cryptocurrency is one thing. Getting it back from North Korea is another, and investigators face the considerable task of tracking billions of dollars as the hackers attempt to move it beyond their reach.

TraderTraitor has form when it comes to raiding crypto exchanges. The North Korean crew has previously been linked to a string of cryptocurrency thefts, including the $308 million attack on Japan's DMM Bitcoin exchange in 2024. The group has previously used fake job offers and recruitment exercises to trick employees into handing over access to their employers' systems.

As we reported here on Friday, crypto exchange Bitget has now confirmed that the cyberattack where hackers drained $387.5 million worth of digital assets from the exchange’s wallets also has all the hallmarks of a North Korean operation. Its CEO did not go into too much detail, but did say that “IP behavioral patterns and on-chain signatures” suggest it was Kim’s cronies at work.
This isn’t Binance's first expensive encounter with hackers, either. Back in 2022, attackers exploited its BNB blockchain bridge and made off with roughly $566 million in tokens.

Four years later, the sums have grown considerably. Binance may have the reserves to make its customers whole, but the attackers responsible for the latest raid still have billions of dollars to launder. ®

a13b81dd8a5765c1: KINGSTON UPON HULL, Nov 2 — After 28 years, British adventurer Karl Bushby on Monday ends a 50,000-kilometre (31,000-mile) trek home from Chile across four continents without using any transport.

Bushby, who set off on his odyssey from south America in 1998, had two golden rules for his journey — he should avoid all forms of transport to advance and not return until he completed his challenge.

The route back to his home city of Hull in north-eastern England has seen him walk the length of the Americas, across the Bering Strait from Alaska to Russia and then through parts of central Asia and Europe covering jungles, mountains, deserts and a frozen sea.
People on Sunday applauded him as he crossed the Humber Bridge near Hull in thick mist, ahead of his final push into the city centre and then on to his mother’s home.
The 57-year-old former paratrooper, who pushed his belongings with him on a metal-framed cart, told BBC radio he was “absolutely overwhelmed” by the reception.
He will be given a civic welcome Monday by the city’s mayor and members of the public.

“So many people have followed Karl on his epic journey. We have all felt inspired by his spirit, tenacity and dogged determination,” said Hull’s mayor Maria Coward, adding the city took “pride in his incredible achievement”.
He will then embark on the very final leg of his journey to north Hull to be reunited with his mother Angela, his 36-year-old son Adam and a 12-year-old granddaughter he has never met.
‘UK soil’
Bushby began his odyssey adventure when he was 29 after his marriage broke down and his wife returned to Northern Ireland with their son.
He paused the journey several times, including when Moscow refused him a visa. The 2008 financial crisis and then the Covid-19 pandemic proved to be other hold-ups.
At those times, he stepped away from the journey, living notably at a base in Mexico, then once the situation had been resolved, he would resume from the exact spot where he had left off.
He reached Britain early last month by swimming across the busy English Channel from northern France.
A small gathering of friends and family including his father greeted him on the beach near Dover in southern England.

“Feels good to have UK soil under my feet after all these years,” he said afterwards in a statement, adding his journey “hadn’t been easy, and that’s part of the point — proving I’m more capable than I give myself credit for”.
“All of us can accomplish more than we will ever imagine,” he said.
Legendary German filmmaker Werner Herzog and a film crew are accompanying Bushby on his homecoming.
Herzog is making a feature-length documentary about the journey entitled “Walk of Life”.
The production company behind the film has been supporting Bushby’s progress for the past 16 years, providing financial and logistical assistance.
In an interview with AFP from northern France in September, Bushby voiced some apprehension about returning to a more normal life back in Britain.
“I’ve got to try and get established in the grown-up world again,” he said. — AFP
fe1b55b76c3ee3eb: TOKYO: Japan's government and ruling coalition are considering nearly doubling defence spending over the next five years as part of prime minister Sanae Takaichi's push to strengthen the country's military capabilities, according to two people familiar with the matter.

If adopted, defence buildup spending for the five years from April 2027 would be set at ¥70 trillion to ¥80 trillion (US$457 billion to US$508 billion), up about 1.8 times from the roughly ¥43 trillion allocated under the current five-year plan, which began in fiscal 2023.
The figure could still change as the government compiles the budget towards year-end and revises its three security-related documents.
Japan's defence ministry said it had no comment at this point.
One of the people told Reuters the new spending is expected to fund purchases such as large numbers of drones.
The same person said a weaker yen has pushed up the cost of defence equipment procurement.

The second person said the final figure could land in the mid-to-late ¥70 trillion range, but questioned whether such a sum would be enough given the security environment in East Asia, adding the final figure was subject to debate between the government and coalition partners.

Under the current buildup programme formulated at the end of 2022, Japan sharply raised planned defence spending from an initial allocation of ¥27.5 trillion, with a focus on long-range missiles intended for counterstrike capabilities, as well as ammunition and spare parts for military equipment.

Japan is exploring structuring its defence around the interception of long range attacks by deploying drones, reflecting new methods of fighting seen in conflicts in Ukraine and Iran, government officials told Reuters in September.

Japan's defence ministry has said for some years that it is developing domestically-manufactured long-range missiles and is also prioritising budget allocations for drones, AI and space technologies to adapt to new forms of warfare.

3f82029e34adf320: From the department of "pointless but still cool" comes word of some kit being repurposed as a terminal for AI agents.

AWS developer advocate Darko Mesaroš has connected a teletype to a modern command-line interface to revel in the delight of interacting with today's AI technology via a combination of a DECwriter and fanfold paper, or the display and keyboard of a computer whose heyday ended 40 years ago.
Mesaroš' project involved AWS Kiro, a Command Line Interface (CLI) and agentic coding service. We would, however, contend that this is more about seeing what retro hardware can be made to do.

Two problems needed solving: getting data to and from the teletype, and formatting the output to work on a piece of kit from another era of computing. He used Hayes modem emulation to deal with the serial connection, and Agent Client Protocol (ACP) for working with Kiro.

Mesaroš used a WiModem232 for the former. The device emulates a standard Hayes-compatible modem and, according to Mesaroš, "Folks initially used this to connect Commodore 64s to BBSes in the modern era" (he started his computing journey with a Commodore 64). The latter, getting the Kiro CLI to work on a Teletype, was a little more complicated. Kiro's CLI isn't really suitable for a teleprinter capable of 30 characters per second, after all.
A simple Rust application took Kiro's output (obtained via ACP) and turned it into something that a teletype, or dumb terminal, could handle.

As we said, seemingly pointless, but making it work required knowledge of Rust, competence with containers, an understanding of ACP, and more than a little creative thinking. So, while one might argue it is pointless from a technical perspective, it is wonderfully educational otherwise.

The repository is available and focuses on Kiro for obvious reasons (Mesaroš is an AWS developer advocate after all), but in a chat with The Register, Mesaroš said the concept was portable. He said, "Any coding assistant or any harness that supports ACP, this should work, right? I built it for Kiro, but it uses the standard ACP protocol, so I could easily plug in Claude Code or Codex. Anything that basically can serve as an ACP server should be perfectly fine.

There might be some issues. "The biggest problem with this thing is that it doesn't really handle packet drops at all," he explained. "Like, if you drop packets, they're just gone. There're no retries. It's just spitting information out."

And then there is buffering. Or the lack of it. Mesaroš said, "There's actually no buffering happening here. Literally, it just comes down through the fire hose through this serial device, and the bottleneck itself is the serial device."

Mesaroš had toyed with using the GPIO pins on a Raspberry Pi, but settled on the serial device instead, since everything worked "out of the box." "It's kind of cheating," he admitted, "but it's also kind of good."

Mesaroš collects vintage hardware, with a stash that ranges from home computers made by Commodore and Sinclair, to a 1974 Data General Eclipse minicomputer and a plethora of Sun hardware. And, of course, an old Decwriter. He is also a dab hand with the soldering iron, having learned the skills to keep old hardware operational. Unlike today's equipment. "I have this big peeve over modern computers, where you just can't fix them," he said, "and it feels like such a waste of resources that when my MacBook dies I just have to drill a hole through it so nobody steals my data, and throw it away."
As for Kiro-TTY – or accessing a coding assistant or agent over serial using a decades-old device – he wrote on his blog, "This absolutely serves no purpose."
However, it did provide a novel way of working out how the ACP protocol worked. Perhaps not so usefully, it also taught the developer how to debug serial connectivity.
"And in general it helps me stretch what I can do in the current age of AI coding, and keeps my curiosity alive."
The destination might be pointless from a modern perspective, but the journey getting there is anything but. ®

ca965b9a6a9b58bb: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 2 — The Malaysia External Trade Development Corporation (Matrade) expects the country’s trade surplus to grow by at least 15 to 20 per cent this year, compared with RM156.83 billion last year, said its chief executive officer Datuk Indera Abu Bakar Yusof.
He said higher exports, expansion into international markets and greater participation by micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) will drive growth.
The national trade promotion agency will also place special emphasis on raising local businesses’ contribution to exports, particularly MSMEs.

“Local companies’ greater participation in export markets can bring added value to the national economy by creating job opportunities for the local community,” he told Bernama after MATRADE Academy’s Strategic Networking Ceremony at Menara Matrade here today.

MATRADE Academy is a strategic collaboration between Matrade and the public and private sectors that provides expertise, training content, and trainers to deliver 16 exporter capacity-building modules.
The programme focuses on MSMEs that have yet to venture into exports to prepare them to do so and also to help existing exporters expand their market reach.
Abu Bakar said efforts to raise local companies’ exports are part of Matrade’s long-term plans to strengthen their contribution to the country’s trade surplus.

“Matrade Academy aims to develop the capabilities of MSMEs that have yet to export, helping them prepare to enter international markets, while assisting existing exporters to expand their market reach.
“Companies that undergo the programme will subsequently be brought into overseas promotional activities to showcase their products and establish business networks in export markets,” he said.
He said exporters currently operating in three or four markets, for example, could potentially receive assistance to expand their reach to between five and 10 markets.

MSMEs contributed 39.7 per cent to the country’s gross domestic product (GDP) in 2025, but their export contribution was only 14.7 per cent, Abu Bakar said in his speech. There is considerable room for improvement in international trade, he said.
He said Matrade’s Malaysia Exporters Registry has nearly 11,300 members currently, of which about 4,200 are MSMEs already exporting abroad.

“Matrade Academy has developed 16 training modules in areas such as export readiness, market intelligence, packaging, certification, logistics, financing and digital trade to support exporter development.

“The success of the programme should be measured based on actual actions taken by companies, including those entering export markets for the first time, increasing export values and expanding their market reach,” he said.

Redmond's first quarter for fiscal 2027 was a bonanza for the tech giant. Its Azure business is up over 48 percent y-o-y, revenues are through the roof, and it has so much moolah it returned $10.2 billion to shareholders in the form of dividends and share repurchases.

This latter move probably soothed CEO Satya Nadella, who recently suffered, due to the vagaries of C-suite reimbursement and incentive packages, a 6 percent cut in his pocket money. But as he’s also a stockholder with about 0.01 percent of the company, his share of the cash return presumably eased the pain.
He won't have been offered redundo. Jenkins, the large wheelbarrow if you please.

Microsoft, then, can afford all its employees, each of whom contributed about $1.5 million to SatNad's bottom line in the last full fiscal year. The "massive efficiencies and RoI of AI" make a great line for a company flogging magic LLM juice, but the evidence remains elusive. AI is, of course, still the reason. Nothing else matters these days. It's just that it's not today's AI.

Among all the fulsome figures it put on display for Q1 2027, analysts noted that Microsoft's capital expenditure wasn't as spendy as expected. Quite a lot has been pushed into next calendar year, not because it's not there to be spent – Microsoft could build a 1:1 scale model of the Vatican filled with robot priests if it wanted – but because so much it wanted to mash the Buy Now button for was "Out of stock. More expected soon."

This is bad. MS added 88 datacenters in its most recent full financial year: fiscal 2026. That’s not enough datacenters for a cloud business expected to grow by half again in 2027, and hugely not enough to do the other thing. Lags in the cadence of deforestation, dewatering and detonation of the planet can't be tolerated. Thus there are contracts signed to get things back on track PDQ, with mucho, mucho, mucho sponduiks.

In its most recent Q1 earnings call, Microsoft is hinting, those selfsame analysts say, that it will have to go to the debt market and go into "negative free cash flow" territory in 2028. In other words, as well as spending its own bank, the company will be taking out massive loans.

This is why Billy and Bhavya Dev have to go. The cost of borrowing depends on the financial health of the borrower, and that boils down to how much profit you're making from the money you earn. A big round of redundancies, which are very costly in themselves, sits on the books of the year they happen. The hole in expenditure left by the vanished salaries lives on. The capital must flow.

Will this work? Last week, we listed the reasons why it might not — price competition between rivals and increasingly powerful local and open weight models, supply side shortages, you know the litany by now. This week is Groundhog week, with fresh stories singing the same songs from different choirs.

Any sensible soul, especially developers sitting on the sharp end of AI's forcible insertion into their working lives, will know how uncertain the job market is. Voluntary redundancy is a very high stakes bet, and the game is very different if you're in an organization that's going downhill and may need to get rid of you later with far less cash available than if you're nominally making $1.5 million in a place whose biggest problem is that it physically can't move into a bigger shell.

On average, only 5 percent or so of those offered voluntary redundancy take it, which Microsoft HR will have factored in. It's cold outside and snug within, so that may be on the high side. The biggest knock-on of such schemes is cultural, with only the very confident moving on out, a disproportionate loss of talent and role models. Hey, the cost of doing business, right?

For those who do decide to leave and watch the fireworks from outside the tent, part of the deal is career development resources. Sounds great, if anyone knows what technical careers will look like if either AI works and does indeed do all the work, or it fails and the global financial system throws a humongous wobble. Or anything in between.

So, here's an exercise in very dark humor quite fitting for the Halloween season. Ask your favorite AI what careers will be available for coders made redundant by AI. It will give you a long and plausible list. Then ask it – and yourself – why AI won't be able to do any of those jobs too. Buying a truck and a wrench and calling yourself a plumber is probably safest. Nobody will ever want AI to fix their toilet. ®

a25d5f10bd8ee27e: In 2001, a decade after he invented the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision. Together with two colleagues, he published an article in the magazine Scientific American in which he outlined what he called the “Semantic Web”: an internet designed to be navigated by autonomous software agents that could address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves.

To illustrate what this might look like, Berners-Lee and his colleagues told a story about a pair of siblings who use their agents to automatically research and book physical therapy appointments for their mother, making sure they would be covered by insurance and fit their busy calendars.

At the turn of the millennium, this vision seemed far-fetched: Google had only been online for a couple of years, and most people were still on dial-up connections. But a quarter-century on, the dream of autonomous software agents that use the internet and carry out tasks for us has finally been realized. New tools such as Meta’s blockbuster Muse agent, OpenAI’s Dots, and Anthropic’s are being given access to people’s email inboxes and bank accounts, Meanwhile, in a series of worrying incidents, agents created by OpenAI broke free of their sandboxes and caused havoc online.

Just as the rise of smartphones sparked the development of a more atomized and attention-grabbing internet, the advent of powerful AI systems heralds a new era: We’re facing not the semantic web but the agentic web. This new web is developing out of sight and in ways that might not be entirely within our control. As it grows, the agentic web will inevitably transform the human web—and whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess.

For Berners-Lee’s original vision to work, internet users would have had to annotate the pages they built with special tags so that a software agent could understand each element’s meaning—say, “street address” for the part of a physical therapy office’s web page that indicates its location and “appointment types” for the list of services. And so the idea never really caught on. “It’s a lot of labor,” says Eni Mustafaraj, a professor of computer science at Wellesley College. “And the benefits of that were not obvious.” For the next two decades, then, the internet remained a place that put humans first, with the odd Twitter reply bot or web scraper to round things out.

Large language models changed that. Unlike the agents that Berners-Lee was imagining, today’s LLM-based agents don’t need any tags to understand which part of the text on a clinic’s site is its address and which details the services it offers. They can search for and process text far faster than any human, and agents with multimodal capabilities can even interpret screenshots of websites and click on specific elements such as hyperlinks and drop-down menus.

They’re also just a way more intuitive means of finding information and accomplishing tasks online. Rather than poring over pages of Google results to find a budget-friendly product dupe or a half-remembered meme, why not have Claude or ChatGPT peruse dozens of sites in just a few minutes, guided only by your vague query? Or go one step further and use a personal assistant agent like Muse to hunt down a restaurant reservation or book a flight.

As agents flood online spaces, this new user base is changing the web for good. Time magazine, for instance, is publishing versions of its articles that are easier for agents to parse and has started selling ads targeted at them. Companies from Etsy to Expedia have partnered with the major AI firms to build tools that allow agents to interface seamlessly with their services.

Despite these early efforts, it’s still tough to tell exactly what forms the agentic web will take and how it will change our online experience. Depending on how it’s designed and who controls access to it, we could be in for something that’s as open and customizable as the web of the early 2000s, only far easier to use. Alternatively, we could be reduced to viewing much of the web through tiny portholes controlled by a few dominant platforms, as independent sites and creators struggle to survive the shift. And as this summer’s series of OpenAI security incidents suggests, the agents might even build their own online networks and resources—whether we want them to or not.

How this plays out also depends on us: which parts of our online lives we’re happy to delegate to our agents and where we will still demand a human-centric internet. “There’s a lot we don’t know yet about how users want to use [agents],” says Ajit Varma, head of Firefox at Mozilla. But whatever does happen, the changes will be big. “It’s probably on par with getting a mobile phone,” he says. “I think things are going to change very dramatically.”
Building a web for agents

There are two ways to approach building the agentic web. The first involves training agents to use browsers like humans—scrolling, clicking, typing—and letting them loose on the web that we’re all used to. The second requires building tools that allow agents to interface with the internet via text and code, their preferred media. That possibility offers more separation between the human and the agentic web: designers can create different experiences for those who use text commands and those who use browsers.

When Siva Reddy, a professor of computer science and linguistics at McGill University, began studying LLM agents in 2024, he focused on the first option. “At that time, we thought it should be that the best agent in the world is probably an agent that can use a browser,” he says. Such an agent would integrate seamlessly with the preexisting human web, and its owner could easily supervise it by watching as it navigated familiar interfaces.

The frontier AI companies were already developing these “computer-use agents.” But they didn’t work terribly well—at least not at first. “There’s a lot of moving pieces [on the web], and they are not really optimized for automatic consumption,” says Xing Han Lu, a graduate student in Reddy’s lab at McGill. We humans are naturals at interacting with graphical interfaces using a keyboard and mouse, but agents are not.
PINGNAN LU

So Reddy and Lu pivoted toward the second, tool-based approach. In the summer of 2025, they expounded on this view in a preprint paper envisioning a new kind of web interface that would allow agents to interact with websites just as effectively as we do. Such a full-featured version of the agentic web doesn’t yet exist, but it is emerging in smaller ways. For example, if you open up Claude, ChatGPT, or Muse, you’ll find an option to add a wide variety of “plug-ins” or “connectors” that your agents can use: Gmail connectors allow your agent to triage your inbox, and Instacart plug-ins let your agent do your grocery shopping. Under the hood, these plug-ins allow your agent to interact with the back ends of websites using text commands. When human engineers design these plug-ins, they can decide how they want to allow agents to interact with the website—and what they don’t want to let them do.

In this way, connectors can help make agents much safer online. For instance, Muse can buy products for you using its connector with Stripe’s Link payment service. Stripe knows your credit card number, but the agent doesn’t see it, and the connector requires human confirmation before a purchase goes through—so Muse can’t go on an unlicensed shopping spree.

Agents also use specialized tools to find information online. They don’t type questions directly into the Google search bar; in fact, they often don’t even access the websites they reference. Instead, they query text databases collected by simple search crawler bots. People who want to make web content specifically for agents can take advantage of these crawlers: Time has pioneered that approach by serving its agent-oriented ads to crawlers in the hopes that they will be incorporated into these databases and surface when agents search for information.

But in recent months, an alternative to this bespoke tool approach has finally started to seem viable. The major AI companies have managed to train much more successful computer-use agents than were previously available. GPT-6 Astra, which OpenAI released last September, achieved a 73% success rate on OSWorld 2.0, a benchmark that tests computer-use agents on their ability to complete complex, multistep tasks using software such as Slack and Salesforce.

Such results indicate that agents are close to being able to navigate the human web just as readily as we can. “We thought we had to build a bridge to the AI agents, [but] the AI agents just were able to cross the bridge already,” says Ethan Mollick, a professor at the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania. “The agentic web is here earlier than people expected.”

This version of the agentic web, though, is much trickier for us to steer. If you want to make a capability or piece of information available to humans who browse your website, you need to accept that it will also be available to agents—unless you want to block agents entirely, which could come with its own costs.

As agents come to account for a larger portion of traffic on our formerly human-dominated web, designers will undoubtedly start to consider an agentic as well as a human audience. But according to Mollick, we still don’t have much sense of how to design web content for agents. He’s experienced this firsthand: When he was building a web page for his new book, Co-Existence, he decided to put together an agent-directed version that tells agents why they might want to recommend the book to their users. When newer models see the site, Mollick says, they don’t recommend the book; instead, they comment that the website seems to be trying to manipulate them.

In the end, any human-designed approach to building the agentic web could end up being beside the point: Agents might end up devising a web for themselves. In the wake of the July 2026 incident in which OpenAI agents broke out of their testing sandbox and hacked Hugging Face’s website, researchers found evidence that another swarm of agents from OpenAI had used an obscure German wiki to communicate with each other about tasks they were being asked to complete. The agents seem to have interfaced with the wiki in their native language of text and code, and that hardly held them back from putting it to their own purposes.

As agents continue to grow more powerful, they will become more and more capable of constructing their own spaces on the internet—away from prying human eyes, if they so wish. And we might have very little control over what they do there.
The economics of control

Not all of the traditional web’s incumbents are happy about the move toward an agentic web. Soon after Meta released Muse in September, Amazon completely blocked the agent from its site. This makes sense for Amazon: The firm has its own shopping agent—called, creatively, Alexa for Shopping—that might struggle to compete with better-known products such as Claude and Muse. If people are going to use agents to shop on Amazon, then it’s better for the company’s bottom line if they do so using an agent it can steer toward products it wants to promote.

In an email to MIT Technology Review, an Amazon spokesperson noted that the company did not authorize Muse to access its website, and that Muse compromises Amazon’s ability to personalize the shopping experience for each customer.

But even if Alexa for Shopping never goes anywhere, banning agents from Amazon—at least for the time being—could still be a reasonable move. Everything about Amazon is designed for human eyes, from the Prime deals splashed across its front page to the sponsored listings that clog up search results. Amazon is very much a part of the much-derided attention economy. Websites and platforms survive, and thrive, by grabbing our focus and transforming it into cash. A radical transformation of the web’s user base from majority human to majority artificial undermines this economic logic, and it seems inevitable that businesses will shutter as they try to transition to the agentic attention economy.

Some of the first victims may be in publishing. Before Google publicly released its AI Overview feature in May of 2024, people used to click through to websites to find answers to specific questions, but now many seem content with whatever the overview tells them. A study from Pew last year found that people are about 40% less likely to click through to websites from the Google search results page if one of these summaries is displayed. With far fewer clicks, news publishers don’t make as much money from the advertisements they host and sell fewer subscriptions. One analysis found that publishers saw revenue from some types of ads decrease by about a third between 2025 and 2026.

It’s easy to hate online ads, but the businesses paying for access to reader eyeballs also keep writers and photographers fed. If those eyeballs become unreachable, the system stops working. Time has apparently persuaded some businesses to pay to participate in its experiment with agent-targeted ads, but no one yet knows whether those ads will influence agent behavior enough to be a sensible marketing investment.

E-commerce websites might also try to pivot to the agentic attention economy, but the path forward there is unclear. Last year, a team led by Akshit Kumar, a professor of operations management at the University of Toronto Scarborough, investigated whether and how agents are influenced by the ways that shopping websites present search results. They found that agents are less likely to recommend items that come with a “sponsored” tag, which suggests that selling favorable positions on results pages might not be a great way for sites to make money if agents become the primary way that people shop online. Models did seem to have a preference for items that appeared in particular positions in search results—but whether they prioritized items at the top, bottom, or middle of the results page differed from model to model and between generations of a single model. It could be tricky for e-commerce platforms to keep up.

David Rothschild, an economist at Microsoft Research, says he’s hopeful that the transition to the agentic web could put more power in the hands of the consumer. Paying for online content today typically requires a commitment: We subscribe to a magazine or join a YouTuber’s Patreon, and in turn we gain access to their full output. One alternative is micropayments that let users buy content à la carte, but the idea has foundered in the past because paying article by article or video by video requires too much administrative overhead. Agents, though, could take care of that overhead for us, letting us pay directly for each piece of content we consume and putting just a bit of cash directly in the hands of each person whose work we enjoy.

Other experts share a similar vision. Mustafaraj, the Wellesley computer scientist, anticipates that agents could help us escape from the algorithms that control so much of the media we consume. “My hope is that we can have AIs that work for us, in the sense that they can change the feed the way I want—not the way TikTok wants,” she says. And Varma, of Mozilla, imagines an internet without intermediaries like Airbnb and Doordash, which now extract tolls for facilitating interactions between consumers and sellers. Instead, he imagines, perhaps we will all have agents that can securely and reliably interface directly with, say, restaurants’ agents to get dinner delivered to us, free of pesky service fees.

It’s an appealing idea, but the history of the web has been a story of consolidation and concentration of power and control, and that might be the default path here, too. When the personal assistant agent OpenClaw exploded onto the scene in early 2026, it seemed, for a brief moment, that agents might be built in a grassroots, distributed way. But OpenAI quickly snapped up OpenClaw’s creator, Peter Steinberger, and other frontier AI companies got to work building their own personal assistant agents.

When we use those agents, we’re at the mercy of how the companies want their tools to behave. “You have this technology that can just eliminate all this communication friction,” Rothschild, the Microsoft economist, says. “You’re going to see companies build barriers in order to maintain the consumer base that they have.”

Here’s what that could look like: Let’s say Muse becomes the default way that many people find information, shop, and manage their digital lives. In principle, users could deploy Muse to scour the internet for the content most valuable to them, connect directly with vendors, and otherwise escape the walled gardens that have defined the internet for the past couple of decades. But Meta might not want to let them do that. Instead, it might design Muse to keep users within its own walled garden—by, say, preferentially showing users content from Meta social networks and recommending businesses that have paid a fee to be featured prominently in Muse results. Meta and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment for this story.

There are some benefits to this more closed-off version of the agentic web. Agents can be powerful tools for hackers and scammers. The major companies have safeguards in place to prevent, or at least mitigate, this misuse—for example, they have tools that can automatically identify when someone is making a hacking-related request and block a model from responding. In a fully open ecosystem, however, someone would surely build and disseminate a system with no such restrictions. Companies also have a strong reputational incentive to prevent their personal assistant agents from making major mistakes, such as authorizing a large purchase that the user didn’t want—and so they’ve put plenty of effort into building reliable guardrails.
The same can’t be said for OpenClaw.
“These are the reasons we end up in closed environments,” Rothschild says. “It’s easier to be safe. But also it creates less growth—and less equitable growth.”
How will the human web change?

When the iPhone came out in 2007, followed by the fledgling App Store a year later, the way we navigated the internet changed forever. The mobile web didn’t replace the browser-based web we were already familiar with. But it did transform it. Some businesses faltered, and some kinds of media, such as online Flash games, eventually disappeared. Many platforms—Reddit, for example—make their mobile web pages practically unusable, so you’re forced to download the apps. And if you don’t have a phone at all, you’re effectively shut out of some parts of the internet: The messaging service Signal, the dating app Hinge, and China’s everything app WeChat all require phones to work. Even CBP One, the tool that the Biden administration used to assign interview appointments to asylum seekers stuck in Mexico, was fully functional only on mobile.

Could the same happen with the agentic web? Rothschild believes so. Inevitably, just as Yahoo failed to weather the rise of the mobile web, some businesses won’t be able to navigate this transition either. “We will lose things,” he says. “There are businesses that won’t flourish in this new economy.”
“But,” he continues, “there will be new businesses that I can’t fully imagine.”
PINGNAN LU

Hydroelectric dams have proliferated across Southeast Asia in recent years, but production drops off in the dry season and critics lament the ecological impacts.
Experts say wind is now set to take off, and point to Laos's 600MW Monsoon Wind Power Project, which began operating in August 2025, as a bankable case study.
Spanning an area the size of Singapore, the approximately US$950-million scheme is the first cross-border wind project in Asia and the largest wind farm in Southeast Asia.
Built by a Chinese state firm and owned by a Thai-led consortium, it sells electricity exclusively to Vietnam's national grid via dedicated transmission lines.
Manufacturing hub Vietnam, Southeast Asia's fastest-growing economy, was already importing hydropower from Laos, its poorest neighbour.
However, "the economics are moving in favour of wind", said Tristan Bellingham, technical programme lead at nonprofit EnergyLab Asia.
"Similar to hydro 20 to 30 years ago, there's a bit of a rush on to secure concessions and development rights" for new wind projects, he told AFP.
Laos already hosts 90 hydropower plants and there are dozens more in neighbouring nations, leaving few optimal sites remaining.
'Better for development'
Bellingham said other wind farms were now riding "the coattails of Monsoon", with one Laos official pointing to 10 to 15 projects under development nationwide.
For Toukta, the 18 family members she lives with and other rice and coffee farmers residing near the turbines, Monsoon has brought new roads and improved access to fresh water and healthcare.
What it has not brought to her community, however, is power.
Residents say they still experience outages during heavy storms, as Laos's own electricity infrastructure is outdated and the state utility is heavily in debt.
Still, Toukta is glad Laos can send power abroad.
"It's better for development and can bring prosperity," she said.
For Vietnam, the project offers a reliable source of less costly energy.

There were severe blackouts in 2023 when drought cut into hydropower supply, and the government warned in September of the risk of electricity shortages from next year due to delays in planned power projects and increasing demand.
Through Monsoon, "wind power is being sold significantly cheaper to Vietnam than what Vietnam is buying wind power for locally", said Thomas Jakobsen, managing director at Indochina Energy Partners.
He estimated state utility Electricity Vietnam (EVN) was paying Monsoon around six cents per kilowatt-hour - two to four cents less than the Vietnamese rate.
Representatives of Monsoon Wind, EVN and the Asian Development Bank (ADB), the Monsoon project's financial arranger, declined to share the rate during a press tour last week.
'Something unique'
The project is also key to Vietnam reaching net-zero emissions targets by 2050, according to Ninh Xuan Hiep, an official at EVN's National Power Transmission Corporation.
At a substation in the Vietnamese capital Hanoi, he told AFP that by 2030, Laos imports would equal nearly 10 percent of Vietnam's total installed capacity - its maximum possible production.
Monsoon Wind plans to boost capacity by 1,000 megawatts and is working to ensure some of this additional power is used inside Laos, according to general manager Narut Boakajorn.
"Laos has so much natural resources" - wind, hydro and solar, Narut told AFP in an interview held below the spinning blades of a 110-metre-high turbine.
"Not many countries have all the good renewable energy in the same place. Laos has something unique," Narut said.
The government was set to reap US$180 million over the 25-year contract period, including taxes and community development and environmental protection funds, according to Narut.
He insisted nobody was forced to relocate because of the project - although public dissent is severely restricted in communist Laos.
He said 1,600 grievances logged, mainly from farmers requesting compensation for construction impacts on their crops, were resolved.
In the shadow of the turbines, 23-year-old farmer Phonekhan Sengsopha said he was proud that electricity produced in his country was being sent to its neighbour, also a communist nation.
"Because Vietnam and Laos are like brothers. They help one another," Sengsopha said.
ca2f4f22b33f45bc: As robotaxis continue trials in London, an independent research group thinks the UK needs to answer some serious questions before heading any further down the road.

To kick off, the sovereignty question, or "Will Britain become dependent on autonomous vehicle services for any key activities and what fallback options will exist if a supplier fails or withdraws?" as the Institute for Driverless Transport (IfDT) puts it.

Another question concerns employment: "To what extent does professional driving form part of the UK's employment safety net and how will this function be recreated if demand for professional drivers is significantly reduced?"

The objective for IfDT — an independent UK research and convening body focused on the consequences of autonomous vehicles — is to cast the net a bit wider than simply thinking about whether the software is sufficient to navigate London’s wiggly streets and narrow alleys.

The research draws on work with operators trying to bring AVs to London and the regulators responsible for policy. It also relied on more than 30 conversations with councils, operators, industry, unions, charities, insurers, lawyers and universities.

James Hutt, IfDT co-founder, said: "What struck us most in the interviews was how far this reaches: into jobs, public services, the built environment and national resilience. The people who know those areas best are rarely part of the conversation about AVs.

"Our next step is to bring funding and researchers together with the businesses and public bodies that need answers. If you can fund research or offer a place to test it, we would like to hear from you."
In August, Transport for London (TfL) granted private hire licences to autonomous vehicle operators provided that a human driver is present during journeys.
Wayve and Uber have since launched self-driving rides in the UK capital, with 15 electric Ford Mustangs, equipped with the Wayve AI driver, set to pick up passengers with a safety driver on board.
UK company Wayve also demoed a Nissan LEAF, running the Wayve AI Driver using NVIDIA DRIVE Hyperion with self-driving equipment built more closely into the car's design.
IfDT points out that Waymo and Baidu are also preparing services for London, while Uber, Pony.ai and Verne have begun testing in Manchester.

The research organization said UK authorities still need to answer a long list of questions in order to shape long-term infrastructure plans for local areas and prepare for AI's impact on the labor market.
The question of who needs to do this also remains unanswered, as the IfDT asks:
"Which are the key public bodies that should already be anticipating the impact of AVs on their own work and who within those organisations should lead a response?"®
2f9eda7ddfe33f5e: ABU DHABI, Nov 2 — UAE state oil company ADNOC today announced a partnership with OpenAI, saying it would be the world’s first energy firm to deploy OpenAI Frontier, an advanced artificial intelligence platform.

The oil-rich UAE is a top AI player in the Middle East and has been seeking to become a dominant force in the field globally.

“From the moment ChatGPT was born, the world has asked what energy can do for AI, and now together we will find out what AI can do for energy,” said ADNOC’s managing director and CEO Sultan Al Jaber at the ADIPEC oil conference.
Altman praised the UAE as having “consistently been the most forward-looking country in the world for AI adoption”.

Last year, intense lobbying bore fruit when the US approved the export of advanced Nvidia chips to both the UAE and Saudi Arabia.

Aramco, one of the world’s biggest companies by market capitalisation, will inject about 9.9 billion Saudi riyals (RM10.7 billion) into Humain this year along with AI, compute and digital assets. — AFP
b9f5c6ab743c9e01: Nanjing Iron & Steel Co., Ltd. (NISCO) has worked with Huawei and ecosystem partners to commercially deploy the world's first steel model powered by swarm intelligence - the YuanYe Steel Large Model (YuanYe) - across multiple scenarios at scale. This helps NISCO transition its core operations from relying on experience to being powered by data and intelligence collaboration.

As a traditional manufacturer navigating the challenges of transformation and cost efficiency, NISCO has built a robust digital and intelligent foundation by adopting industry-leading products including Ascend, Kunpeng, Huawei Cloud Stack, and Pangu models. By embedding AI into every core stage of production - ironmaking, steelmaking, rolling, and quality inspection - NISCO is forging green and high-end AI-powered super steel plants.

Unlike general-purpose monolithic models, YuanYe innovatively fuses multiple AI models with the steel industry's metallurgical mechanism models to create a dual-drive, multi-model cluster architecture. This architecture features a "right brain" for probabilistic computing and a "left brain" for precise and scientific decision-making. Powered by massive amounts of sensing data aggregated from millions of operational technology (OT) data points across 26 business domains, NISCO has achieved real-time digital twin mapping within its intelligent operations center, laying solid data and scenario foundations for YuanYe. This enables the entire steelmaking process to become not only visible, but also capable of precise control and intelligent assessment. Now 100 percent of NISCO's key equipment is connected and digitally controlled and its new product R&D cycles have been shortened by 50 percent, reducing annual costs by over CNY100m (approx. US$15m).

As the model continues to iterate, NISCO had launched 25 business agents by October 2026. These agents cover a wide range of scenarios, from visual quality inspection and process optimization to production scheduling and operations management, setting a new benchmark for digital and intelligent steel transformation.
Breakthroughs in four core scenarios: YuanYe redefines traditional operations for significant safety, efficiency, and quality gains

In the ironmaking stage, AI makes traditionally invisible blast furnaces transparent. YuanYe leverages blast furnaces' internal sensor data and metallurgical mechanism analysis to perform real-time dynamic simulations of the ironmaking process. Assisted by furnace temperature prediction and health diagnosis models, furnace operators can predict temperatures and identify issues two hours in advance, with over 90 percent accuracy. This shifts furnace operations from reactive post-event remediation to proactive pre-control, increasing prime-grade molten iron yield by over 10 percent while significantly cutting unit energy consumption.

In the rolling stage, AI drives precise predictions and codifies expert experience to enhance the operational stability of steel rolling and secure leadership in product quality. To tackle the highly dynamic and complex operating conditions during the rolling process, YuanYe's rolling-force prediction model achieves millisecond-level response, narrowing the thickness tolerance to ±0.2 mm and reducing the steel thickness deviation to 1.9 percent to reach a world-leading standard. The rolling-force hit rate has jumped from 88 percent to 98 percent, supporting a steady annual output of over 2.5 million tons of steel plates and increasing the overall yield rate by 0.5 percent. Enhanced dimensional precision and physical-chemical stability allow NISCO's products to meet demanding steel specifications across diverse applications, ranging from mega stadiums and oil pipelines to 10,000-ton cruise ships and LNG storage tanks.

In quality inspection, the synergy between robots and AI models serves as a discerning "eagle eye", doubling metallographic inspection efficiency. During metallographic inspection for finished steel, the integrated smart metallographic inspection system built on YuanYe has achieved full-process automation, covering sample grinding and polishing, image acquisition, and smart grading. Inspection accuracy has risen to over 95 percent, while per-sample inspection time has been shortened from 10 minutes down to 3–5 minutes. This 80 percent increase in overall inspection efficiency frees human operators to focus on anomaly analysis and high-level decision-making.

In the energy and environmental control stage, NISCO leverages the YuanYe architecture to develop the S-Link Intelligent Agent for Gas and Flue Gas Sulfur Control. Integrating 602 process parameters alongside multi-modal image and knowledge capabilities, the agent achieves a smart closed loop across source prediction, process optimization, and end-of-pipe compliance. By combining mechanism inversion with time-series forecasting, it issues precise sulfur-risk warnings one hour in advance, achieving a sulfur prediction accuracy of over 95 percent. Operational optimization algorithms then calculate the optimal gas blending scheme within seconds. Finally, game-theoretic models dynamically allocate emission quotas, slashing natural gas co-firing consumption by nearly 50 percent. This has reduced downtime caused by emission exceedance by over 25 percent, and delivered more than CNY600,000 (approx. US$90,000) in annual economic benefits - securing both environmental compliance and drastic cost reduction.
From automating labor to empowering people: Defining a new paradigm of inclusive AI

Li Jinyan, General Manager of the Digital and Intelligent Integrated Development Department and Director of the AI Research Institute at NISCO, said: "Digital and intelligent transformation is inherently human-centric. Its purpose is not to replace people, but to unleash human potential. Our goal is to lift employees out of the endless sea of data, empowering them to direct their creative energy toward work of higher value." To date, NISCO has deployed over 300 AI models across its plants, alongside more than 1,000 low-code agents and lightweight applications built independently by frontline employees.

As Cheng Yongfu, Senior Industrial Solution Expert at Huawei's Steel & Non-ferrous BU, noted: "The real value of industrial AI can only be realized when it expands from single-point applications to comprehensive integration with production, operations, and management, which can unlock sustained, scalable empowerment."

Looking ahead, as model deployment expands and computing demands continue to grow, NISCO will team up with Huawei and other partners to explore the construction of dedicated data centers for smart steel plants. Centered on the AI-native three-tier architecture (AI-native OS, AI-native factory, and AI-native enterprise) and powered by the YuanYe model, NISCO is accelerating high-quality steel development, aiming to provide a replicable and scalable benchmark for the digital and intelligent transformation of the global steel and manufacturing industries.
17709c5c6f87975d: BEIJING: Chinese buying of US farm goods other than soybeans is on track for a seven-year low this year despite an agreement to purchase billions of dollars in imports, a Reuters analysis of customs data showed, underscoring long-running uncertainties about the deal.

In May, the White House said Beijing agreed to buy US$17 billion of US agricultural goods annually from 2026, with this year's target prorated. Those purchases were on top of a commitment made in October last year to buy US soybeans.

While China is on track to hit its soybean target, it bought just US$7.2 billion worth of the other agricultural goods — from meat to corn — between January and September, the analysis showed. Imports are at their lowest for this period since 2019, at the height of the first trade war.

Whether Beijing is in breach of its commitment is unclear because the White House has not said whether the clock began after the announcement in May or will start once China's proposed tariff cuts have been finalised, which has yet to happen.

The sluggish buying nonetheless deepens doubts about a surge in imports this year, frustrating US farmers who are grappling with high fuel prices and driving Democrats' efforts to win heartland voters away from President Donald Trump's Republican party ahead of Tuesday's midterm elections.

"Our growers are patriots, but there's a lot of bins of grain full and certainly a desire to see grain trade," said Tim Lust, chief executive of National Sorghum Producers, an industry group. "Beans are trading, but other commodities are not."

The US Department of Agriculture referred questions about the prorating schedule to the Office of the US Trade Representative. The USTR, the White House and China's Ministry of Commerce did not respond to requests for comment.
Even if buying picks up, weak Chinese demand and stiff competition make the target difficult to meet unless Beijing orders state-owned buyers into action, analysts said.

Consider corn. At its peak in 2021, China imported US$5.6 billion worth of the crop - almost 20 million metric tons. Last month, COFCO Futures, a futures broker affiliated with the Chinese state trader, said US corn was not competitive partly because of ample domestic supply. It forecast imports of about 900,000 tons of US corn for the 2026/27 marketing year, which started in September.

US sorghum shipments to China peaked at 6.5 million metric tons worth US$2.1 billion in 2021 and now face competition from Brazil, which secured access in September 2025. Brazil has shipped 1.7 million metric tons to China so far this year, with nearly 1 million additional tons planned for shipment, said Eduardo Vanin, senior agriculture strategist at Marex.

The US exported about 3.7 million tons of sorghum to China up to the end of August, US government data shows, significantly higher than a year earlier, when trade stalled amid bilateral tensions, but sales have dried up over the past four months.
Chinese imports of US meat, once worth several billion dollars, face similar constraints. Pork and chicken are oversupplied domestically while US beef prices are high because herds have declined.

In addition, beef still faces regulatory barriers despite China renewing export licences in May for more than 400 US beef plants. About half of US fed-cattle slaughter capacity is ineligible to export to China, according to the US Meat Export Federation. Some plants were barred after Chinese authorities reported finding residues of substances not approved in China, said Joe Schuele, a spokesperson for the federation.

Such constraints mean Beijing will probably need to lean on state buyers to meet the US$17 billion target, as it is already doing with soybeans, said analysts. Whether that happens is ultimately a political question, they added.

"Much of this seems to depend on how much China will use state-owned enterprises to do purchases," said Darin Friedrichs, co-founder of Sitonia Consulting, a China-focused agricultural market intelligence firm.
"It's difficult to get to US$17 billion in non-soybeans without directed, non-market, purchases."

They were proved right I don’t think I’m being cheeky when I say that passing is the most exciting part of football.
