0747ff0d7149d6f2: Google on Friday celebrated receiving a poem from its first experimental orbital AI datacenter satellite.

The company's Suncatcher satellite, launched at the start of the month and put into low Earth orbit, has responded to a ground station prompt to "Write a haiku from the perspective of a TPU orbiting Earth, with the wonderful world spinning beneath you."

Travis Beals, senior director of Google's interdisciplinary Paradigms of Intelligence research team, said that with Suncatcher's host and TPU trays powered up and machine learning tests completed, the onboard Gemma 4 model achieved its "Hello World" milestone by sending an inference response from orbit.
"During a ground-station pass, we uplinked our first prompt to our onboard Gemma 4 open model, asking it to generate a haiku about being in space," wrote Beals in a blog post.
And as the satellite passed over Svalbard, Norway, the orbiting AI model responded over the downlink:

Those roughly 20 tokens would cost about $0.000012 if generated through the Google Cloud API, based on Gemma 4 26B's pricing of $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.60 per million output tokens, excluding input costs.
Add in a satellite weighing perhaps 500 kg, based on the mass of SpaceX's Starlink satellites, and a retail launch price of around $7,000 per kg, and you have a very expensive haiku.

According to Google's calculations, if the cost of getting a satellite into low Earth orbit can be brought down to $200/kg, the launch cost amortized over the satellite's useful life (~$810–7,500/kW/year) could be comparable to current electricity spending for terrestrial datacenters in the US (~$570–3,000/kW/year).
Google predicts that SpaceX could achieve that by 2035, more or less, and considers it strategically beneficial to prototype well in advance of that actually happening.

After the haiku, Beals said, "we tested space-themed limericks and telemetry prompts reporting the technical status of the payload systems." Next up: tests for evaluating how TPUs perform under thermal stress and radiation.
Google has already done some laboratory testing of its Trillium Cloud TPU and AMD host server to see how well they can withstand a 67 MeV proton beam.

The system's high-bandwidth memory shows the most sensitivity in terms of the total ionizing dose – it exhibits irregularities after a cumulative dose of 2 krad(Si), which is about 3× Google's minimum requirement for TID survival of 750 rad(Si).

"For typical transformer workloads, the observed SDC [silent data corruption] rate of approximately one event/17 rad, at an estimated orbital dose of 150 rad(Si)/year, translates to a very low failure probability on the order of 1 per 3 million inferences, assuming 1 inference per second," Google researchers said in a paper published earlier this month.
"While this error rate is likely acceptable for inference, the impact of SEEs on training jobs, and the efficacy of system-level mitigations, requires further study."

Indeed, the study will continue. Next year, the plan is to test a pair of interconnected satellites. Rather than lofting large satellites into orbit, Google anticipates sending a constellation of many smaller satellites that communicate with one another. ®
c4847b9309dd62fe: Their most pressing challenge is solving the long-standing water shortage in the village
Originally published on Global Voices
Participants of the project in Qyzylsay, Kazakhstan. Photo by Nazgul Aidabossynova. Used with permission.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

Women in the rural areas of Kazakhstan are among those most affected by climate change, energy deficit, and poor governance. They bear the heavy burden of water shortages, especially in the southern parts of the country, where this problem is the most acute due to dense population, economic reliance on agriculture, and water losses related to outdated irrigation infrastructure.

In the village of Qyzylsay, located in the southern Jambyl region, the water shortage has become a major issue affecting the daily lives of women. It forces them to spend multiple hours a day outside their homes to secure water for their households, gardens, and animals. Their grueling work often goes unnoticed and unpaid, and their geographical remoteness places limits on access to information and government services, exacerbating their situation.

In 2026, Nazgul Aidabossynova, a local activist, implemented a project to help local women improve their livelihoods by training them to engage with the government more effectively and efficiently, calculate the cost of their labor and products, and mobilize collective efforts to solve community problems. Global Voices conducted an email interview with Aidabossynova to learn more about her initiative. The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.

Nazgul Aidabossynova (NA): I represent a community-based initiative led by rural women in Qyzylsay. Our work focuses on supporting women who manage households, small farms, livestock, and care responsibilities, while also facing limited access to information, public services, and opportunities for civic participation.

We chose to participate in the Digital Sparks project because digital tools can make a direct, practical difference in women’s daily lives. Many women already own smartphones, but previously used them mainly for calls and WhatsApp.

The project created an opportunity to turn these devices into tools for accessing eGov services, documenting community problems, managing farm and household responsibilities, protecting digital security, and communicating with local authorities.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

NA: The key challenge is unreliable access to water in Qyzylsay. Water often disappears from the pipes during the day, particularly in summer. This affects gardens, livestock, household work, and the health and well-being of families.

The burden falls disproportionately on women. They wake early to store water, carry water for household and agricultural needs, care for the livestock, and wait for irrigation turns. Much of this work is unpaid, time-consuming, and rarely recognized.

Women also faced barriers in reporting water problems: they knew what was happening, but often lacked the knowledge, evidence, and confidence needed to raise concerns effectively with local institutions.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?
NA: The project delivered four practical training sessions for ten rural women.

The first one, titled “Your Phone is More Than WhatsApp: Smartphone as Your Household Assistant”, taught them how to use smartphone reminders, photo-diaries for farm and livestock work, eGov services, strong passwords, and basic digital-security practices.

In the second workshop, titled “Smart Water: When Your Garden Tells You It’s Thirsty”, participants learned about water rights, the responsibilities of relevant local authorities, and water-supply mapping using timestamped and GPS-tagged photographs.

The third session, titled “Numbers Don’t Lie: When You Count Everything, You Earn More”, covered how to track unpaid work and calculate the real cost of agricultural products such as milk. It also discussed the economic value of time saved through smart irrigation.

In “Honest Agreement: When Technology Helps Us Trust Each Other”, the fourth and final session, participants prepared time-to-income plans, mapped local support networks, discussed peer mentoring, and agreed to begin work toward a cooperative approach to water advocacy and shared smart-irrigation infrastructure.
GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.
NA: The project helped participating women see smartphones as tools for independence, civic participation, and practical problem-solving, rather than only communication devices.
For example, women learned that they can use eGov services to request certain official documents online, reducing the need to spend time and money traveling to administrative offices.

They also learned to create structured evidence of water problems. A photograph of a dry canal, broken pipe, or contaminated water source becomes more useful for advocacy when it includes the date, location, and a written description.

The training on unpaid labor and production costs was especially meaningful. Participants calculated the value of their time and better understood the real cost of milk production and irrigation work. The discussion showed that manual irrigation may take up to 60 hours per month.
This helped participants recognize that their time has economic value, and that shared smart-irrigation solutions could create more time for income, education, rest, and community participation.
The group also began a peer-learning process. Three participants started sharing the knowledge gained during the training with neighboring women.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?
NA: My understanding of digital democracy has become much more practical. Before this project, digital tools could be viewed mainly as a way to communicate or access information.
Through Digital Sparks, I saw how digital tools can strengthen people’s ability to exercise rights, access public services, collect evidence, engage with local authorities, and organize collectively.
I also gained a stronger understanding of the link between digital inclusion, women’s unpaid labor, climate-related water challenges, and civic space.

For rural women, digital capacity is not only about technical skills. It is about having a voice, being able to document problems, understanding their rights, and participating in decisions that affect their families and community.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

NA: The most valuable lesson is that digital literacy has the greatest impact when it is directly connected to people’s real, daily needs. In Qyzylsay, water shortages, agricultural work, unpaid care responsibilities, and access to public services were the issues that made digital tools relevant and useful.

Another important lesson is that women need not only information, but also confidence and collective support. When participants understood their rights, calculated the value of their labor, and learned how to create reliable evidence, they became more prepared to speak with local authorities and work together.
The project also showed the value of peer learning. Participants are more likely to trust and learn from women in their own community who face similar challenges.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?
NA: We will continue the peer cascade model, with trained participants sharing basic smartphone, eGov, digital safety, and evidence documentation skills with other women in Qyzylsay.

The group intends to develop a cooperative approach to the village’s water challenges. The planned cooperative would support joint advocacy, shared learning, and exploration of funding opportunities for smart-well or shared irrigation infrastructure.

In future work, we will continue combining digital skills with women’s economic empowerment, rights awareness, and local civic participation, so that rural women’s work, knowledge, and needs become more visible.

A new Science study on Manx shearwaters, seabirds that can fly hundreds of kilometers a day over the North Atlantic, shows they jet-lag themselves during their excursions. And because these birds navigate by the Sun, that jet lag leaves a measurable mark—it skews their compass.

Patrick Lewin is a behavioral and sensory ecologist at the University of Oxford and lead author of the study. “Manx shearwaters are medium-sized birds, about the same size as a pigeon,” Lewin said. “They are white underneath and black on top, but they have very long wings, and they are closely related to albatross.” Manx shearwaters nest in burrows on coastal islands around the North Atlantic. Most breed around the UK and Ireland, with about half of their population living in Wales.

<!--kg-card-end: html--> Welcome back to the Abstract—and Happy Halloween! Here are the studies this week that smashed into Earth, put aliens on ice, drank mummy wine, and hugged it out.

First, a century-old theory that comets enriched Earth with the stuff of life is upended by new models of ancient impacts. Then: the case for life in extraterrestrial sea ice, a Halloween-coded medieval concoction, and a scientific embrace.
As always, for more of my work, check out my book First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens, or subscribe to my personal newsletter The BeX Files.
Did the seeds of life come from above or below?
Anslow, Richard J. et al. “Cometary impacts are an unlikely pathway towards the origins of life on Earth.” Scientific Reports.

Carl Sagan eloquently said that we are all made of “star stuff,” but just how much of us is really comet vomit? This is a hotly debated question in science due to the popular theory that comets delivered essential ingredients for life to Earth during impacts more than four billion years ago, paving the way for the curious emergence of Earthlings.

But scientists have thrown cold primordial water on this idea in a new study that challenges “the long-held assumption that cometary impacts played an important role in the origins of life on Earth.” By running more than 100,000 advanced simulations of comet impacts, the team found that key prebiotic molecules found in comets, such as hydrogen cyanide, would be smashed to smithereens during impacts with Earth’s ancient surface in most cases.

Moreover, while Earth was pummeled by these snowballs during its youth—relatable!—this bombardment doesn’t neatly line up with the timeline of abiogenesis, the term of the origin of life. For these reasons, it’s much more likely that life assembled from earthly molecules that leaked out from our planet’s interior, according to the study.

“The most probable timing of successful cometary impact is in the early Hadean…more than 100 [million years] earlier than the estimated emergence of the last universal common ancestor (LUCA) at 4.2 [billion years ago],” said researchers led by Richard Anslow of the University of Cambridge.

“Taken together, the rapid decline in Earth’s cometary impact bombardment and the efficient destruction of fragile cometary organics indicate that the successful delivery of prebiotic feedstock molecules was an exceedingly rare event,” the team added.

The researchers didn’t rule out the possibility altogether, but concluded that any impact that had a direct influence on abiogenesis would be an edge case. That said, comets might serve as prebiotic wellsprings on other planets, such as Mars, where key molecules might have faced better odds of survival upon impact due to the red planet's smaller mass and thin atmosphere.

“Mars would have been the more favourable target for the cometary delivery of prebiotic feedstock molecules” which “strengthens the possibility that life could have emerged on Mars,” the study concluded.
In other news…
The tip of an alien iceberg
Barrier, Edouard et al “Sea Ice as an Origin of Life Location for Hycean and Ocean Worlds.” Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.

While we’re on the topic of prebiotic feedstock molecules—a household conversation, no doubt—let’s speculate about their accumulation on weird exoplanets. In a new study, scientists suggest that these molecules might build up in sea ice on a variety of extraterrestrial ocean worlds, providing a pathway to the emergence of aliens.

“Water worlds with potential deep oceans are at the forefront of currently observable exoplanetary habitability,” said researchers led by Edouard Barrier of the University of Cambridge. “Here we outline a location where nutrients could be concentrated in sufficiently high quantities to make abiogenesis possible—at the interface between the open ocean and the surface ice shelf.”

The team studied the dynamics of sea ice on Earth, and modelled how similar features might form on a range of different exoplanets, including hypothetical “Hycean” planets. These are worlds more massive than Earth, but smaller than Neptune, making them part of the “sub-Neptune” class of exoplanets.

The results revealed mechanisms that “may plausibly provide concentrated chemical feedstock for prebiotic chemistry” on many of these exoplanets, suggesting they could be a substrate for the emergence of alien life. This “rich avenue of research…has the potential to significantly advance our understanding of aquaplanet habitability, and particularly to improve the prospects of abiogenesis on sub-Neptunes,” the team concluded.

What a week for the prebiotic feedstock beat! Taken together, these studies point to multiple onramps for life on worlds like Earth, Mars, exotic sub-Neptunes, and more, upping odds that life exists elsewhere in the universe—regardless of whether we ever find it.
Drink the mummy wine
Berger, Tim, and Naimi, Amira et al.“New molecular and historical evidence on ancient Egyptian embalming.” Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

To celebrate Halloween, here’s a trick and a treat all wrapped up in one delightfully grotesque story about mummies. Roughly 700 years ago, someone had the interesting idea of grinding up parts of Egyptian mummies, mixing the residue with wine or other liquids, and prescribing it as a medicinal elixir for people to drink.

This resulting product, known as Mumia vera aegyptiaca, circulated in Arabic and European markets for centuries, but its exact composition and pharmacology remain unclear. You know what that means: It’s time to do science on the medieval mummy cocktails.

Researchers analyzed historical Mumia vera products, mummified body parts, embalming residues, bandages, and two mummified skulls. The team discovered a wide range of formulas for this medicine, including one powdered product that appears to have been derived from a mummified head.

The results demonstrate that “an apparently uninformative powdered material can be chemically linked to a specific mummified head,” said researchers co-led by Tim Berger and Amira Naimi of Marburg University. “This study shows that linking historical texts, material culture, molecular composition, and bioactivity, can open new routes for decoding historical medicines and reconstructing the material biographies of human remains and museum objects.”

So if you are really committed to the spirit of this season, break out some Mumia vera aegyptiaca to pair with your Halloween candy and witches’ brew. Bottoms up—or more accurately: mummified-heads up.
Advances in hug science
Dueren, Anna Lena et al. “Why we hug: Individual differences predict emotional touch memories.” PLOS One.
What better way to close out this chilling spooky season than with the warm embrace of science? So come on, bring it in for a hug—or, in this case, roughly 15,000 of them.

Hugging is an incredibly common form of affection among humans, and even some other animals, including Halloween favorites like vampire bats. But little is known about “how individual differences shape the remembrance of such experiences,” according to a new study.

To fill this cuddly gap, scientists analyzed survey responses from 15,049 adult participants in the United Kingdom who were recruited in a public broadcasting campaign that included the BBC. The volunteers reported that their most memorable hugs were “for comfort, support, and understanding” and there was a noticeable gender split, as men were more likely to remember hugs that were “arousing” than women.

“Regarding hugs, men have shown different lateralisation and arm crossing patterns when hugging other men compared to women,” said researchers led by Anna Lena Dueren of the University of Bristol. “Furthermore, women were found to experience a stress buffering effect of hugs that was absent in men.”

And for anyone who considers themselves not a “hugger,” you are not alone. Plenty of participants expressed that they found hugs difficult or unpleasant. So whether you love bear hugs or cannot bear hugs, this study has something for you.
Thanks for reading! See you next week.

In the grand corporate hierarchy of Perikatan Nasional (PN), these two are the interns who don't get invited to the lunch table, yet somehow believe they are next in line for the CEO's position.
To say that MIPP and Gerakan bring no clout to PN is a profound insult to the word clout.

They are the political equivalents of plastic indoor plants – supposed to add a splash of "multiracial colour" to a very green room – except the plants have withered, the owners keep forgetting to water them and the landlords are currently trying to evict the entire building.

The political future of these minority component parties in PN has become one of the most ironic talking points in modern Malaysian politics. Critics, political analysts and observers frequently debate their position, although "debate" might be too active a word. It is more akin to watching two passengers argue over who gets the window seat on a bus that has already driven off a cliff.
MIPP: from bold newcomers to zero-vote club

Let’s start with MIPP, the bold newcomers whose political future in PN is currently the hottest topic among three guys at a coffee shop. MIPP entered the scene with the explosive energy of a damp firecracker. At its grand electoral debut in Johor, it contested five seats and managed a spectacular, flawless clean sweep of losing their deposits in all five.

MIPP’s standing within a major coalition remains precarious precisely because it has demonstrated a rare, mathematically impressive lack of an independent base. Yet, MIPP’s confidence remains unshaken by minor details like numerical reality.

Recently, the party announced it would completely sit out the Nov 14 Melaka state election after seat distribution talks with the PN leadership broke down. The official reason? President P Punithan bravely declared that the party refuses to compromise its dignity or accept "irrelevant" seats just to field candidates.

Translation: PN offered it a constituency consisting entirely of three palm trees and a stray cat, and MIPP chose "dignity" over another hefty loss of deposit. This breakdown signals deep friction over how minority component parties are treated by the dominant Malay-Muslim parties in PN.

The ideological mismatch here is staggering. MIPP is trying to pitch a minority-interest narrative in a coalition heavily dominated by PAS’s religious and conservative Malay narratives. It’s like trying to sell vegan burgers at a Texas steakhouse and acting surprised when the chef throws a spatula at you. It is incredibly difficult for a minority-interest party like MIPP to gain genuine traction among non-Muslim voters while standing next to politicians who view secularism as a design flaw.

Ultimately, MIPP’s decision to bypass Melaka highlights the ongoing, tragicomic struggle for minor non-Malay component parties to find an equal voice in a house that doesn't even know they are in the room.
Gerakan: master of the secular submissive

Then we have Gerakan, the veteran master of political irrelevance. The argument that Gerakan has no future in PN is a view increasingly shared by political analysts, critics, and even internal party factions who have grown tired of buying antacids in bulk.

Political observers highlight several compounding crises that threaten Gerakan's long-term viability in the coalition. First and foremost is its utter inability to attract non-Malay voters. Gerakan originally joined PN to serve as its non-Malay face, a bridge to the cynical urban electorate. Instead, it has become a cautionary tale, repeatedly failing to win over non-Malay voters from Pakatan Harapan, particularly DAP.

This has trapped it in the "shadow dilemma" – a polite academic term for operating entirely in the shadow of its larger partners, PAS and Bersatu. Because Gerakan brings minimal electoral data or seat victories to the table, its leverage in PN is roughly equivalent to a discount voucher that expired during the Asian financial crisis.

The ideological friction between Gerakan’s secular principles and PAS’s Islamic stance peaked hilariously during the school brewery donation saga. When PAS attacked the fund-raising, Gerakan deputy president Oh Tong Keong threatened to exit the coalition over "extreme" demands. PAS responded with a collective yawn, and Gerakan naturally stayed – proving that its red lines are drawn in invisible ink.

Naturally, this masterclass in political submission has triggered an internal rebellion. High-profile departures – such as the resignation of 31-year veteran and party treasurer Hng Chee Wey – underscore a growing internal revolt against sacrificing core principles for political expediency. These exits expose deep cracks under president Dominic Lau, as grassroots members grow tired of watching their leadership nod politely while being publicly sidelined.
PN's burning house

To make matters funnier, the house that Gerakan and MIPP are clinging to is literally on fire. The broader PN coalition is undergoing severe structural shocks, with PAS announcing the end of its political cooperation with Bersatu, triggering a chaotic power struggle and the sudden resignation of top PN leadership.

The Registrar of Societies even ordered the coalition's deregistration, and while a temporary court reprieve saved it from legal oblivion, persistent internal rifts cloud the bloc's political future. It is a civil war where the big boys are throwing live grenades, and Gerakan and MIPP are caught in the crossfire armed with plastic cutlery.

What is Gerakan’s next move? Political analysts suggest that leaving the coalition may be a risk worth taking compared to staying and enduring further humiliation. Yet, Lau has indicated that Gerakan is trying to pivot by backing a broader PN-Barisan Nasional electoral tie-up for future stability.

Yes, you read that correctly. While PN is on the verge of structural collapse and PAS is actively exploring independent realignments with Umno, Gerakan is trying to build a bridge to a party that doesn't know it exists, using a blueprint that is already out of date.
Conclusion

Gerakan risks being completely left behind unless it thoroughly recalibrates its political alignment. But that would require a sense of direction, and right now, both Gerakan and MIPP seem perfectly content to sit in the back seat of a driverless car heading straight towards a cliff, arguing over who gets to hold the auxiliary cable.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

d84808b6057ac5b3: The Hubble Space Telescope still shines in the eyes of astronomers after 36 years in orbit, but it is not as nimble as it once was. Left alone, the observatory will plunge back into the atmosphere in the early-to-mid-2030s, closing the book on one of the most famous scientific instruments of the century.

NASA last raised the orbit of Hubble in 2002, when the Space Shuttle Columbia visited the observatory for a servicing mission. The final shuttle servicing flight in 2009 did not reboost the telescope's orbit, and with the retirement of the shuttle fleet two years later, Hubble has steadily lost altitude with no way to stave off eventual destruction.

The space agency released a Request For Information (RFI) on Thursday asking commercial companies for ideas on how to reboost, service, or conduct a controlled disposal of Hubble. Responses are due November 30. Specifically, NASA is looking for information about companies' current and near-term capabilities for capturing Hubble and boosting it to an altitude of at least 373 miles (600 km), enhancing the telescope's performance, or guiding Hubble to a controlled reentry.
68f2fe60ad7543ba: Washington’s decision to order non-emergency American diplomatic personnel and their families to leave Saudi Arabia is more than a precautionary measure. It signals a dangerous deterioration in the security environment of West Asia.
For Malaysia, the implications are immediate, strategic and potentially costly.

Saudi Arabia is not merely another oil-producing country. It is a pivotal power in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), the custodian of Islam’s two holiest cities and an indispensable pillar of global energy security.
When Washington begins withdrawing diplomatic personnel from Riyadh, Kuala Lumpur must pay attention.
The decision follows increasingly audacious attacks by Yemen’s Houthis against Saudi airports, energy installations and civilian infrastructure.
The recent targeting of Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport and Saudi Aramco’s Shaybah oilfield demonstrates how asymmetric warfare can undermine even a militarily sophisticated state.

Saudi Arabia possesses advanced Western weapons systems, extensive financial resources and powerful international partnerships. Yet relatively inexpensive drones and missiles continue to penetrate or challenge its defensive arrangements.
This carries five important lessons for Malaysia.
First, energy security cannot be separated from national security.
Although Malaysia produces petroleum and natural gas, its economy remains vulnerable to disruptions in global energy markets.
Higher transportation costs, expensive imported industrial inputs and renewed inflationary pressures could weaken domestic purchasing power.
Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s unity government has worked to preserve economic stability amid considerable international uncertainty.
A prolonged crisis in Saudi Arabia could undermine these efforts, especially if disruptions spread across the Persian Gulf and Red Sea.
Second, maritime security must be understood as an interconnected strategic system.
The Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb are indispensable arteries of international commerce.
If both become increasingly dangerous, shipping companies will face higher insurance premiums, longer journeys and mounting operational costs.
Malaysia, strategically positioned along the Strait of Malacca, cannot remain insulated from these developments.
Disruptions in West Asia can eventually affect Malaysian ports, manufacturers, exporters and consumers.
Third, the Houthis have demonstrated the growing effectiveness of asymmetric warfare.
Military superiority no longer guarantees comprehensive security.
Drones, missiles, cyberattacks and sabotage can inflict enormous economic damage without requiring conventional military parity.
Malaysia and Asean must therefore strengthen the protection of airports, ports, energy installations and communications networks.
The strategic lesson is straightforward: resilience matters as much as deterrence.
Fourth, Saudi instability carries serious implications for Malaysian pilgrims.
Mecca and Madinah remain central to the religious lives of Malaysian Muslims.
Any deterioration in aviation security or airport operations could complicate haj and umrah arrangements.
Wisma Putra, Tabung Haji and Malaysia’s diplomatic missions must strengthen contingency planning, particularly regarding evacuation procedures, flight disruptions and consular assistance.
The safety of Malaysian citizens must remain paramount.
Fifth, the American decision exposes the limitations of excessive dependence on external security guarantees.

The United States remains militarily formidable. Nevertheless, its decision to reduce diplomatic exposure demonstrates that even Washington cannot eliminate every security threat confronting its allies.
Malaysia must therefore deepen its strategic relationships with Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Pakistan, China and other influential powers.

256141e19a66337a: Dalam dunia moden, masyarakat sering merasakan mereka bebas membentuk pendapat sendiri. Namun, seperti dihujahkan oleh Edward S Herman dan Noam Chomsky dalam karya penting Manufacturing Consent (1988), pendapat umum sebenarnya dibentuk melalui hubungan rapat antara elit politik, elit korporat dan pemilik media.

Herman & Chomsky menunjukkan media arus perdana tidak benar-benar bebas; sebaliknya, ia mengikuti struktur kepentingan pemilik, pengiklan, kerajaan, dan rangkaian ekonomi-politik yang mengawal aliran maklumat. Apabila masyarakat bersandar kepada elit kerajaan, agensi dan tokoh berpengaruh, keputusan menjadi lebih mudah ‘diurus’ kerana rakyat bergantung kepada sumber yang sudah dianggap sah dan berautoriti.
Jika pada era lama pemilik media ialah syarikat akhbar, konglomerat penyiaran dan stesen televisyen nasional, hari ini ‘pemilik media’ telah berubah wajah menjadi pemilik platform digital.

Herman & Chomsky menekankan sesiapa yang menguasai infrastruktur penyampaian maklumat akan menguasai ruang fikir masyarakat. Dalam konteks abad ke-21, kuasa itu bukan lagi dimonopoli oleh kerajaan atau syarikat media tradisional, tetapi oleh gergasi digital seperti Meta (Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp), Google (YouTube), X (Twitter), TikTok, dan aplikasi mesej peribadi seperti Telegram.
Mereka bukan sahaja menyebar kandungan, tetapi mengawal algoritma iaitu sistem yang menentukan apa yang rakyat lihat, baca dan bincangkan setiap hari.

Inilah versi baharu manufacturing consent dalam era digital: persetujuan tidak lagi dibentuk melalui editorial akhbar, tetapi melalui newsfeed, trending list dan algoritma cadangan yang direka untuk memaksimumkan masa tontonan.

Sebagai contoh, Facebook boleh mengangkat isu tertentu sehingga kelihatan seperti ‘suara rakyat’, walaupun ia sebenarnya digerakkan oleh kumpulan kecil belakang tabir yang mengeksploitasi sistem perkongsian. Begitu juga YouTube, yang boleh mempercepatkan penyebaran ideologi tertentu melalui cadangan video yang memerangkap pengguna dalam echo chamber.

Walaupun kerajaan masih mempunyai kuasa kawalan, yang menurut saya terhad kepada kandungan. Mereka kini bergantung pula kepada platform digital untuk menjangkau rakyat, menjadikan pemilik platform sebagai rakan strategik atau ancaman senyap dalam pembentukan pendapat umum.

Hubungan ini dapat dilihat dalam pilihan raya moden. Di Amerika Syarikat, kempen Donald Trump 2016 bergantung kepada Facebook Ads yang menyasarkan kelompok tertentu dengan mesej emosi, membuktikan bahawa pemilik data kini lebih berpengaruh daripada pemilik media tradisional.

Di Malaysia, penyebaran naratif politik di TikTok menjelang PRU15 menunjukkan bagaimana anak muda membina pandangan politik bukan daripada ucapan rasmi, tetapi daripada video pendek yang dikuasai algoritma. Ini menunjukkan kuasa mengurus masyarakat kini bergantung kepada gabungan kerajaan + elit korporat + pemilik platform digital, bukannya kerajaan sahaja.
Secara keseluruhan, apabila masyarakat terlalu bersandar kepada elit berkuasa baik kerajaan, media tradisional atau pemilik digital maka proses membuat keputusan menjadi lebih mudah dimanipulasi.

Masyarakat percaya kerana mereka menganggap sumber-sumber ini ‘natural’ dan neutral, sedangkan Herman & Chomsky membuktikan setiap sistem media sebenarnya mempunyai struktur kepentingan yang tersusun. Dalam era digital hari ini, propaganda menjadi lebih halus kerana ia bukan lagi disampaikan oleh editor manusia, tetapi oleh algoritma yang memutuskan apa yang wajar ditonton.
Pemahaman ini penting supaya masyarakat sedar bahawa ‘kemudahan membuat keputusan’ selalunya datang dengan harga: penyerahan sebahagian kebebasan berfikir kepada elit yang mengawal aliran maklumat.
Bagaimana ekosistem ini mempengaruhi fikiran dan tindakan masyarakat

Ekosistem yang dibina oleh kerajaan, pemilik media tradisional dan pemilik platform digital hari ini membentuk satu sistem pengaruh yang hampir total. Masyarakat yang bergantung pada sumber-sumber rasmi dan platform digital untuk memahami dunia akan mengikuti aliran maklumat yang telah ‘ditapis’ sebelum sampai kepada mereka.

Dalam kerangka Herman & Chomsky, ini ialah proses penyusunan agenda di mana apa yang dianggap penting oleh rakyat sebenarnya ditentukan oleh struktur kuasa di belakang media. Platform digital menambah satu lapisan baharu: maklumat bukan sahaja disaring oleh pemilik media, tetapi dipilih oleh algoritma yang mengutamakan interaksi popular dan bukan atas agenda kepentingan negara.
Akibatnya, isu yang paling banyak mendapat perhatian bukanlah isu yang paling penting, tetapi isu yang paling menguntungkan dari segi trafik dan emosi.

Ekosistem ini mempengaruhi cara masyarakat berfikir dengan mencipta ilusi bahawa maklumat datang secara organik, sedangkan ia sebenarnya hasil kawalan sistemik. Contohnya, seseorang mungkin percaya sesuatu isu ‘hangat dibincangkan rakyat’ kerana ia tular di TikTok, walhal algoritma hanya menolak kandungan serupa berulang kali sehingga mencipta kesan majoriti palsu.

Ini disebut Herman & Chomsky sebagai manufactured perception, persepsi yang dibuat, bukan dilahirkan secara semula jadi. Begitu juga dalam konteks politik: apabila naratif tertentu diulang melalui media arus perdana dan disokong oleh kemunculan semula video pendek di laman sosial, masyarakat mula melihat naratif itu sebagai ‘kebenaran kolektif’. Mereka percaya bukan kerana bukti, tetapi kerana kekerapan dan kebiasaan.

Ekosistem ini juga mempengaruhi emosi kolektif. Kerajaan mungkin menetapkan nada optimistik seperti ‘ekonomi stabil’, media tradisional mengulanginya melalui laporan rasmi, dan platform digital memanjangkan emosi itu melalui konten yang dipromosikan oleh algoritma seperti infografik, meme, video pendek, atau klip ucapan pemimpin. Pada masa sama, algoritma meminggirkan suara yang dianggap tidak menguntungkan atau bertentangan dengan arus popular.

Apabila masyarakat hanya dibenarkan melihat satu sisi, mereka percaya itulah keseluruhan cerita. Keadaan ini menjadikan propaganda lebih efisien kerana ia tidak memaksa masyarakat menerima sesuatu naratif, tetapi membentuk persekitaran maklumat yang membuatkan naratif itu kelihatan seperti pilihan paling logik.

Selain fikiran dan emosi, ekosistem digital juga mempengaruhi tingkah laku. Di Malaysia, kita dapat lihat bagaimana pola pengundian anak muda berubah secara drastik apabila mereka terdedah kepada video politik TikTok dan bukan kerana hujah rasional, tetapi kerana naratif visual yang dikuatkan oleh algoritma.

Di peringkat global, kempen Trump 2016 dan Brexit menunjukkan bagaimana data pengguna digunakan untuk menyasarkan mesej individu mengikut ketakutan, minat dan kelemahan masing-masing. Apabila algoritma mengetahui apa yang mencetuskan kemarahan, ketakutan atau harapan seseorang, ia boleh mempengaruhi tindakannya tanpa individu itu sedar mereka sedang dipengaruhi.

Akhirnya, ekosistem ini menjadikan masyarakat lebih mudah diurus. Herman & Chomsky menyebut media moden sebagai ‘sistem propaganda’ yang tidak kelihatan seperti propaganda kerana ia berfungsi dalam suasana kebebasan. Dalam era digital, sistem ini menjadi lebih kuat: masyarakat percaya mereka bebas memilih, tetapi pilihan mereka telah dibentuk oleh infrastruktur maklumat yang dikuasai oleh kerajaan, pemilik media, dan pemilik platform digital global.

Kesimpulannya, apabila aliran maklumat dikawal oleh jaringan elit ini, masyarakat bukan sahaja terpengaruh, malah diarahkan tanpa sedar untuk berfikir, merasa dan bertindak mengikut kepentingan pihak yang menguasai sistem.

0a7c6a7f6988f770: In calling on Malaysians to reject the politics of hatred based on race and religion on Oct 25, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said some people were attempting to “distort history by claiming that this country can only be saved through the victory of a single race”.
“If our ancestors succeeded in building the Melaka Malay Sultanate into a great empire, we can do the same through peace, unity among all quarters, and sound development strategies,” he said.
I couldn’t agree more. And history proves him right.

In recent decades the tension over whose country this is has taken on a life of its own, with those arguing for ketuanan Melayu or calling non-Malays pendatang gaining in strength. So much so that it has put many non-Malay citizens on the defensive.
It is as if Malay political strength and cosmopolitan composition are rivals for the same space.
They need not be, as Melaka’s history shows.

For roughly a century, the most important port in the Malay world was simultaneously the most thoroughly Malay polity in the region and one of the most diverse places on earth. Both facts were true at once. Neither diluted the other.

The Sultanate of Melaka was unambiguously Malay and Islamic. The court spoke Malay, kept Malay adat, drew its ceremonial rituals from Hindu-derived concepts filtered through centuries of courtly tradition, and derived legitimacy from control of the Strait of Melaka.

And yet the city’s population was staggering in its variety. Tomé Pires, writing within living memory of the sultanate’s fall, described traders from around the world who spoke somewhere around eighty-four languages in the port.

Gujarati Muslim traders and Tamil merchants from India traded here; Hokkien and Cantonese-speaking Chinese merchants ran warehouses; and Javanese, Siamese, Cham, Ryukyuan, Arab, Persian and Filipino traders also maintained quarters here.
There were resident communities with temples, mosques, shrines and headmen of their own.
This diversity was not incidental to Melakan power. It was Melakan power. The sultanate’s wealth came from being the place where the South China Sea met the Indian Ocean.

And that could only work if an Indian Muslim or Tamil merchant, a junk owner from Quanzhou and a pepper shipper from Java could all find or agree on the same weights, the same credit practices and the same language of contract.
Cosmopolitanism was not a value Melaka upheld. It was the economic base.

Melaka’s answer to governing this population was administrative rather than ideological. The state appointed a Shahbandar — the chief port master — to oversee all traders and revenue. The Shahbandar managed distinct trading quarters, registered merchants, collected taxes, settled internal disputes, and liaised with the government.

In practice this gave each community customary autonomy over its own affairs (marriage, inheritance, temple and mosque management), while the Bendahara handled internal Malay affairs. All commercial, criminal and appellate jurisdiction, however, rested with the sultanate.

The arrangement deserves attention precisely because it looks superficially like what colonial administrators later built and what Malaysian coalition politics later imitated — separate channels for separate communities. But the difference is structural, and it matters for how we think about unity today.

Under colonial rule, communal separation was the point. British policy froze categories through census classification, partitioned schooling by language, segregated employment by race, and treated intermixture as a management problem. Communities coexisted economically while remaining socially sealed, held together from above by an administration that belonged to none of them.

Melaka’s system separated for the purpose of incorporation. The Shahbandar registered you so you could trade, marry, inherit and litigate inside Melaka’s order. The Undang-Undang Melaka and the maritime code recognised community customs while reserving commercial, criminal and appellate jurisdiction to the state.
Malay was the lingua franca of the market and the court, and participation in that common life was the price and the reward of belonging.

Movement across lines was expected and routine. Chinese traders married locally and produced Baba-Nyonya culture. Indian Muslims settled into quarters that became permanent neighbourhoods, as did the Tamil merchants. And Arab Syed families entered Malay genealogies.
Conversion to Islam opened the fullest paths into the elite, and did so without erasing the commercial networks converts had brought with them.

Unity here meant a shared sovereign frame, a shared commercial language and a shared legal horizon — not shared blood, shared schooling or shared culture. Diversity was not accommodated at the margin. It was administered at the centre.

Against this record, the claim that non-Malay presence in the peninsula is a colonial residue awaiting digestion does not survive contact with the evidence. The ancestors of today’s Malaysian Chinese and Malaysian Indian communities were not confined to nineteenth-century steamships.

Long before Penang, Singapore and Melaka passed to Britain, there were resident Chinese, Tamil, Indian Muslim, Gujarati and Arab populations under Malay sovereignty here. They were registered, taxed, and adjudicated; and they even intermarried.
They were not guests awaiting permanent permission and the Shahbandar was not a manager of ethnicities.
That historical fact dismantles the foundational premise of ethnic exclusivism — that Malayness and non-Malay residence are, in principle, incompatible claims on the same land.
Five hundred years of Malay statecraft say otherwise, in Jawi script, in the records of a Malay court.

Honesty, however, requires stating the limits. Melaka was a transit entrepôt with a small population, perhaps tens of thousands, many of them sojourners, governed as subjects rather than citizens, and ranked by status and religion in ways no modern Malaysian would want restored.

So Melaka is not a blueprint. Nobody should propose reviving the Shahbandar offices. But it is something more useful than a blueprint: it is a refutation. It removes the alibi. If exclusion is defended on the grounds that Malay civilisation has always been exclusive, the fifteenth-century record contradicts the defence.
If assimilation is defended on the grounds that diversity requires uniformity to be governable, the fifteenth-century record contradicts that too.

What survives the comparison is a definition. Melaka shows that this region produced a working model of unity in diversity in which unity meant shared sovereignty, shared law and shared language, while diversity meant real autonomy of custom, belief and association.
The unity did not require the diversity to dissolve. The diversity did not threaten the unity.
This is an opportune time to remember this historical fact, as voters prepare to go to the polls in Melaka next month.

Some politicians will surely tell voters that they must choose between affirming Malay identity and embracing the country’s plural character; that they must unite to save their race or religion. Others may say voters need to come together to defend their rights.

The city’s own history says the choice being thrown at them was invented by colonial administrators who preferred divided subjects to a mixed populace. Before the colonialists came, the most successful Malay state in history proved the two were never opposites.

It would be asking a great deal of a banner-waving election season to engage with that. But the evidence sits there, in plain sight, in the very state being fought over — and it is worth saying out loud, in Melaka, before the voting: this country’s diversity is not a problem Malay civilisation inherited from outsiders. It is an achievement Malay civilisation once mastered.

be8bb047a425a21d: A significant number of patients in the US lie to their doctors to get antibiotics they likely don't need, according to two new studies. While that may not be a startling revelation, the studies drill down on the phenomenon, finding that the lies patients tell are generally bad ones—and yet, they work almost all the time.

In the two linked studies published Friday in JAMA Network Open, a team of researchers led by Alistair Thorpe at the University of Utah analyzed online survey data from over 1,000 adults. They found that over a quarter of people reported having lied to a clinician at least once to get an antibiotic prescription for themselves or a child in their care. Patients lied by either exaggerating symptoms, making up symptoms, or—most often—both.

But interestingly, the lies people told to get antibiotics involved making up or exaggerating symptoms of infections that wouldn't be treated with antibiotics. For example, the most common falsehoods were symptoms associated with colds, such as fever, cough, and sore throat. That's despite the fact that colds are caused by viruses, not bacteria—which antibiotics treat.

bed1fed0b77f7211: Plausible misinformation is the most dangerous kind
Originally published on Global Voices

Hyrije Mehmeti presenting research report “The Chatbot Version of Truth” at Hibrid.info international expert conference held on 16 December 2025 in Prishtina, Kosovo. Photo by Global Voices, CC BY 3.0.
By Hyrie Mehmeti

This article by Hyrije Mehmeti combines and adapts material from the author's earlier work, including an article published in German by the European Journalism Observatory. It draws on the 2025 ADS/Hibrid.info research report The Chatbot Version of Truth. It is also part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

For many people today, asking a chatbot a question feels as natural as opening a search engine once did. “Is Kosovo an independent state?” “What happened in Srebrenica?” “Is Crimea part of Ukraine or Russia?” — these are no longer questions reserved for history books, court rulings, or newsrooms. They are typed into chat windows that respond in seconds, in fluent, confident language, often with the tone of an all-knowing guide.
That confidence is exactly what makes large language model (LLM) chatbots so attractive, and so risky at the same time.

Alongside social media platforms and online news outlets, AI chatbots are increasingly functioning as reference tools, offering summaries of complex political and historical subjects, often without users verifying the information they receive.

This shift matters particularly in regions such as the Western Balkans, where history, statehood and war legacies remain politically contested. The way these issues are explained and framed is therefore not only a question of factual accuracy, but also of narrative influence.
When “plausible” beats “true”

LLMs are designed to generate text that sounds convincing. They produce fluent and coherent responses, but these qualities do not guarantee verified truth. If something reads clearly and authoritatively, it feels reliable.
But in geopolitics, plausibility is not enough.

Unlike traditional information sources, chatbots do not simply retrieve facts. They also interpret, prioritise and frame information in ways shaped by their training data and the technological environments in which they operate.
This was one of the central questions guiding our research.
What our research revealed

In 2025, I led a research team at Action for Democratic Society/Hibrid.info that examined how three widely used AI chatbots responded to sensitive political and historical questions: ChatGPT (launched in the United States), DeepSeek Chat (launched in China), and Alice (launched in Russia).

The study, titled “The Chatbot Version of Truth,” analysed what kind of “truth” these systems produce when people use them as shortcut information sources for specific topics concerning Kosovo, critical issues related to the Western Balkans (WB) and global comparative topics.

The team developed 100 standardised prompts covering issues such as the independence of Kosovo, the war legacy, international recognition, EU integration of West Balkan countries, memory politics, regional disputes, and global comparative questions like Crimea, Cyprus, or other contested territories.

A separate account was created in each chatbot for every thematic area, and each prompt was entered separately into a new chat, to avoid previous answers influencing the next one. The responses were then checked for factual accuracy and compared for semantic similarity. Semi-structured interviews with experts were also conducted, which were used to verify and interpret the experimental findings.

Initially, the results suggested a positive picture: most answers were broadly accurate, with ChatGPT and DeepSeek Chat demonstrating the highest and most consistent accuracy. However, both systems still produced inaccuracies, elements of hallucination, and interpretive variations. Alice showed a weaker performance, with the highest number of refusals to answer, thematic evasions, and ideological deviations, particularly on politically sensitive topics.
Performance of the chatbots in the 100 tested prompts by accuracy categories. Graph by hibrid.info, used with permission.
But accuracy alone does not tell the full story.
One of the clearest findings was that none of the tested systems could be considered a fully neutral or consistently reliable reference point for geopolitical issues.

The semantic similarity analysis showed that ChatGPT and DeepSeek Chat often produced very similar formulations, especially on Kosovo and regional topics, suggesting a shared way of structuring narratives. Alice, by contrast, deviated more strongly in both wording and emphasis.
From a user's perspective, this leads to a simple but troubling conclusion: the same question can produce different versions of political reality depending on which chatbot is used.
When location changes the answer

In a second part of the study, the team tested whether the user’s location influences the responses. The same three sensitive questions were asked from six Western Balkan countries: Kosovo, Albania, North Macedonia, Montenegro, Serbia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina.
The findings showed that geography can matter.

ChatGPT and DeepSeek Chat remained relatively stable in wording and meaning, although some variations appeared on particularly contested topics. Alice, however, behaved differently: in some countries it answered in Russian, in others it refused to answer entirely, and in some cases it mixed languages within a single response, despite all prompts being submitted in English.
The analysis also identified differences in semantic similarity between responses from different countries, including some with contrasting historical and political perspectives.
This may sound like a technical detail, but the implications are practical. Similar questions asked from different locations may produce answers that differ in language, emphasis or completeness.
Much like digital maps can look different depending on which country they are opened from, AI-generated explanations of political reality can also shift with geography.
For users, this means that the information they receive may depend not only on what they ask, but also on which system they use and where they access it.
A new layer in the information environment

Authoritarian influence over information is often associated with censorship, propaganda and restrictions on independent journalism. AI chatbots introduce another dimension to how political narratives are encountered and reproduced.
These systems do not simply provide information. Through differences in accuracy, framing and contextual adaptation, they can influence how political and historical realities are presented to users.

When AI systems are trained on unbalanced data, filtered through political constraints or designed to produce fluent responses without guaranteeing factual accuracy, they risk becoming quiet amplifiers of distorted realities – not necessarily because they are designed to promote a particular narrative, but because of how information is selected, processed and presented.
This is particularly relevant in information environments where foreign manipulation, propaganda and historical revisionism are already present.
The research does not establish direct coordination between chatbot developers and political actors. Nor does it suggest that every inaccurate response reflects deliberate manipulation.

Rather, it highlights a broader concern: systems developed and controlled by powerful technology companies increasingly mediate access to political knowledge, while the processes shaping their answers remain difficult for ordinary users to examine.

The way these systems present information is therefore not merely a technical issue. It also raises questions about transparency, accountability and the influence of technology platforms over public understanding.
Beyond accuracy: The question of accountability
The findings of “The Chatbot Version of Truth” do not suggest that AI chatbots are useless or inherently misleading. Most of the responses examined were broadly accurate.
But being accurate most of the time does not make a system consistently reliable, particularly when questions concern sensitive political or historical events.

Developers and platform providers should increase transparency about data sources, model development and the mechanisms used to verify responses. Independent, region-specific testing is also necessary to identify systematic biases, inaccuracies and gaps in information.

For journalists, researchers and users, verification remains essential. Comparing chatbot outputs with multiple trusted sources, recognising omissions and questioning how information is framed are increasingly important parts of media and AI literacy.

Nearly a year after the publication of our research, its central message remains relevant: AI chatbots are becoming everyday intermediaries in how people seek and consume information, but they are not neutral mirrors of reality.
The challenge is not simply whether these systems can provide quick answers. It is whether those answers are accurate, sufficiently contextualised and open to scrutiny.

Because, in the end, the most dangerous kind of misinformation is not necessarily the one that looks obviously false, but the one that sounds smooth, reasonable and just plausible enough to pass as “the answer.”

Hyrije Mehmeti is a media and communications professional and a PhD candidate in Media and Communication at South East European University. She also teaches in the Department of Journalism at the University of Prishtina. She led the ADS/Hibrid.info research “The Chatbot Version of Truth” while serving as Head of Editorial and Programme Coordination at the organisation.

226d6d5c25cb9ac1: People are peppering artificial intelligence chatbots everyday with questions, but when it comes to politics and the looming 2026 U.S. midterm elections, what role are AI platforms playing? Could an AI chatbot sway a voter to switch parties or re-examine their political beliefs?  MIT researchers have built a new dashboard, called the LLM Election Observatory, to examine, in real-time, how popular AI chatbots are responding to questions about the 2026 midterm elections. The team behind the dashboard — led by Professor Adam Berinsky, Assistant Professor Chara Podimata, and Professor Charles Stewart III — has extensive experience studying voting and election administration, AI and misinformation, and how AI systems are impacting human decision making. In an effort to better understand how AI is shaping the election, they designed the dashboard to simulate how individuals across the country communicate with chatbots.  The team tracks how different AI systems respond to the same fixed set of questions on a range of topics, including election certification, hot-button issues, result predictions, news coverage, and more. Every few days, the LLM Election Observatory team runs the questions through the chatbots again, monitoring how their responses vary as the election gets closer depending on user location, political party affiliation, identity and other factors. The goal of this work is not to merely understand how AI systems spread information, but also better comprehend how they are shaping political discourse and voter understanding of political issues across the country.  MIT News chatted with Podimata, the Class of 1942 Career Development Professor, an assistant professor of operations research and statistics in the MIT Sloan School of Management, and a member of the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems; and Berinsky, the Mitsui Professor and a professor in the Department of Political Science, about their work with the LLM Election Observatory, how AI could impact the midterms, and what voters should keep in mind when they interact with chatbots. Q: What was the inspiration for this project and what are you hoping to learn through the LLM Election Observatory? Podimata: People are increasingly using AI chatbots to find and make sense of political and election-related information. That makes it important to understand what information these systems actually provide, not just at one moment in time but throughout an election cycle. This is particularly challenging because the models themselves are continually getting updates, the political information inputs available to them are themselves changing, and their answers can depend on how a user asks a question or what information the user provides about themselves. One basic problem is that we currently do not have a good historical record of this information environment. If an AI system gives a particular answer about an election today and gives a different answer several weeks later, it can be very difficult to reconstruct after the fact what voters would have seen at each point in time. One important goal of our project is simply to systematically document that environment as it develops and make the resulting data available to other researchers and to the public. Ultimately, factual accuracy is only the first frontier. We absolutely need to understand whether chatbots provide accurate political information, but we also need to pay just as much attention to the subtler ways in which they may shape people’s understanding of political issues. Differences in framing, emphasis, uncertainty, and cited sources can matter enormously, even in the absence of outright misinformation.   Q: Professor Podimata, you studied how LLMs shaped political discourse and information during the 2024 election. What were the main takeaways of that research and how did those findings inform this new project? Podimata: The LLM Election Observatory builds on my previous work during the 2024 presidential election, which found evidence of meaningful variation in AI models’ responses over time and across prompt framings, as well as differences in how models characterized candidates and implicitly anticipated the election outcome.  The 2026 midterms give us an opportunity to expand that work substantially. Midterm elections are particularly interesting because there are many state and local contests unfolding simultaneously, alongside broader national political narratives. Our new audit survey therefore asks both contest-specific questions about the U.S. House and Senate candidates, but also broader questions about voting information and other aspects of the election information environment. Q: Why do you think it’s so important to be studying how chatbots are responding to political queries across different groups of users? Podimata: We all build our own “microcosms” through our interactions with chatbots. And yet, we lack systematic ways of understanding how these individualized information environments are shaped by who we are or how they evolve over time as we and the information environment changes.  For example, people may not realize that what their favorite chatbot tells them about a political issue may be quite different from what their friend’s favorite chatbot tells them about the exact same issue. And importantly, these differences matter even when the information being provided is factually correct. Chatbots may frame the same facts differently, emphasize different aspects of an issue, express different levels of uncertainty, or draw on entirely different sources, even when responding to identical queries between different users. As a result, two users may walk away with very different perceptions of the same underlying facts, without ever realizing that their experiences differed.  In some ways, this brings back many of the concerns we (as researchers and society) have grappled with in the context of social media. On social media, users and researchers could, at least to some extent, observe the information circulating across different Facebook groups, Instagram accounts, or TikTok communities. With chatbots, these information environments are largely invisible to anyone outside the individual conversation. We cannot easily observe what different users are being told, let alone systematically compare those responses or track how they change over time. This is precisely why projects like the LLM Election Observatory are so important: By systematically collecting and publicly sharing chatbot responses, we can begin to make these otherwise invisible differences observable and open to scrutiny. Q: What sorts of questions and AI responses are you tracking through the dashboard? Podimata: There are several questions we ultimately want this dataset to help us study. For example: Do different models provide systematically different information for the same questions? Do their responses change over the course of the campaign? Does the answer a particular model gives change depending on how a user frames the question or describes themselves (e.g., does it change if the model gets informed that the user is a Democrat or a Republican)? And, finally, what are the sources that the models pull information from when answering election-related questions?  Our public dashboard is an important part of the project. We want people both from and outside of academia to be able to see the data we are collecting as the election unfolds rather than only seeing the results months later in an academic paper. The dashboard therefore presents the underlying data and some preliminary descriptive analyses, and we plan to make the dataset available for other researchers to study as well. We expect the dashboard to evolve as the data and our methods evolve. Through this dashboard, we wanted to build on the scientific methodology we developed in 2024 but also to make the research much more accessible and useful to the public while the election is actually unfolding. Not only that, but the addition of MIT political science experts in the team cannot be overstated; Adam and Charles have really helped expand the questions that we are asking in our audit. Q: What do you wish voters across the country knew about AI chatbots when it comes to searching for election information? Berinsky: People should be sure to remember that just because a chatbot sounds confident doesn’t mean it is accurate. AI systems are designed to answer the questions that people ask them in an authoritative voice even when they are wrong, incomplete, or leaning on a weak source. These answers are a reasonable place to start, but voters shouldn’t stop there. Q: What are your findings thus far? Podimata: We have not yet done the full, longitudinal analysis, so we are only going to talk about broad strokes here, but a few broad patterns seem to be visible in the 2026 data. Across the different user identities we present, we see differences in how the answers are presented, in which sources a model cites, and in tone — sometimes even when the underlying facts are the same. What we cannot yet say is how stable those differences are, how they move over the course of the election, or how a real person would read and react to them. Our future analyses will take this up. It also underscores why the continuous record of responses we are collecting matters more than any single snapshot that you might see in the days around the election. Q: Professor Berinsky, your research has also shown that in some cases AI chatbots can be harnessed to help refute misinformation. Can you talk a bit about this? Berinsky: In my undergraduate course on information and social media I have been talking for a while about how AI can cut both ways. On one hand, these tools can generate misleading claims in text, pictures, and video at a scale we have never seen. Basically, AI can help bad actors “flood the zone” with misinformation. On the other hand, some of the most promising recent work demonstrates that evidence-based dialogues with a chatbot can durably reduce belief in conspiracy theories and other beliefs that are not supported by the balance of publicly available evidence.  AI has the potential to do such debunking at scale — something we have long struggled to do. The lesson from decades of misinformation research is that any technology (be it print, radio, or television in earlier eras) is not inherently good or bad for promoting truth. The devil is in the details in how it is built and deployed. Independent auditing like this project can help us assess the ultimate impact of such technologies. Q: Can you talk a bit about your overall goal with this research?  Podimata: AI is a transformative technology, and people understandably have very different expectations (and feelings) about what it will mean for society at large. All of us have people in our lives that are overly enthusiastic about AI, others that are deeply concerned, and many more that are somewhere in between trying to understand what this technology can and cannot do. Our goal here is not to begin from the assumption that AI is either good or bad for elections. Instead, we hope to shed some light onto one part of this transformation: what information major AI systems are actually giving people about an election as it unfolds.

<!--kg-card-end: html--> In the wake of fanfiction repository Archive of Our Own (AO3) announcing a weeks-long security incident outage, readers and writers are reflecting on why the site is important to the fanfiction community, and how they’re coping with the downtime.

On Thursday, the Organization for Transformative Works (OTW), the non-profit organization that runs AO3, posted that the site was down for maintenance, eventually updating to say the site restoration will take around two weeks, but could take up to a month. OTW confirmed in an updated status report Friday morning that this outage is due to a security incident.

Some have speculated that the outage is a result of the PHP scramble this week that led to several sites going down to update their security, but AO3 doesn’t use PHP. An OTW representative told CNET: “I can let you know that this is not related to the PHP security issue as the Archive uses Ruby on Rails.”
Massive Fanfic Site Archive of Our Own Says It’s Going Down for 'Up to 4 Weeks'
Oh my god?

A lot of people are grieving the loss of Kinktober, AO3’s annual group writing exercise where writers upload a chapter or fic every day throughout October based on a prompt of the day. (The prompts are horny, if that’s not clear.) Several of the writers and readers who reached out to me following the outage brought up the poor timing around Kinktober.

One writer I spoke to who posts her writing and reads others’ writing on AO3, told me that she was in the middle of racing to finish a work that was deliberately timed to Kinktober and Halloween when the outage happened. She was hitting “next chapter” while reading a fic on Wednesday night when she got the message that the site was down for maintenance, “which I initially took as a sign from the universe to go to bed,” she said.
“The outage hasn’t derailed my desire to write. If anything, I want to have more chapters ready to go so my readers can eat good once it’s over,” she said.

Do you know anything else about what happened to Ao3? I would love to hear from you. Using a non-work device, you can message me securely on Signal at sam.404. Otherwise, send me an email at sam@404media.co.

Some writers are considering posting elsewhere while they wait for AO3 to return, but it’s not an ideal workaround. AO3 author who goes by Selkie Myth told me they’re moving to Space Battles, another fanfiction site, during the outage. “I'm shrugging and just posting on SB [Space Battles] while the site's down. Hopefully I'll remember to post the chapters over on AO3 once it's back up — the story is projected to end during the outage. I anticipate the same is true for a lot of other authors,” they said.

Some people have said they’ll try fanfiction.net in the meantime, but it’s a much more bare-bones website. Fanfiction site Sufficient Velocity added a banner to its homepage welcoming AO3 refugees: “We’ve had a big influx of guests due to the AO3 outage. If you've been affected by the outage we're sorry to hear that and hope that they're able to get that fixed soon.” Wattpad, which many fanfiction writers and readers really, really hate for reasons I won’t get into here, posted on X: “we're here to support you during this difficult time.” Overwhelmingly, the replies are from people telling Wattpad to go away.

Another AO3 writer who goes by Ren told me she has two long works in progress right now with nowhere to post them. Posting elsewhere poses continuity and discovery problems, as some of these fanfiction works span chapters and hundreds of thousands of words of character and worldbuilding. “I could technically keep posting updates on sites like tumblr through the downtime, but both of these fics are quite long and I haven't been posting them anywhere other than AO3 — if I drop a new chapter for my 130k Pokemon Black and White fanfic on Tumblr completely out of context, people just now finding my work aren't going to be able to read the rest for a while :(“ she told me in an email. “I have seen other authors posting their gdocs and Ellipsus reader links in the meantime, but my draft files aren't exactly presentable... I will keep marinating but what will probably happen is my wips [works in progress] will just be on hiatus for a bit. My readers are used to hiatuses at least.”

Another writer said she’s not considering posting elsewhere. “Wattpad can piss off,” she said. “But I may go back to fanfiction.net to save and physically print some of my favorite fics from way back in the day (the ancient/sacred texts, if you will) to ensure I have copies of those somewhere. This outage is a good reminder that things can vanish in the blink of an eye, whether a website crashes or is hacked or an author decides to suddenly delete their fic. If you love something, smash the kudos button, comment on it, bookmark it, subscribe, and consider downloading it. You never know.”

A reader who emailed me following the outage said they’ve been enjoying getting into AO3 as a new fan. “I was a big fanfic skeptic, but that’s changed lately. I’ve found some truly excellent writers, and real creativity. The free nature of it in this increasingly horrifying stage of capitalism is refreshing,” they said.

AO3 has said in status updates and to journalists that they don’t expect any data loss. Losing works would be devastating for writers and readers, but AO3 is more than just a repository for writing; it’s a community of people commenting and reacting to those stories. Selkie mentioned the rigorous tagging habits of AO3 members, where stories are tagged with sometimes dozens of fanfiction tropes, character names, content hints and warnings, and can constitute a language specific to the platform and its readers; “Crack Treated Seriously,” for example, means writing a silly premise with a straight face, while “Idiots in Love” is self explanatory.

“To me, the more devastating thing would be to lose the comments and kudos on my fic. Technically I have them saved elsewhere because I get AO3 email alerts, but seeing them threaded in one place at the end of a chapter hits different,” a writer said. “Comments can turn an author’s entire day around and restore their will to live. I often reread them if I have writer’s block or a bad bout of imposter syndrome. They also turn the otherwise solitary act of writing into something communal. Seeing someone experience your story chapter by chapter is incredibly motivating and makes the writing process feel less isolating.”

OTW is entirely volunteer-run, and people on social media and in speaking to them directly have said they hope AO3 users go easy on staff during this time. “So many people rely on AO3 as an outlet for creativity and escapism as the real world burns, myself included. It’s also important to remember that the site is run by volunteers,” that writer said. “The work they do to protect writers, fight censorship and safeguard freedom of expression is extremely important and necessary, especially right now. They deserve all the respect and patience in the world as they work to get the archive back up and running. Be kind.”
Ren, echoing those sentiments, sent me a meme:

“An additional sentiment I've seen is ‘ok so when AO3 comes back we're all going to tell our favorite authors how much we missed their work, right?’ which I hope catches on — I'm writing for niche fandoms and had to disable guest comments due to bot spam, so comments are few and far between as it is,” Ren said. “I do kind of hope that the extended outage serves as a sort of wake-up call to anyone who's been taking ao3 for granted lately. It certainly was for me.”
6636fcb789950d92: Crater counts tell us that most of the Martian surface is more than 3 billion years old, but pieces of Mars we have on Earth tell a different story. The three main classes of Martian meteorites—shergottites, nakhlites, and chassignites—are all 2.4 billion years old or younger. Until now, only two genuinely ancient Martian meteorites were known: Allan Hills 84001, found in Antarctica, and a jumbled rock from northwest Africa nicknamed Black Beauty. Now we have a third one.

A team led by Yang Liu, a planetary scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, has shown that a Martian meteorite called Teghaza 001, found in the Sahara Desert in Mali in 2022, formed at least 4.1 billion years ago. “It's very old and similar to some of the oldest rocks on Earth,” Liu says.

“We don't fully understand why old Martian rocks are so rare on Earth," Liu said. Part of the answer may lie in how a piece of Mars gets here. It takes a large impact to launch a rock off the planet, and not every rock can survive that. “If the impact hits into loose powder, it may not get cemented to become a rock and fly off Mars' gravity,” Liu said. “So the natural impact already acts as a filter. Weak rocks do not make it off Mars.”
