<!--kg-card-end: html--> Researchers have amassed a trove of more than 25,000 calls to a support hotline for people during and after psychedelic trips, making it “the largest dataset of psychedelic support interactions ever assembled—exceeding the combined sample sizes of all published psychedelic clinical trials by an order of magnitude,” according to a study published on Friday in Science Advances.

Despite the popularity of psychedelics as recreational drugs, and increasing interest in them as medically-prescribed therapeutic treatments, there is very little research about the effects of these substances outside of clinical settings with carefully-selected patients. That, scientists say, is limiting what we can learn about the effects of these drugs, because the vast majority of psychedelics are consumed by all kinds of people in homes, festivals, ceremonial gatherings, or other uncontrolled environments.

The Fireside Project, a nonprofit founded in 2020, has filled this knowledge gap with its Psychedelic Support Line, which connects callers who are on bad trips, or who are seeking more information about psychedelics, with trained volunteers who offer confidential peer support.

The team has now published a compendium of 25,419 anonymized interactions with 220 hotline volunteers that took place between April 2021 and February 2026. The database opens an unprecedented window into the experiences of people on psilocybin, ketamine, MDMA, LSD, ayahuasca, and even cannabis, which is not generally considered a psychedelic but can trigger similar effects, such as mild hallucinations.

It’s a “treasure trove,” said Félix Schoeller, a senior research scientist at the Institute for Advanced Consciousness Studies, a California-based nonprofit, who led the study, in a call with 404 Media. “In general, we're really lacking any evidence and data beyond what exists in the underground world, if you will, for psychedelic therapy.”

“There's different types of knowledge,” continued Schoeller, who is CEO of ReWire Neurotechnologies, a startup focused on novel experiential treatments for depression. “Some cultures and communities have been doing that for thousands of years. But there's a question about how to do this in a way that follows the principles of biomedical science.”

The interactions included phone calls and text exchanges with hotline volunteers who provided support by talking through the experience or connecting callers with emergency services in the most urgent cases. About 40.2 percent of callers (10,208 interactions) were actively tripping, while 32.1 percent of callers reached out after they had tripped, a period known as “integration.”

The rest of the calls fell into smaller categories, such as informational inquiries about certain substances, requests to prepare or buy drugs, or calls from “trip-sitters” assisting a person on psychedelics.

Psilocybin was the most commonly reported substance (9,348 callers), followed by LSD (2,247callers), cannabis (2,004 callers), and ketamine (1,194 callers), and MDMA (682 callers), with ayahuasca and other drugs logging much smaller numbers.

Surprisingly, callers who had used cannabis reported the highest distress rate—47.2 percent had bad experiences with the drug. Though cannabis has a reputation as a low-stakes substance, the study confirms that it can induce real distress in some cases that warrant consideration for harm reduction. The distress rates for the rest of the commonly used psychedelics were only slightly lower than cannabis, ranging between 40 to 42 percent.

The study also revealed 43 rare but disturbing instances of “facilitator abuse,” including at remote retreats or ceremonial gatherings involving ayahuasca. In these cases, callers reported abuse from the people providing psychedelics, such as reports they had deliberately been given extra doses without consent.

Those reports “provide the first quantitative documentation of this phenomenon in a community help-seeking sample,” according to the study. “The pattern of these reports—clustering in ceremonial settings involving plant medicines, presenting primarily as trauma-processing calls, and involving callers with elevated rates of prior PTSD diagnoses—suggests that even modest surveillance through existing peer support infrastructure can detect harm occurring in unregulated psychedelic settings.”
Some calls also came from people who said they suffered from schizophrenia, or had taken multiple psychedelics, offering a rare glimpse of situations that could not be observed in clinical settings.

“This kind of data can inform us on these topics in the context of legalizing these drugs and making them accessible,” said Schoeller. “I'm glad that there's this data that exists that people can look into to support or contradict the claims that they make as to how these things should be done.”

The study also outlines several limitations, including its sample bias of people who are inclined to call a hotline in the first place—which is not representative of psychedelic consumers at large—as well as self-reported accounts of doses, among other factors that are impossible to verify.

Despite the noisiness of the data, however, it contains helpful clues about avenues for future research. In Schoeller’s view, one of the most important revelations was that the success of a call was strongly linked to the perception that the hotline volunteer showed genuine care and empathy toward the caller. Using 2,777 postinteraction satisfaction surveys, the team found that the few negative experiences with the hotline tended to stem from feelings that the volunteer was dismissive, or didn’t seem to care about the caller.

“My takeaway is that the number one thing that predicts whether a support call will not work” is “the volunteer being perceived as genuine,” Schoeller said. “That's something that, in many ways, poses a problem to the biomedical system of centralized hospitals. I'm not trying to be ideological in any way, but when you create a centralized institution where you throw everybody to a single place to get care” then “clinicians become burned out.”

For this reason, Schoeller and his colleagues plan to follow up on the role of perceived care and empathy in treatment, and to emphasize this factor in guidance for community-based peer support for people in crisis due to psychedelics. It also reinforces the value of the Fireside Project’s hotline, which provides a safe and confidential service for people who might be reluctant to contact emergency services because of the criminalization of these substances or fear of incurring medical debt.

“For many people, they have experiences with psychedelics, and they may not be required to go to the ER, but they still need someone to help them navigate the difficult experience,” Schoeller concluded. “The hotline can truly be a lifeline for them.”

0e346d4a2bbac184: The campaign of U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola of Alaska, a Democrat, has been rocked by accusations it recruited a spoiler candidate for the ballot. AP/Mark ThiessenLess than a week before Election Day, The New York Times reported that people with links to Alaska Democrat Mary Peltola’s U.S. Senate campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee had recruited a candidate to the race whose name is nearly identical to that of the incumbent Republican senator, Dan Sullivan, whom Peltola was challenging. The plan aimed to siphon votes from the incumbent senator and help Peltola win, according to the reporting. The story has driven calls for prosecutions, lawsuits and state action. But as a political scientist who studies election law, I can say that the spoiler candidate is one of the oldest tricks in the American campaign toolbox, and the law has rarely touched it. Early ballots 19th-century voting usually involved casting a ballot printed by political parties, such as this electoral ticket for the Free Soil Party from 1848. Smithsonian National Museum of American History For most of the 1800s, American elections were conducted with ballots designed and printed by the parties. There were no official ballots printed by the state. In those days, the addition of a rival name to a party ballot by an insidious printer could swing countless votes to the opposing party. The tactic was well known, and voters were often warned to look out for the “Spurious Ticket.” By the 1890s, the government-printed ballot had gained widespread adoption and ended the practice of counterfeit tickets. But that would not be enough to deter those who wanted to deceive voters. Power of a name As observers in Alaska have noted, recruiting candidates with similar or identical names is not a new move. In John F. Kennedy’s first congressional primary, his opponent was a city councilor named Joseph Russo. An aide to Kennedy reportedly paid a janitor with the same name to enter the race. The real Russo complained, but in the end, Kennedy took more votes in the 1946 race than the Russos combined. Eight years later, the name Kennedy worked the other way, when a Gillette stockroom supervisor named John Francis Kennedy, no relation, was elected as a Democrat to the position of treasurer and receiver-general of Massachusetts, owing in large part to the familiarity of his name. Names can move votes, so namesakes can be worth recruiting. Spoilers as surrogates Some spoiler candidates are not necessarily meant to win votes. Sometimes they are there to amplify a message. In 1978, Republican Carroll Campbell was running for an open House seat in upstate South Carolina. His opponent was Max Heller, the mayor of Greenville and a Jewish refugee from Nazi-occupied Austria. Days before the election, Don Sprouse, an independent running for office for the first time, held a press conference and declared that Heller was unfit for office as he had “not made clear to the voters he is not a Christian” and was “not as qualified to represent the Christian people.” Although Campbell condemned the remarks and Sprouse received only 1,693 votes, Heller lost the race. The allegations, still unproven, of Sprouse being a “stalking-horse” for Campbell only surfaced years later, but they continued to dog Campbell when he ran for governor in 1986. Sprouse wasn’t going to spoil the election with the votes he could win, but he could be a spoiler with his message, an antisemitic appeal that Campbell would not make directly. A spoiler candidate who made antisemitic remarks in a 1978 South Carolina campaign for the House of Representatives became a campaign issue eight years later. New York Times archive Candidates who don’t even know they’re running A different type of ballot shenanigan skips the recruitment and simply puts candidates on the ballot. This was the case in 2010 when two Oakland County, Michigan, Democratic officials put candidates on the ballot under the Tea Party label in three races. The candidates didn’t even know they were running. In this case, the law did come back to bite. The county party chair and operations director were charged with perjury and forgery, but the crime was forging signatures, not their strategy. Some state election codes specifically discuss false declarations or forged election paperwork, but many don’t contemplate this type of scheme. Forgery and perjury, however, are illegal across the country, and it’s almost impossible to put an unwitting person on the ballot without one or the other. Alaska: No barriers In Alaska, this tactic can be used cheaply. There is no petition requirement to get on the ballot, just a $100 fee. Moreover, the parties can’t vet candidates in the primary. The state’s unique top-four primary system lets candidates choose their own party label. The saga of Daniel J. Sullivan, the schoolteacher known as “Petersburg Sullivan” because of where he lives, and Sen. Dan S. Sullivan goes back longer than recent revelations. Petersburg Sullivan filed to run as a Republican in the Senate race just three days before the deadline; state officials tried to bar him from the ballot. In June a judge said there was nothing in Alaska law to prevent him from appearing on the ballot, and the state Supreme Court subsequently agreed. Since he couldn’t be removed, the state Division of Elections took unusual steps on their ballot design to help distinguish the two candidates. They listed Sen. Dan S. Sullivan as a Republican, marking him as the incumbent, and left Daniel J. Sullivan without a party designation. This had not been done for previous incumbents in at least a decade. What the law can do Assuming there is no forgery of documents with an unwitting and unwilling spoiler candidate, there is little the law can do. History shows us that the real legal exposure in these cases usually lies where it most often does in politics: money. In a 2020 Miami, Florida, race, a former state senator turned political operative was convicted of three felonies related to efforts to recruit and pay a decoy candidate with the same surname as the Democratic incumbent. In another Florida case, a local Republican Party chair was convicted in connection with a scheme to plant a progressive alternative to siphon votes from the Democratic candidate. In both cases the prosecutions focused on campaign finance crimes, not simply on putting the spoilers on the ballot. The state of Washington is an outlier, where it is a felony to run under a rival’s surname if the intent is to confuse voters. In 2024, two Bob Fergusons were recruited by conservative activist Glen Morgan to run for governor against state Attorney General Bob Ferguson. Both opted to drop out of their race under threat of prosecution. There is nothing comparable to these laws in Alaska, however, and whether laws like this could prevent this type of thing in a federal election is still untested. Under the Supreme Court’s decision in U.S. Term Limits v. Thornton in 1995, states cannot add their own qualifications for Congress. Read your ballots! The advice from 1860 – “Watch your tickets on election day. There’s a scheme on foot …” – when newspapers urged voters to read their tickets before casting their vote, is still relevant long after the demise of the party ticket. It is unlikely that the law can solve this problem, because to do so would be to wade into the First Amendment waters of why people run for office. Regulating thought and intention is a dangerous proposition under the Constitution. The old answer is the best one. Self-government depends less on clever rules and more on citizens paying attention. Read your ballots! Drew Kurlowski does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

da44a73a639653f3: <!--kg-card-end: html--> On Friday, Andy Yen, the CEO of Proton, cancelled a series of nearly company-wide ‘re-interviews’ that would have forced employees to explain how they are using AI, with the clear intention that they may be fired if not using it enough in the eyes of Proton leadership, according to six current Proton employees and audio of an around two hour all-hands meeting obtained by 404 Media.

The move came after 404 Media published an investigation on Thursday, which showed how Yen was aggressively pushing AI across Proton, in some cases despite security concerns from employees. In one exchange, an employee in the company’s security Slack channel urged Proton to at least take a few days to pentest newly written code before pushing it live. “That’s bullshit and loser thinking. Of course it’s possible to be fast and secure,” Yen wrote in the channel at the end of August. “Stop thinking always of how to be slower, and focus more on how to be faster.” Yen added, “stop lovingly handcrafting all our code and use AI more.”

The re-interview cancellations likely don’t address the concerns of many Proton users, who are more focused on Proton’s deprioritization of security; many Proton users have blasted the company’s leadership on social media over the last 24 hours and explicitly called for Yen to resign.

The investigation was based on conversations with eight current and one former Proton employees, Slack chats, meeting audio, and an AI manifesto written by the company’s CTO Bart Butler. It painted a picture of Proton that is very different to the public’s perception of a company carefully protecting privacy. Instead, Proton is barreling ahead with AI in large part to achieve more annual revenue. The investigation also found a culture of fear across Proton, where employees have genuine concerns about security or being asked to develop security-focused products with AI, but feel unable to voice them because Yen mocks or insults employees in front of everyone else.
“I don’t think he will change anything, and I think the only reason we had this meeting is because he has a rebellion on his hands,” one employee told 404 Media after the all-hands meeting on Friday.
db28dde45a2fbb76: For the first time in the country, a candidate managed to turn the results in the run-off
Originally published on Global Voices
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva waves Brazil’s flag surrounded by a crowd of supporters in São Paulo, during the 2026 election campaign. Photo by Ricardo Stuckert/Lula Oficial on Flickr (CC BY-SA 4.0).

On April 7, 2018, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who had been president of Brazil twice, waited in the building of the Metalworkers’ Union, in São Bernardo do Campo, São Paulo state, where his political life started in the 1970s, to be arrested by the Federal Police following convictions for corruption and money laundering.

Gilberto Carvalho, one of his oldest allies, later recalled that they hoped for a crowd of 50,000, but only 10,000 people waited outside. Lula looked through the window, grabbed his arm, and said, “Gilbertinho, we go to war with the soldiers we have.”
Eight years and six months after that day, on October 25, 2026, Lula was elected president of Brazil for the fourth time, supported by millions of people in the streets and an army of his own online.
The convictions against him were later annulled by the Federal Supreme Court (STF), which ruled that the lower federal court lacked jurisdiction and was biased. Lula spent 580 days in prison.

His latest victory was also the first time a candidate was elected after losing the first round in Brazil. In 20 days, Lula, a member of the Workers‘ Party, managed to turn Flavio Bolsonaro’s advantage of 2.2 million votes into a win by a 4.4 million-vote difference.

As the BBC explained, both candidates increased their votes in the second round, in an election with the lowest abstention rate since 2006. The leftist’s victory came from five million new voters, with a drop in absences, blank and nulled votes, says UOL news portal. Also, it left the world in awe, wondering just how he did it.
On the streets and an online army

Lula gathered the support of massive crowds in the streets and an online army led by federal deputy André Janones, who poses with him during a livestream. Photos by Ricardo Stuckert/Lula Oficial on Flickr. Collage by Global Voices on Canva Pro.

Lula reset his campaign in the second round, bringing new people into his team and riding on the so-called R-factor — ruas e redes, Portuguese for “streets and networks” — which started organically and was embraced by his team. On October 5, while many were dispirited by the first-round results, students from UFF (Fluminense Federal University) took to the streets in the city of Niterói, Rio de Janeiro state, in a pro-Lula act that spread nationally in the following weeks.

Lula’s official events also left the stage used in the first round and instead moved to the streets for massive marches, during which he led the crowds from a truck and talked to supporters about his proposals, his own history, and the threats presented by his opponent, all while waving Brazil’s flag.

On October 7, federal deputy André Janones posted about an initiative that would hack social media and contribute to turning the election around. On X, Janones wrote that he had recruited 1.5 million people for a WhatsApp channel, inviting more to join and saying: “This is the ONLY way of bursting the bubble, since Meta only organically delivers right-leaning content.” After threats of being taken down by the electoral court, by voting day, the public channel had 11 million people.

Janones’ guide for social media, nicknamed “cultural Janonismo,” included ignoring opponents’ posts and setting coordinated actions, like the viral trend of Lula’s supporters wearing the national team's yellow jersey, a symbol hijacked by the right for over 10 years. Every command delivered to the soldiers of “Lula's Army” — new hashtags, a post to engage, a live feed to watch — Janones would follow up in capital letters with an order: “EXPLODE.” The methodology is already inspiring people in Spain and France.
ATTENTION! People are mistranslating what I said!
I NEVER said people should block far-right accounts. I said they should IGNORE THEIR POSTS!
Blocking actually works against this strategy because the algorithm will understand that you didn’t see the content simply because you blocked the account.

However, when a post appears in your feed and you ignore it, you don’t read it, don’t like it, don’t comment on it, or engage with it in any way, the algorithm will interpret that content as irrelevant because it was shown to you and you chose not to engage with it!
THERE IS A HUGE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN BLOCKING CONTENT AND IGNORING IT!
— André Janones (@AndreJanonesMG) October 28, 2026

During the campaign, users accused Meta of affecting their engagement when posting pro-Lula content. On October 16, Folha de S. Paulo reported that Meta employees admitted that Lula’s accounts “were hindered by ‌restrictions.” The tech company denied any political bias after the electoral court ordered it to give equal treatment to both candidates.

The campaign was also boosted by a change of rhetoric, says anthropologist Rosana Pinheiro-Machado. “This was not mobilisation in a vacuum. Lula focused less on sovereignty and more on people’s concrete concerns.”
On voting day, the pro-Lula mobilization also resulted in Brazilians over 70, who are not required to vote, showing up, some brought by relatives, in the call for democracy.
The Bolsonaros’ risk

On the other side, bolsonaristas began the second round by celebrating their candidates’ major wins in seats for state governments, the federal senate, lower chamber, and state parliaments from north to south. Two of Jair Bolsonaro’s sons, his wife, and one of his brothers were elected.

But in the 20 days that followed, scenes from bolsonarista events led many Brazilians to question what country they wanted. In an act by Flavio’s campaign, at Paulista Avenue, in São Paulo, a traditional point for political protests, his supporters carried an inflatable missile with the message “Trump nuke Brazil,” which many saw as a treasonous statement. In another event in Rio, a white man was seen holding a Black man in plastic chains, with Lula’s name on his back. The man told the police that the idea was to represent the leftist leader as Satan. There was also an escalation of political violence, including threats, beatings, and killings.

Add to those the weight of the Bolsonaros’ own history, along with a growing anti-Bolsonarista sentiment. Jair, the father, is under house arrest for a coup attempt that included a plan to assassinate Lula, his VP Geraldo Alckmin, and a Supreme Court justice. Flávio himself vowed to change the 1988 Constitution, created after the military dictatorship, once elected.

Forty-five-year-old Flávio was always considered less radical than his younger siblings, despite selling himself as anti-establishment, even as an elected politician since 2002. This always guaranteed him a privileged forum and protection when investigations drew closer. In 2020, former judge Sergio Moro, who convicted Lula, resigned as Jair Bolsonaro’s justice minister after the president tried to intervene in the Federal Police to protect Flávio, then a suspect in “an embezzlement and money-laundering” scheme within his state deputy office.

During the 2026 campaign, Flávio’s links to other scandals were exposed by the Brazilian press. Among them, the money he received from a disgraced banker for his father’s movie biopic (Dark Horse), without ever proving the final destination of the funds.

Flávio is currently under investigation in three different inquiries at the Supreme Court. After he lost the election, he fled to the US after the Federal Police asked to seize his passports (he also has Italian citizenship), considering him a flight risk.
Lula’s last dance
Brazilians waiting in line to vote, in Brasília, the country's capital, on October 25. Photo by Fabio Rodrigues-Pozzebom/Agência Brasil. Used with permission.

On voting day, both campaigns asked the electoral court (TSE) to extend the voting period. Lula’s campaign requested the extension following reports that Bolsonaro-allied mayors reduced public transportation in some capitals, while Flávio’s claimed storms in states where he had stronger support affected voter turnout. After the TSE failed to rule on the requests, they were referred to the Supreme Court, where Justice Cristiano Zanin, Lula’s former defense lawyer, appointed by him to the court, ruled that polls should remain open for two more hours. Zanin was randomly selected for the case.

Despite having his own request answered by the ruling, Flávio has been using this as a motive to contest the results, even though they were recognized by the electoral court's president Kassio Nunes Marques, a Supreme Court justice appointed by Jair Bolsonaro, following Flávio’s suggestion. His own party — PL, Liberal Party — also published a note acknowledging Lula’s election win. Around 34,000 votes were registered during the extended period, which had little impact on the final numbers.

The 2026 candidacy was Lula’s seventh time running for president and his fourth election. Even though he is known as a popular leader, back in August, 43 percent of Brazilians disapproved of his government. The campaign underestimated frustration with the government’s fiscal performance, public debt, inflation rates, and how people still link corruption scandals to the left, even when right-linked figures are at the center.

Flávio’s counter-medicine at the beginning of the campaign was the promise of a super-scissor cut to all public spending, modelling Javier Milei’s steps in Argentina. One of the people appointed to his economic team talked openly about privatization. This brought many investors and the upper classes to his side. On the second turn, however, eyeing the election, he toned down and started promising to keep all social programs from Lula’s governments, without explaining the math of his actual government plan.
With the majority of bolsonaristas and right-leaning politicians in both the Senate and the Lower Chamber, Lula will start the most challenging of his four terms next year.

Besides dealing with the 11 trillion BRL of federal debt (around USD 2 trillion), he promised in his victory speech: “This will be the term in which I'll listen to the Brazilian people the most about what they want me to do in this country. We'll work to make our digital communication stronger. And I even got a cell phone now. Get ready.”
Written by Global Voices Brazil
b3f5e32588f49f07: A new report from the analytics firm Quilty Space confirms that, outside of China, the world faces a significant shortage of rockets over the next five years.

The firm estimates that between now and 2030, there will be a shortfall of about 150 launches compared to demand from satellite operators and civil space agencies. If demand from the US military is added in—and SpaceX does not extend the Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy program to accommodate increased national security needs—the shortage could be doubled.

"What we wanted to get at is to understand how severe this launch crisis is and when will it be resolved," said Caleb Henry, director of research at Quilty Space. "What we learned is that the launch crisis is more severe than we thought and that it will not go away this decade for sure, and it might not abate until sometime late in the 2030s."

This was a company that once charged $19 for a polishing cloth, asked $200 for a VESA mount, and sold $700 wheels for the Mac Pro. Now it’s borrowing tired ideas from its competitors and launching hardware its previous leaders rejected.

The once dominant company is struggling to find its feet in an AI-driven post-Tim Cook world. John Ternus is the new CEO — a 25 year veteran of the company with a track record of pushing harebrained hardware schemes like the much reviled Touch Bar and lawsuit inducing butterfly keyboard.

<!--kg-card-begin: html--> <!--kg-card-end: html--> With Ternus at the helm, I feel there’s a good chance Apple’s best days are behind it, that it will have to make do with less, that it’s déclassé. Apple, blindsided by AI and relying on crowdpleasing hardware gimmicks, is downwardly mobile. It’s in its slop era. The company that once asked consumers to “Think Different” is now releasing hardware that’s just like everything else on the market.

Apple is not adjusting to this new position well. AI boosters agree that Siri AI is awful. Apple HomeView is a $300 Apple Watch meant to replace the family hearth. The iPhone Duo has only been out for a few days and all people can talk about is the cracks, yet Ternus is on the cover of Time Magazine this week holding the folding iPhone Duo and staring at the camera. “The other examples in the world felt kind of cheap and crappy,” Ternus told Time. Many people holding cracked iPhone Duos this week are learning just what (not) cheap and crappy looks like.

Flailing from crackgate, Apple announced the launch of a touch-screen laptop, an idea Steve Jobs extensively tested and said “doesn’t work,” an idea Cook once compared to combining a toaster with a refrigerator. What’s next? What if the toaster-refigerator folded? Ternus has been trying to make an 18-inch foldable iPad happen for years. Maybe Apple will solve the screen cracking issues by then. Or maybe Ternus will continue to try to put a hat on a hat.
I have been waiting for this moment for more than a decade. I am relishing Apple’s recent trajectory more than I should. I confess I harbor a secret and petty grudge.

In 2010, when Apple released the iPhone 4 I was working as a floor manager at a Banana Republic in Dallas. I was interested in smart phones, of course, but Dallas is an expensive city and the iPhone was a luxury. I made do with my Motorola Razr. But the suit-wearing middle management retail psychopaths that were my coworkers saw my lack of an iPhone as a weakness. It was not, as they say now, On Brand.

I had started at the store in the stock room, working my way up to manage the backroom before ascending to a coveted position on the sales floor. The other managers made it clear that a Razr was a “backroom” phone and someone in a prominent position on the floor needed to be seen using an iPhone.
At first, I was not told to buy an iPhone. The message came in the form of subtle and not so subtle bullying deployed over weeks.
“Still using that old phone?” they’d say.“Didn’t you get a raise?” someone would ask a week later.
“Try not to use that thing on the sales floor,” one co-worker told me, pointing at my Razr. “We’re trying to project a certain image here.”

The social pressure had the opposite of its intended effect. I resisted. Eventually one of the friendlier managers pulled me aside. He told me that my colleagues thought it was weird that I didn't have an iPhone. He said I needed to buy one to fit in and he said the store could give me an advance on my paycheck to make it happen.

Ever the contrarian and pissed I was experiencing high school style bullying as a full grown adult, I threw in with Google instead. I got an HTC Dream. My coworkers weren’t happy, but they stopped bringing up the iPhone.

I’ve been an Android user ever since and studiously avoided Apple products until I broke down a few years ago and bought a Macbook Air. Time heals all wounds and Windows laptops are garbage. I’d even been considering changing from Android to iPhone because the privacy features are more robust. I’ve never been averse to a fast food meal either and maybe I’m a little more comfortable with Apple now that the cracks are starting to show in the foldable phone.
01e3da261c2e8c21: A court-ordered reassessment will set new values for every property in Allegheny County. Robert D. Strovers/Moments Collection via Getty ImagesAllegheny County will undergo a countywide reassessment of every property it taxes for the first time since 2012. A county judge ordered the reassessment in August 2026, requiring the work to begin by July 1, 2027, and finish within five years. The goal is to bring property values in line with today’s market. That could shift the tax burden among property owners across the county. State anti-windfall rules may require local governments to lower their tax rates after a reassessment to ensure they balance and equalize the tax reassessments. Individual bills may go up or down. For many homeowners, property taxes are confusing. Terms such as assessment, millage rate and school district tax come up often, but taxpayers may not know what they mean or how each one affects their annual tax bill. In Pittsburgh, property taxes pay for schools, parks, libraries, public safety and other local services. I research and teach government finance at Penn State Harrisburg, including a course on state and local taxation. Here’s a plain-language guide to how Pittsburgh’s property taxes work. What your home is worth – on paper The first concept is the property assessment. Allegheny County’s Office of Property Assessments gives every property an assessed value. That value is the basis for calculating property taxes. The Allegheny County Courthouse is also home to the county treasurer’s office, which collects county property taxes. tupungato/iStock Collection via Getty Images Plus An assessed value isn’t necessarily what a home would sell for today. Some places, such as Philadelphia, assess property at full market value. Other jurisdictions assess property at a set percentage of market value. In Cook County, Illinois, which includes Chicago, homes are assessed at 10% of their market value. That doesn’t mean Chicago-area homeowners pay less. When assessments are a smaller share of market value, tax rates are set higher to raise the same amount of money. Allegheny County assesses at full value, but it uses what properties were worth in 2012. The court-ordered reassessment is meant to close the gap between those 2012 values and today’s market. Allegheny County’s 14-year gap would be unusual almost anywhere else. Pennsylvania is the only state that doesn’t require counties to reassess on a regular schedule, while most states do so at least every six years. Within Pennsylvania, though, Allegheny is far from the worst: Butler County hasn’t reassessed since 1969. Homeowners can look up their assessment on the county’s real estate portal. What a mill means Once a property has an assessed value, each local government applies a millage rate to figure out the tax owed. One mill equals $1 of tax for every $1,000 of assessed value. A home assessed at $100,000 has 100 units of $1,000 in value. Pittsburgh property owners pay property taxes to three government entities: Allegheny County, the City of Pittsburgh and Pittsburgh Public Schools. Each one sets its own millage rate. For 2026, the city’s general rate is 9.67 mills. The city also charges 0.5 mill for parks and 0.25 mill for libraries. Pittsburgh Public Schools charges 10.457 mills, and Allegheny County charges 6.43 mills. Together, those rates add up to 27.307 mills. For a city home assessed at $100,000, that comes to about $2,731 a year before any exemptions or discounts. The county’s property tax worksheet and the county treasurer’s millage rate page list current rates. These rates are set each year, and all of them will be cut when reassessed values take effect, since the law requires rates to drop as total values rise. The biggest slice: Schools School taxes are often the largest share of a homeowner’s property tax bill. In Pennsylvania, property taxes are a major source of revenue for public schools. They help fund salaries for teachers, updates and maintainance for buildings, transportation, and technology and educational programs. School tax rates vary widely across Allegheny County. Pittsburgh Public Schools charges 10.457 mills, well below the suburban districts around it. North Allegheny, one of the lowest-taxing suburban districts, charges about 20.4 mills for the 2026-27 school year. Two of the highest are Mt. Lebanon at about 32 mills and Penn Hills at about 32.6 mills. The county treasurer publishes a full list of school district rates. Help for homeowners and seniors Some homeowners qualify for programs that lower their tax bills. The Allegheny County Homestead exemption, known as Act 50, cuts $18,000 from the assessed value of a qualified, owner-occupied, primary residence property’s county taxes. There’s no income limit: Any homeowner who lives in the property as their primary residence qualifies. A home assessed at $100,000 is taxed on just $82,000, which saves about $116 a year. Enrolling in Act 50 also automatically applies Pittsburgh’s $15,000 exemption, which covers the parks and library levies, and a larger Pittsburgh Public Schools exemption that is set each year. Applications for this exemption are due March 1 and need to be filed only once. The senior citizen tax relief program, known as Act 77, takes another 30% off county taxes for homeowners who are at least 60, have household incomes of $30,000 or less and have owned and lived in their home for at least 10 years. For a qualifying senior with that $100,000 home, the county bill would drop from about $527 to about $369. If you think your assessment’s too high Homeowners who believe their assessment is too high can appeal their assessment to the county’s Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review. Filing is free; appeals can be submitted online, by email or in person. Appeals are filed the year before the tax year they affect. The appeal window for 2027 bills closed Sept. 1, 2026. The next window, for 2028 bills, is expected to run from July 1 to Sept. 1, 2027, around the time the reassessment is set to begin. At an appeal hearing, homeowners can argue their property’s value using either 2012 prices or today’s market. Recent sales of similar homes nearby can help show whether an assessment is out of line. The board can lower the assessment, leave it as is or raise it. What reassessment means for you Pittsburgh property taxes come down to two elements: the property’s assessed value and the millage rates set by the county, the city and the school district. Understanding how these elements work together can help homeowners read and comprehend their tax bills and better plan for one of the biggest ongoing costs of owning a home, next to the mortgage payment. That understanding will matter more as the reassessment gets underway. When new values take effect, some homeowners will see their share of the tax burden rise and others will see it fall. The direction depends on how their property’s value has changed compared with changes of other similar properties since 2012. Read more of our stories about Pittsburgh and Pennsylvania. 62c5ca7a60baabf4: Economic pessimism among Americans in both political parties is deepening ahead of the November midterm elections, amid factors such as high energy prices and cost-of-living pressures. AP Photo/Jeff ChiuPolling is looking grim for Republicans ahead of the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3, 2026, due in large part to deep pessimism among the public about the economy. At first glance, this might seem surprising. With the exception of inflation, many economic measures remain strong, including gross domestic product growth. But consumer sentiment continues to languish. This has prompted a debate over whether mere “vibes” are in play, or whether these long-used metrics are no longer capturing something fundamental to Americans’ economic well-being. This debate matters politically because voters are placing an overwhelming priority on the economy as an issue in the midterms. A Pew Research survey in early October 2026 found that 84% of registered voters said the economy was very important to their vote, and the concern is bipartisan. Among the issues in that Pew survey, for example, “the economy” was the least polarizing, with 82% of Republicans and 88% of Democrats ranking it as very important. Meanwhile, the overall drop in voters’ economic outlook has largely been driven by growing pessimism among Republicans. While Democrats remain much gloomier about the economy than Republicans, the gap is narrowing. These trends help explain why Democrats are expected to make significant gains in Congress: This election will likely be seen as an indictment of how well the economy is working for ordinary Americans under President Donald Trump and the Republican-controlled Congress, despite strong macroeconomic measures. So what is going on? As a scholar of financial markets and global inequality, I believe the relationship between how people see their own finances and their view of the broader economy is also changing on a more fundamental level. And this shift will affect how they judge the next class of lawmakers in power. Reality versus ‘vibes’ When scholars try to understand how people judge the economy – and how they separate their own personal circumstances from the broader economy – one of their key reference points is the University of Michigan’s consumer sentiment index. It asks respondents about their personal finances, their short-term and long-term economic outlook, and whether they think it’s a good time to make major purchases. This gauge has historically tracked key economic measures of consumer spending and inflation: The state of the broader economy usually shapes the way people think about their own financial well-being. But in recent years, these have diverged. By many measures, the economy is doing well, but people feel they’re falling behind. And this has only become more pronounced ahead of the midterms. Despite strong consumer spending, robust business investment and low unemployment, consumer sentiment keeps slipping and is now 10% below where it was a year ago, according to the Michigan index. Some commentators point to ongoing inflation as the reason for gloom. It has remained stubbornly above the Federal Reserve’s annual 2% target rate due to drivers like tariffs, energy price hikes stemming from Middle East turmoil, and massive amounts of investment in the artificial intelligence build-out. But what’s really happening is that consumer sentiment data and inflation data have become untethered. Inflation has actually dropped sharply from its 21st-century peak of 9.1% in June 2022 after the pandemic to 3.7% in September 2026, but consumer sentiment is lower now than it was even then. What about wages? Here, too, the data also doesn’t fully explain this disconnect. While inflation makes consumer goods pricier, it also lifts pay. Inflation-adjusted wages actually increased between 2022 and the first half of 2026, all while consumer sentiment remained weak. What has changed in recent months is that inflation-adjusted wages are now falling – which could help explain the darkening outlook among voters. Inequality versus growth One possibility is that deeply entrenched inequality explains this divergence. Compared with other eras of moderate-to-high inflation, the U.S. economy today is much more unequal. Income inequality has increased over the past 20 years, narrowing only during the 2008 and 2020 crises before quickly widening to prior levels. This trend is important for understanding which consumers are shelling out cash. The Fed has consistently cited strong consumer spending in its economic assessments, but the richest 10% of Americans account for half of that spending today. Meanwhile, spending by the bottom 80% of earners has fallen behind inflation. In other words, the strong total consumer spending figures reported as official data are being driven by very wealthy Americans and fail to reflect the experience of typical consumers who are the bulk of the electorate. This trend of increasing inequality has been particularly acute in terms of wealth: The top 0.1% of American households together own five times as much wealth as the bottom 50%. Much of this reflects the uneven gains of the stock market boom and how wealth is taxed. In short, Americans’ economic malaise might be driven by concerns over income and wealth that conventional measures don’t fully capture. A surging stock market in 2026 helped boost Americans’ retirement accounts, but it hasn’t translated into greater consumer confidence. AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura It’s not just about me When it comes to consumer surveys like the University of Michigan index, economists generally assume that the answers reflect the personal experience of respondents. But I agree with other scholars who argue that sometimes these answers may be based less on people’s own circumstances and more on how they view the economy as a whole. This assessment could reflect, for example, concerns like equity, equality of opportunity and economic justice. When responses are driven by a concern for collective well-being rather than just personal material self-interest, social scientists refer to such perceptions as “sociotropic.” This last point isn’t just theoretical. Research suggests voters tend to weight their perceptions of the economy more heavily than their personal financial circumstances when deciding whether to vote for the incumbent party. Trade is one good example. Americans’ preferences for trade policy are driven less by how a particular measure, like tariffs, would impact them personally and more by how they think it would affect the country as a whole. If consumer sentiment follows a similar path, that could explain the divergence between generally strong economic trends and weak consumer sentiment. People are thinking not just about their own conditions but those of the U.S. as a whole, and it’s possible that their understanding of “the economy” includes its relationship to inequality. Understanding the disconnect between the economic data traditionally used to assess the economy’s health and Americans’ perceptions of that economy is important not just to the scholars trying to make sense of it – it could also help set an agenda for the incoming Congress. If economic insecurity punishes the governing party at the polls, the next Congress will be expected to do something about it once sworn in. Voters generally back the incumbent party when the economy is doing well and the out-party when it’s not. But how they judge the health of the economy is not straightforward, and the past six years suggest that improving headline measures of economic health – without regard to Americans’ lived experience and their concerns about what kind of economy is being built – may not be enough to assuage voters’ concerns. 114920bae2772585: Nissan has a new version of its bestselling Rogue SUV, and it’s launching the model here with the latest version of its e-Power hybrid system, which Ars tested in February. Most hybrid cars you can buy today are parallel hybrids, which means that they have an internal combustion engine and an electric motor, both of which drive some or all of the wheels—everything works in parallel. But there’s another approach. Instead of connecting the engine to the wheels via a transmission, it can act as a generator and charge the traction battery, which in turn powers the electric motor. Since the engine and motor work in series, this is known as a series hybrid.

That’s mostly how the Chevrolet Volt worked. As does Honda’s hybrid CR-V. Well, mostly; engineers worked out it was more efficient for those cars' gasoline engines to directly drive the wheels at highway speeds, something that to this day makes a certain subset of hybrid car enthusiasts irrationally angry. If you know anyone like that in your life, send them to wherever the nearest Nissan dealership is, because the 2027 Rogue Hybrid is exactly what they’ve been asking for.

Under the hood, with its crisp shut line and slim horizontal lights that give me something of a Range Rover vibe, there’s a 1.5 L, three-cylinder turbocharged direct-injection engine that generates 148 hp (110 kW). It only revs to 5,200 rpm because it’s optimized to charge the battery, not cope with the various loads of an engine connected to a gearbox and the wheels. That also allows the engine to operate at a rather impressive 42 percent thermal efficiency—we would need to look at Formula 1 engines to find higher.
298d4aed9fdf5e94: My colleagues and I discovered a new species of extinct crocodile from a fossil found in the same rocks used to carve the Great Sphinx of Giza. Today, there are only two species of the long-snouted gavial crocodile, both of which are endangered: Gavialis gangeticus and Tomistoma schlegelii. They are found only in freshwater environments on the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia. However, the fossil record of gavials goes back 80 million years, to the time of the dinosaurs. It shows that they were once diverse, with more than 40 species known, and lived all over the globe. So how did a group of crocodiles that today cannot tolerate saltwater once live all over the world? Our discovery may help to solve this puzzle. Although the distribution of the continents differed from today, most were already separated by oceans. My colleagues and I have been trying to understand how gavials achieved this cosmopolitan distribution, while also seeking to unlock what led to their current predicament. Studying the anatomy of the skeletons of living and fossil gavials has given us a better understanding of the group’s evolution in recent years. CT scans have enabled us to look inside their skulls, giving us a window into their brains and sensory systems. This has revealed new anatomical information that helps differentiate species, and has allowed us to infer aspects of the biology and ecology of some of the extinct species. For example, in an extinct group of crocodile relatives known to have lived entirely in the ocean, other researchers found thickening of the outer wall of their inner ear to cope with the higher pressures seen at ocean depths. My colleagues and I have found similar evidence for a marine lifestyle in some fossil gavials. This ability to live in the ocean was lost in living species, which are restricted to rivers and lakes. Several of the gavial fossils we have been studying from Africa and Europe were first reported in the late 19th and early 20th centuries and they were often described as species of Tomistoma, i.e. closely related to Tomistoma schlegelii, one of the two living species of gavials. Our previous work and that of others has shown that some of these extinct species are not closely related to Tomistoma, with new names given for some of them. However, many of these historically described species remain neglected. Led by my former PhD student, Paul Burke, now a researcher at the Swedish Museum of Natural History in Stockholm, along with colleagues from Egypt and Germany, we re-examined one of these species in a new study. In the 1920s, several fossils were collected from northeastern Egypt. These were found in a limestone rock, known as the Mokattam Formation, that had formed 45 million years ago in a shallow marine environment when sea levels were higher. This region was submerged at this time. These fossils, including a nearly complete skull, were described in 1927 as belonging to Tomistoma, because of their superficial resemblance to the living species, Tomistoma schlegelii. However, aided by the use of CT scanning, our team was able to identify several anatomical differences, including the presence of raised rims around the eye sockets, which are absent in Tomistoma. The Great Sphinx of Giza. Fernanda-Belen/Shutterstock The Mokattam Formation already has a legacy: 4,500 years ago, these rocks were used to carve the Great Sphinx of Giza. The gavial skull shares more than this origin story though. Just as the Sphinx is famously missing the tip of its nose, the fossil is also missing the tip of its snout. This coincidence led us to name the new crocodile Herugavialis cairensis after the Egyptian falcon-headed god Heru (also known as Horus), who is often thought to be the inspiration for the iconic Sphinx. Both northern Africa and southern Europe hosted a high diversity of gavials (and other crocodiles) during much of the last 80 million years, with these species thriving in the shallow, marine environments that covered much of the Mediterranean region at the time. Unlike living gavials, it is likely that some of these species could cross oceans. This diversity appears to have persisted through the devastating mass extinction that wiped out the dinosaurs, and probably fluctuated during alternating warmer and cooler intervals over the next 60 million years, tied to higher and lower sea levels, respectively. However, crocodiles disappeared from the Mediterranean region approximately 6 million years ago and never returned. Their demise coincides with an event known as the Messinian salinity crisis, when the Mediterranean essentially dried up as a result of being sealed off from the Atlantic Ocean. As the seawater became increasingly salty with the heightened evaporation of water, it would have become ever more intolerable to the animals inhabiting it, even those usually able to live in saltwater, leading to the loss of crocodiles and many other species. The signature of this event can still be observed today, with the Mediterranean Sea still much saltier than the oceans, and crocodiles entirely absent from this region. The remaining living gavials live far away from the Mediterranean, but the loss of the adaptations that would allow them to live in saltwater means that they would not be able to survive there regardless. Rapid and extreme changes in temperature, sea level, and aridification are critical components of the current climate emergency, and events such as the Messinian salinity crisis show that they can have a lasting impact on biodiversity, spanning millions of years. a0833c45fb9a0973: In 2015, biomedical entrepreneur Elizabeth Holmes was Silicon Valley's golden girl, lauded as the youngest and richest self-made female billionaire thanks to the company she founded, Theranos, which was valued at $9 billion at the height of its success. Then it all came crashing down when accusations of fraud surfaced about the company's signature blood-testing device, culminating in a sensational trial. Holmes is back in the headlines thanks to a new film, You Can See Everything, which depicts the final days before Holmes, having exhausted her appeals, went to prison. Co-directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, it's a surreal, absurdist piece that has largely been received with gushing enthusiasm and no small amount of hype, with some declaring it the best film of the year. A few contrarian voices have emerged over the past week with much-needed reality checks, but there's no denying the film is destined to be an awards-season darling.

Pardon me for joining the buzzkills, but I cannot in good conscience jump on the You Can See Everything bandwagon. Sure, it has its moments, and the second half is highly entertaining, but there's nothing here to warrant all the breathless hyperbole. For all their much-touted access, Oppenheim and Fielder have produced a surprisingly shallow film that runs in circles, yielding very little fresh or novel insight—into Holmes, personally, or much else.

edf030352b667085: GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are one of the biggest biotech breakthroughs of the last decade. But to some clinical psychologists, they can represent something more sinister—a potential trigger for eating disorders.

A new report suggests that the global incidence of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa shot up between 1990 and 2023—by a whopping 71%. By 2023, there were an estimated 18.1 million people living with one of these two disorders.

What’s worse is that the number is likely to be much higher than that once we factor in other eating disorders. And, disturbingly, those in the field are already starting to see GLP-1 weight-loss drugs exacerbating the issue.

Cheri Levinson is a clinical psychologist at the University of Louisville in Kentucky who has specialized in eating disorders for almost 20 years. She says she’s now seeing more patients with more severe symptoms than at any other time in her career, and that many of them are misusing GLP-1s. “This is the worst I’ve seen things,” she says.

Eating disorders are mental health conditions in which people’s eating behaviors impact their health. They include anorexia nervosa (defined by a fear of weight gain), bulimia nervosa (in which people binge and purge), binge eating disorder, and others.

It’s thought that some people have a genetic predisposition to certain eating disorders, but that some external factor is what triggers their onset. That might be stress, or social pressure to be skinny. Often, simply restricting food intake can trigger an eating disorder, says Levinson.

Eating disorders—along with the pressure to look thin—were already prevalent in the 1990s (the heroin chic era springs to mind). To find out how things might have changed since then, Ruhai Bai at the Children’s Hospital of Nanjing Medical University in China and his colleagues pulled together data from studies and surveys conducted on populations around the world. The team used statistical models to fill in any data gaps.

That research allowed the researchers to estimate the annual incidence of two eating disorders—anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa—for each of 204 countries and territories between 1990 and 2023. They also estimated the impact those disorders had on global health by calculating their disability-adjusted life years (one DALY represents a year of healthy life lost).

The findings, published in JAMA Psychiatry on Wednesday, are unsettling. Between 1990 and 2023, there was a 71% increase in the incidence of those two eating disorders, the team found. Those conditions had a huge impact on global health, too. In 2023, they “cost the world the equivalent of about 3.83 million years of healthy life,” says Bai.

Bai and his colleagues expect these figures to continue to rise. In 2023, an estimated 18.1 million people had either anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa; by 2050, the team predict, the two conditions could affect 21.8 million people.

It gets worse. Those two conditions represent less than half of all eating disorders, says Levinson, who was not involved in Bai’s study. The true impact of these disorders is “probably three times the rate that they’re reporting,” she says.
Bai and his colleagues didn’t explore the reasons for this rise (although Bai points out that it can’t be entirely explained by population growth). So how did we get here?

Social media may have played a role. “Social media comparisons, influencers, challenges, diet trends can all be precipitating … events for an eating disorder,” says Cynthia Bulik, a clinical psychologist at the University of North Carolina, who was not involved in the new study. Bulik has been studying and treating eating disorders since the early 1980s. “Between 1990 and 2023 there has clearly been an upsurge of those types of environmental exposures,” she says.

Many social media users are exposed to filtered and modified images of skinny influencers who may have undergone cosmetic surgery or extreme dieting and who are promoting “thinspiration” or “fitspiration” content. But users with eating disorders appear to be more likely to engage with this content—and to be fed more of it as a result.

When researchers at the University of Melbourne investigated this phenomenon a couple of years ago, they found that the algorithms of TikTok users with eating disorders delivered 4343% more “toxic eating disorder videos” than those of users who didn’t have the disorders. They also got more content focused on dieting or exercising. Many were fed over 1000 problematic videos per month. Bulik describes social media as “quicksand” for people with, or at risk of, eating disorders.

The covid-19 pandemic—and the social isolation that accompanied lockdowns—also appears to have contributed to the rise in eating disorders. Research conducted in 2021 found that the number of people hospitalized with eating disorders in the US doubled between 2018 and 2020.

Researchers don’t yet have good data on how trends in eating disorders might have progressed since 2023. But anecdotally, things seem to be getting even worse. “There are more eating disorders, more severe eating disorders… and we’re seeing earlier ages of onset,” says Levinson. “We’re seeing eight- and nine-year-olds with eating disorders.”
“From what I’m hearing and seeing, I am not going to be surprised if that number isn’t at least doubling again,” she adds.

Levinson particularly worries about the impact of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs, which have exploded in popularity in recent years. A Gallup survey conducted earlier this year suggested that 15% of Americans had used one of these drugs for weight loss. And they’re becoming more accessible—drug companies are working on new formulations that are both easier to take and more effective, and many people can buy versions of these drugs from compound pharmacies or dubious online sources.

In a small study published earlier this year, Levinson and her colleagues found that 30% of people with eating disorders had used GLP-1 drugs. The drugs might benefit some of those people. But 10% appeared to have misused the drugs. And Levinson thinks that figure is also an underestimate.

Levinson says she and her colleagues have seen children develop eating disorders after being prescribed GLP-1s for medical reasons. They’ve seen others—even children as young as 11—buy versions of these drugs over TikTok.

“We’re very concerned that GLPs will lead to even faster and more extreme weight loss in people with anorexia nervosa, and that patients will come to us in even more advanced stages of illness that become difficult to reverse,” says Bulik.

Both Bulik and Levinson are continuing to study the impacts of these drugs in eating disorders. In the meantime, both urge medical professionals to consider the risks GLP-1s might pose to people with those disorders. Bulik contributed to a set of research and clinical guidelines, published earlier this month, that recommends doctors screen for eating disorders before prescribing the drugs, for example. The guidelines also recommend more patient education and more robust monitoring of people who take GLP-1s.
If you think you or someone you know might have an eating disorder, you can find information and support at the National Eating Disorders Association.

5baff2e67cd0deb4: ‘Let us eat what we produce; that way, we all win’
Originally published on Global Voices
REB Lokal founder Rébetha Charles stands with a jar of peanut butter (manba lokal). Photo courtesy of Rébetha Charles, used with permission.

For several decades, due to the significant reduction of tariff barriers on foreign goods — particularly those from the United States and the Dominican Republic — Haiti has depended heavily on imported products for local consumption.

The arrangement began under various structural adjustment programmes that were initiated between 1994 and 1995, through agreements between the Haitian government and international financial institutions like the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank. Since then, imports have practically invaded the Haitian market, creating inequitable competition for local farmers who rely on subsistence agriculture and traditional, rudimentary equipment, and significantly weakening national production.

Complicating the economic reality is Haiti’s ongoing struggle with gang violence, political instability, and the absence of adequate infrastructure; yet, many Haitians continue to take on ambitious initiatives. Take Rébetha Charles, a 38-year-old woman entrepreneur. Originally from Jérémie, Charles studied agronomy, works in the Grand’Anse department in Haiti’s southern region, of which Jérémie is the capital, and created an agri-food enterprise called REB Lokal.
Rébetha Charles. Photo courtesy of Rébetha Charles, used with permission.

REB is a short form of her name; Lokal speaks to the pride inherent in making local products. Her company buys products from small farmers and, in its small manufacturing plant, transforms these local harvests into healthy, sustainable, tasty products.

In a WhatsApp interview, Charles says she is proud of a few key things. First, her company adds value. Through a manufacturing process that produces authentic, nutritious, and 100 percent local products, farmers have a much better guarantee of not losing their crops, whereas before, various obstacles, including spoilage, prevented them from selling their produce at market.

Charles explains that the REB Lokal project is an enterprise that transforms local agricultural products: “We work with a supplier network of almost 2,000 people, including agricultural producers and small traders. We have more than 20 employees, so we work every day to grow the project even more.”

Second, Charles is pleased with the company’s focus on providing safe, fresh food that meets modern food processing standards — its approach places value on Haitian culinary traditions to preserve the natural taste and nutritional value of local ingredients. Finally, REB Lokal makes a point of avoiding chemical additives and artificial ingredients, as part of its commitment to providing consumers with healthy, accessible, community-friendly food.

Charles didn’t initially see herself as an entrepreneur. Before she decided to enter the agro business, she was working at an international humanitarian organisation, but resigned because of a culture — fairly common in Haiti — of sexual harassment. “In Haiti,” she stresses, “a woman’s life is not easy when it comes to work. Instead of competence, sometimes there are other things they ask from us. Sometimes, some of us stand up and say, ‘No, we do not agree,’ because we went to school just like everyone else, got experience where we needed — and after that, there are things we choose not to do.”

That professional environment left her with “such a disgust for work” that, even though she had been offered other opportunities in bigger organisations, she decided to put everything on pause. Charles finally submitted her resignation letter on August 31, 2020, and launched the REB Lokal project the very next day.
Workers packaging chocolate balls at the factory. Photo courtesy of Rébetha Charles, used with permission.

It wasn’t easy for Charles, especially at the beginning. In an interview with Chef Cassy, she said she started the business doing papita — breadfruit and banana chips — but spent more than five months making it, every single day, without getting it right. It was only by the sixth month that the papita started coming out well, and she began selling it in supermarkets. After that, things started moving quickly; every day, customers would place more orders — not bad for a small business that began with about USD 8.50, selling papita.

The business has now evolved to the point where it offers a broad range of widely available products: “We sell [our products] in the Grand’Anse department, we sell them in the south, in the west, in several other departments in the country, and we also sell internationally in the United States and Canada.”
Everything has grown out of her core commitment to Haitian farmers by purchasing their crops, and encouraging Haitian consumers to eat local products:

Mwen panse li lè li tan pou peyizan yo kapab vann sa yap pwodui. Donk, mwen santi m toujou gen yon responsabilite depi m pase yon kote ki gen dennre, bagay nou yo kap fèt nan andeyò yo, mwen anvi fè yon bagay. Ann manje sa nou pwodui, ann manje sa nou fè. Sa ap pèmèt peyizan yo pa bezwen deplase kite lakay yo pou yo ale lòt kote; yo ka rete nan zòn yo, yap travay, n ap achte, n ap kondisyonnen, nap transfòme, ou menm wap konsome. Konsa, nou tout ap soti gayan, e nap gen yon lòt peyi, nap gen yon lòt kominite.

I think it is time for farmers to be able to sell what they produce. So, I always feel a responsibility whenever I pass by a place that has crops, or things made in the countryside; I want to do something. Let us eat what we produce, let us eat what we make. This will allow farmers to not need to leave their home to go somewhere else; they can stay in their area — they work, we buy, we process, we transform, and you consume. That way, we all win, and we will have another country; another community.

Inside REB Lokal’s processing facility feels different from what one would expect. There are production rooms, transformation rooms, and packaging rooms where employees work in white coats, hairnets, and gloves.
Customers inside the REB Lokal store looking at products. Photo courtesy of Rébetha Charles, used with permission.

There is also a shop front full of shelves with finished products — now much more diverse than just papita — displayed for sale. There are roasted peanuts, sakalapina (cornmeal with avocados), papita in both chicken and fish flavour, konparet (spiced ginger-coconut cake), corn chanchanm (traditional Haitian sweet, made from roasted corn and peanuts), honey, sugar cane syrup, chocolate powder and balls, cocoa butter, breadfruit, corn, cassava and plantain flour, baby food (made without chemicals under the supervision of paediatricians and nutritionists), alcoholic drinks, fruit juice, and castor oil.

To Rébetha Charles, who grew up in an idyllic rural community, the work of REB Lokal is close to her heart. Yet, running a business in an insecure country comes with its challenges. Gangs’ control of the main roads can make delivery slow and limit production, as the lack of access prevents products from reaching many communities. A true entrepreneur, Charles finds ways around such obstacles as best she can. She still believes that Haiti has a future, so she perseveres, believing the impossible can become possible through vision and sheer willpower.
Written by Jude Pierre Louis

95fcfb629e87abc5: At the end of Star Trek: Generations (1994), surveying the wreckage of the crashed USS Enterprise he captained for nearly a decade, Jean-Luc Picard (Patrick Stewart) muses to his first officer, William Riker (Jonathan Frakes): … time is a companion that goes with us on the journey, reminds us to cherish every moment, because it will never come again. What we leave behind is not as important as how we’ve lived. Smiling, he quips to Riker, “After all, Number One, we’re only mortal.” Passing away this week at 86 years old, we are sadly reminded of that mortality with the death of Sir Patrick Stewart: actor, dramaturge, Shakespearean exemplar, mutant professor, and distinguished Starfleet captain. From humble beginnings Born in Mirfield, England, in 1940, Stewart grew up poor during the worst days of the second world war. He found his calling to theatre as a child, thanks to a keen-eyed English teacher and a copy of Shakespeare’s plays. He left school at 15 to become a working actor in community theatre. His extraordinary talent would lead to a stay at the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, membership with the Royal Shakespeare Company, and a host of acclaimed theatre performances. Despite the many screen roles for which Stewart would later be known, his Shakespearean roots are indelibly intertwined with almost every performance he gave. They would also give him – and many of us – something to lighten the load of COVID lockdowns. Stewart used social media in 2020 to read the internet a Shakespearean sonnet each day, later turning his delightful orations into an audiobook. For most, Stewart will best be remembered as a kaleidoscopic titan of film and television. Beginning as a firefighter on the British soap opera Coronation Street in 1967, Stewart’s illustrious screen career spanned more than 50 years and a vast array of roles. To name only a few, he was: a flamboyant interior designer a stoic Atreides weapon master in a screen adaptation of the Dune books the irreverent king of England a foul-mouthed CIA deputy director an enigmatic cult leader, and a megalomaniacal egg-alien overlord. Two key roles From his storied body of work, two roles loom largest. He was the telepathic mutant and academic Charles Xavier of the X-Men film series – a role he played for more than 25 years, including a posthumous appearance in Avengers: Doomsday (released this December). As Professor X, Stewart embodied a beloved superhero with paternal warmth and secretive, calculating intellect. He was an empathetic leader of a team of extraordinary people who had been shunned, threatened and harmed by the world for their differences. One cannot help but think this role enabled Stewart to channel much of his real-life allyship with marginalised queer communities and his support for survivors of domestic violence (which was based on his own childhood experiences). In this role, Stewart acted alongside his long-time friend Sir Ian McKellen, who played the mutant antagonist and master of metal Magneto. Ironically, McKellen had once warned Stewart not to forsake the theatre for the screen, advising that a career in film and television would go nowhere. Stewart and McKellen’s endearing friendship and acclaimed X-Men performances became the stuff of internet legend, particularly when McKellen officiated Stewart’s wedding to US singer Sunny Ozell in 2013. Stewart’s work in Star Trek as Jean-Luc Picard – captain (later admiral) of the USS Enterprise – is equally revered. As Stewart’s first major American television role, he took the captain’s chair in Star Trek: The Next Generation in 1987. He would eventually appear in seven seasons, four theatrical films, and the recent sequel series Star Trek: Picard. Despite initial reservations – including an infamous on-set incident where he stoically told his rambunctious Next Generation colleagues that “we are not here to have fun” – Stewart later embraced the role of Picard. He will be remembered as one of Star Trek’s most acclaimed and legendary performers. As Picard, Stewart created a potent role model in a franchise focused on an inclusive, utopian future. Stewart’s Picard was a respected leader, intergalactic explorer, keen orator, Shakespeare enthusiast, thoughtful diplomat, archaeology aficionado, and prolific tea-drinker – as he and other characters famously said, “tea, Earl Grey, hot”. This captain was an inspiring beacon of hope, curiosity and discovery. He advocated Starfleet ideals of exploration and community, but encouraged his crew – and, by extension, all of us – to seek out knowledge. He urged us all to solve problems with rationality and empathy, and work toward a better future for humanity. An enduring inspiration Like many others who grew up in the 1990s with Picard on the television, I still find the character’s ethos and Stewart’s performance have a profound impact on me as a scholar and educator who strives to live and teach by those ideals. Were it not for the inspiration Picard and Stewart provided me as a child, I may not have become an academic. Stewart lived the kind of important life that Picard would admire, and leaves behind a cherished body of work, as well as a legacy of dedicated social advocacy. Now, he boldly goes where you and I have not gone before.
