74a19f23c8f72af9: Whenever you scan the headlines, a heart-breaking reality stares back: several Muslim-majority nations are trapped in devastating wars and armed conflicts. These crises range from full-scale international warfare to intense civil strife and localised insurgencies.

Tragically, from Iran, Iraq and Syria to Yemen, Saudi Arabia, Sudan, Somalia, Pakistan and Afghanistan, Muslims are often locked in conflict with other Muslims. This deep friction naturally prompts a difficult, uncomfortable question: can the Muslim world ever truly achieve unity?
On paper, the global ummah is bound by the most foundational of principles: belief in one God and the guidance of the Quran.
Yet, the reality on the ground is starkly fractured. It is easy for casual observers to look at this discord and assume that Islam itself is the root problem.

But if you pull back the curtain, it becomes clear that these conflicts are rarely about theology. Instead, they are driven by the exact same catalysts that spark wars anywhere else on earth: politics, money and human greed.
The truth is, most internal conflicts in the Muslim world are old-fashioned power struggles. Factions, regimes and politicians compete for control, territory and resources, plain and simple.

Consider the Sunni-Shia split. While it dates back to a seventh-century political disagreement over who should succeed Prophet Muhammad, these communities lived side-by-side in relative peace for centuries.
The divide only becomes weaponised today because authoritarian regimes and militant groups exploit it to manufacture an "us versus them" mentality.

Leaders routinely wrap their political ambitions in religious rhetoric because it remains a highly effective tool to manipulate the masses, justify violence and safeguard their power. This has been the norm in many failed Muslim states.

This dynamic plays out on a massive scale through regional chess games. Major powers like Saudi Arabia and Iran have long been locked in a geopolitical rivalry, turning vulnerable nations like Yemen and Syria into proxy battlegrounds.

Compounding the issue is that many modern borders in the region are fragile, artificially cutting across deep ethnic and tribal lines. When a central government collapses – as seen in Iraq or Libya – it creates a power vacuum that local armed groups immediately resort to violence to fill.
Coincidentally, many of these conflict zones are endowed with rich oil and gas reserves, making them highly attractive to foreign powers.

These natural resources are a double-edged sword: while they should guarantee prosperity, mismanagement leaves many states impoverished, even as the wealth draws predatory external interests. When warring domestic factions face defeat, they readily invite foreign intervention. Superpowers then step in under the guise of aid, though their true drivers are their own economic and strategic interests in the region.
Ultimately, a shared religious identity is not enough to sustain stability when states are hollowed out from within.

You cannot talk about unity without addressing daily survival. When high poverty, a lack of economic opportunity, systemic corruption and oppressive governance collide, they create a recipe for desperation. If citizens cannot build a decent life through peaceful or democratic means, sub-state conflicts and insurgencies become inevitable.

The path forward for the Muslim world is about repairing broken systems. Unity will only shift from a theological ideal to a political reality when leaders begin prioritising stable governance, economic fairness and basic human dignity over their political survival.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

ccbf2f56503f85ee: It seems like another season, but it was early this month when Anfield was meant to be the bear pit that would maul and then spit out the bad boys of Manchester City.

It was the first game after their guilty verdict and we all know how it went. Forgotten is that Liverpool gave City as good as they got before two harsh yellow cards to Ryan Gravenberch turned it all around.The bear was declawed and Liverpool’s 10 men couldn’t live with City, who ran out comfortable 3-0 winners.

That the Reds matched them for an hour didn’t fit the narrative of City defiance. Owners fiercely maintaining their innocence, players with a siege mentality, fans with inflatable bananas… all wallowing in victimhood.
They managed to win their first seven games, but then United stole their thunder with yet another crisis of their own.
After this Mancunian monopoly of headlines, it is time to go back to Liverpool, not least because Arsenal are the next visitors.
Smarting from their loss to Fleetwood, the champions will be a good test of where Liverpool are in the pecking order right now.
For there is the unmistakable whiff of meaningful momentum about them.
The roar that greeted Wesley Fofana’s penalty miss in midweek was more like the Kop we knew.
It was only a shoot-out, only the League Cup, and there were extra decibels for Chelsea, but it resonated.
Not ‘off the Richter’ like the Kop’s deafening best, but it saluted another win, their fifth in a row since the loss to City.
Two were in the Champions League (against Villarreal and LASK) that helped them to third place in the table with a 100% record.
Two in the EPL against hard-to-beat Brentford and Brighton, and now this to reach the last eight of the Carabao Cup.
And there was the added satisfaction of beating two former employees.
Xabi Alonso, who had been warmly welcomed as Bayer Leverkusen boss, was made aware what a cardinal sin it is to join Chelsea, at least in the eyes of the Kop.
But it was former skipper Jordan Henderson, who came in for most of the stick.
“Hendo’s” sterling service in Jurgen Klopp’s greatest sides was brusquely erased from memory by the sight of him in Chelsea blue.
Besides being loftily placed in three competitions, there are many reasons for optimism around the Reds right now.
The rebuild is not yet finished, but there has been unexpected progress.
Top of the list is that the stalled £400m strike force is firing.
Even the most recent – and expensive – addition, Bradley Barcola, is showing why the Reds paid PSG £125m for him after a sluggish start.
His pace is electric and although he’s very different to Mo Salah, his versatility is giving the attack more flexibility.
But the biggest improvement has come in the form of Alexander Isak, who had such a horrendous start to his Anfield career.
The Swede is now looking more like the player they broke the club record for. Cody Gakpo is also more of a force than last season, having brought his international form to the EPL.
This leaves Florian Wirtz. To say that Iraola is getting a tune out of the £116m man may still require a hearing aid.
He’s had better moments but is still way short of the little maestro they thought they were getting.
Then there’s the waspish Munoz buzzing across the entire attack, and it’s no wonder with assets like these, the Reds are mostly on the front foot.
Coupled with the ‘coming out’ of Rio Ngumoha ahead of schedule, and the teenager’s ability to flourish on both wings, too, manager Andoni Iraola has the sort of headache he doesn’t mind.

He’s been rewarded for his faith in youth by the emergence of Trey Nyoni too, and in a position where the club offered £100m fees in vain a couple of seasons ago. Ngumoha and Nyoni, a magical pair and money-savers too.
Let’s not forget Hugo Ekitike, who hopes to return from his ruptured Achilles by the end of the year.
The good news for Liverpool is that the Frenchman, who was by far the best signing of the previous transfer window, is already back working on the ball.
With that type of injury, there’s no guarantee he’ll be as lightning-fast as he once was, but his recovery is on course.
If he does return to his old form, Liverpool could boast the best attack in the business.
If attack is Liverpool’s forte, there’s encouragement all over the park. Ronald Araujo has been a masterly piece of business and gone from stopgap to cult hero playing out of position.
Whatever Barcelona want for the Uruguayan must be paid, according to his adoring fans.
Jeremy Jacquet has also made a brilliant start and looks to be Virgil van Dijk’s successor already.
And Giorgio Mamardashvili may have finally won the sceptics over with his showing against Chelsea.
The prevailing view is that Iraola has done well to fit them into the jigsaw so quickly and return Liverpool to something more like the heavy metal style of Klopp.
A slow starter – he went 10 games at Bournemouth before claiming his first win – and with the huge step up in size of club, it was felt he might need a few months to get it right.
But to have the team where they are before the end of October suggests he could become a major managerial figure.
Having come out on top – albeit narrowly – over one of his former Basque colleagues in Alonso, he now faces another in Mikel Arteta.
It’s too soon to talk of a title challenge, but if he can find a way to beat the depth of the Gunners, it won’t mean Liverpool are back, but that they are coming back.
That’s pretty good given the upheaval the club has been through.

ff28614e0b2a21a4: ‘No independent body regularly monitored developments in prisons and communicat’d this information to the public using data.
Originally published on Global Voices
Screenshot from Prison Agenda‘s Substack page, used with permission.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

In Turkey, a team of two journalists and human rights activists launched a digital publication, Prison Agenda, to report on what is happening inside the country’s prisons and prison system, information that is often hidden from the Turkish public and the world.

As the Nordic Monitor noted in 2025, Turkey’s prison population has reached an unprecedented level. Citing figures from the Directorate General of Prisons and Houses of Detention, the website states that as of September 1, 2025, Turkish prisons hold 419,194 individuals. This includes 356,710 convicted prisoners and 62,484 people in pretrial detention. The figure exceeds the official capacity of 295,000 and places immense strain on the country’s penal system.

Le Monde also wrote in 2026 that a commissioned report on prison conditions among Council of Europe member states showed that France and Turkey each had 131 inmates for every 100 places, making them the two most overcrowded prison systems.

For the relatives of people in prison, as well as for national and international human rights organizations and agencies, the information provided by the Prison Agenda publication can be vital. A similar organization — Russia Behind Bars — used to work in Russia. While it did not function exclusively as a publication, it received letters from prisoners and their relatives, published news about torture or other human rights violations, and reported how the prison population had been drafted, in the hundreds of thousands, to fight Russia’s war with Ukraine. Unfortunately, it had to shut down its work within Russia because of the regime’s prosecution, but it continues to inform from abroad.

Civil society organizations, such as the publication about Prisons and Prisoners, are vital to the country and the world; they need to continue their important work within one of the most opaque systems in the world.
Global Voices interviewed one of Prison Agenda’s founder, Ahmet Kavruk, by email.
GV: Please tell us about your organization, and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Spark project?

Ahmet Kavruk (AK): Prison Agenda is a digital publication that covers data on Turkey’s prisons, legislative changes relating to prisons, and human rights violations within them. It is guided by an independent, rights-focused approach to journalism.

We launched in January 2026. Our aim is to make the often complicated and scattered information about prisons more accessible to the public by presenting it in a clear and understandable way, and to highlight the human stories behind the statistics.

Shortly after launching in January, we reached a crossroads. We could either continue as a passion project, publishing solely in Turkish, which would be easier to sustain, but would not fulfil our potential, or evolve into a publishing model that would require more intensive work, but enable us to reach a wider audience.

It was precisely at this decision-making stage that we came across the Digital Spark call for proposals. It was one of the few support programmes capable of creating space for initiatives working in specific and often overlooked fields, such as prisons. We, therefore, drew up a plan and, should we be accepted into Digital Sparks, began to focus on the question, ‘How can we grow the Prison Agenda?’

We were particularly impressed by Digital Spark’s approach, which focuses on amplifying the voices of marginalized groups and strengthening civic participation. The fact that the project’s core objectives aligned so closely with our own area of work was a decisive factor in our decision to join the programme.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

AK: We are currently a team of two. We are both individuals with over 10 years’ experience working and producing within the prison sector in various capacities. We were aware of the growing problems in Turkey’s prisons. Through our voluntary work, professional lives and social networks, we have been trying to raise awareness of these issues.

However, our work in this field revealed not only these problems, but also a significant shortcoming. No independent body regularly monitored developments in prisons and communicated this information to the public using data. The data was scattered, technical and often difficult to access. Meanwhile, media interest tended to intensify only when there was new legislation or a high-profile incident.

Drawing on our background in journalism and our experience in human rights monitoring, we believed we could address this gap. We, therefore, launched Prison Agenda, aiming to present existing information to the public in a clear, accessible, rights-focused manner.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?

AK: The most significant change for us during this project was launching our bilingual publications. By switching to English, we were able to reach beyond our existing Turkish audience and connect with a very different group of readers. The feedback from this new audience further strengthened our belief in the project’s potential.

While we initially had just one e-newsletter, we diversified our publications over time, increasing our regular e-newsletters to three. Today, Prison Agenda has evolved from a publication that shares news into a comprehensive digital media organisation that produces investigative reports, data analyses, data visualisations, thematic content, and opinion pieces.

This transformation aligns with our initial project goals of bilingual publishing and data-driven content production. In the first six months, our Turkish and English newsletters reached a total of 435 subscribers.
AK: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.

AK: While our Turkish-language publications are mainly followed by the press, legislators and civil society, we have noticed that our English-language publications are attracting the attention of diplomatic missions from various countries and international-level bureaucrats. This was a significant development for us as it created an opportunity to raise awareness of prison issues in Turkey within a wider international network.

Throughout the project, we received collaboration proposals from different organisations and groups. The number of news articles citing our data and content increased, raising Prison Agenda's profile. Additionally, we started providing advice on data, sources and content to journalists reporting on prisons.

This has ensured that the information we produce is not limited to our own readers, but is made available within a wider ecosystem. We hope the network of readers and stakeholders established by Prison Agenda will help to raise awareness of prisoners’ rights and the need for humane prison conditions. The project’s aim was, indeed, to strengthen civil oversight and accountability by making information more accessible.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?

AK: Prisons are, by their very nature, a rather closed field of work, with limited overlap with many other areas of rights. For this reason, we are not always able to collaborate with other civil society organisations.

One of the most significant opportunities that Digital Sparks has created for us is the chance to share a space with different civil society organisations and learn about their work first-hand. We have met groups working on issues outside our own field, developing different methods, and those who are just starting out. These encounters have enabled us to share knowledge and view our own work from an outside perspective.

One of the most significant realisations for us during this process was that civil society is much larger and broader than we had previously realised. Because Prison Agenda works in a very specific field, we realised that we were sometimes limited to our immediate circle. However, Digital Sparks showed us that this field is much broader and that there are far more areas where different struggles can intersect.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

AK: Digital Spark was the first support we received. Although we had previously been involved in various projects as part of a team, this was the first time we had been part of a project where the full responsibility rested directly with us. For this reason, it was also a new learning experience for us.

This was actually the part that challenged us the most. We learnt that a project is not limited to simply producing content and activities; it also requires managing its budget, administrative processes, reporting and responsibilities.

One of the most tangible things we learnt during this process was financial reporting. While our previous experience in this area was limited, carrying out the reporting processes required by the project provided us with valuable practical experience.

Consequently, Digital Sparks was not merely a project through which we developed Prison Agenda’s publishing capacity; it was also a significant experience in a small team transforming into a structure capable of standing on its own two feet, managing its responsibilities, and planning for the future.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

AK: Although we’re a very new organisation, we’re just as eager and enthusiastic. We have many options before us that could take us in different directions, as well as ideas that we’re keen to develop.

For example, we’re currently refining a public prison database project, and we’re also preparing to run a training course on prison journalism in the new year. We have a wide variety of datasets at our disposal that we want to make accessible to a wider audience. In the long term, we also plan to increase the number of areas we cover and deepen the content we produce in these fields.

We believe that we have not yet reached our natural limits. The digital capacity we have developed through Digital Sparks has opened up significant scope for us to expand these limits. In the near future, we intend to use the knowledge and experience we have gained to prioritise our readers, understand their requirements, and integrate their feedback into our editorial strategy.

Our aim is to transform the Prison Agenda into a structure that produces more content and enables more people to access information on prisons, bringing together different stakeholders in the process.
Written by Daria Dergacheva
6d0c83d2b64fda06: So now “gomen” employees can’t use Waze, the popular navigation app. This is a truly funny-but-not-funny situation. Somebody must have invoked some scary natural security scenarios about the dangers this US-owned, Israeli-founded company poses to our nation.

Here’s why this isn’t trivial. A company I once worked in experienced a massive computer hack. Experts from overseas were brought in to investigate. Panic reigned at the top. What I remember most from the briefings by the experts was the experts saying that everyone in the industry has either been hacked, or has been hacked and didn’t know about it.
I felt rather naked knowing somebody somewhere has a lot of detailed info about me, even if the only juicy details were about at which street corners were the best char kuey teow stalls.

It turns out one of the easiest ways to hack a human target and steal information more critical than just the locations of char kuey teow stalls is to hack their co-workers, assistants, family, friends, or football buddies and not necessarily the targets themselves.

That’s not as exciting as what happens in a James Bond movie, but rather the more plodding and low-key style of a John le Carre novel. One way or another, though, with enough cunning and guile and resources, people can find out a lot of things that others would prefer left hidden.
Why they snoop

Digital surveillance has become a massive business as well as a national security tool – checking what, when, and where we went or bought or spoke, as well as where we browsed on the internet and what social media content we generated or consumed. Artificial Intelligence has made it all easier.

The purpose of all this snooping is often just to sell you stuff, but increasingly it’s also becoming a way to control people and societies and even conduct warfare - as in the case of Elon Musk personally throttling his Starlink and Starshield services to Ukraine, thus harming Ukraine’s war efforts. That was one of the reasons many European nations are building digital alternatives to what Musk and the US offer, a trend that’s only gaining speed.

They're not just looking for alternatives for the latest digital stuff, either. Many nations have begun cutting off links they have relied on for decades with nations they no longer deem reliable for software, data centres and cloud services, computer chips, critical scientific research etc.

The big powers, especially the US and China, have been manipulating each other and others for years. China, which is fast catching up with the West in digital capabilities, looks safer today by comparison, but certainly they’re playing this same game too.
The Malaysian way

After banning Waze, Malaysia took the obvious next step by recommending the use of a home-grown alternative called TuJu, an app apparently running off the same backbone as Waze, but hosting all the captured data in some secure local data centres.

I haven’t downloaded TuJu, or used it in any shape or form. I know the locations of the best char kuey teow stalls by heart and can get there come rain or shine or traffic jams or anything else, up to a haze API level of 200. I'm fine, thank you.

Of course, we’re going about this the typical time-honoured Malaysia-Boleh way. First the government declares a critical national objective – industrialisation, national security, safety, pandemic response, etc.—and then, lo and behold, there appears a ready-made Malaysian solution!

We’ve seen this all before. The secrecy behind such decisions is often at a high level. Don’t forget even a toll highway concession agreement between the government and private parties is considered a sensitive national secret. Malaysia Boleh often actually means Malaysia Tak Boleh for the rest of us.

What little I know about TuJu doesn’t give me much confidence. The names associated with it seems to be the usual cast of characters of door openers to lucrative government contracts and not quite young genius alumni of the world’s top research universities or tech corporations or research institutions.
The other way

When it comes to high-tech, especially digital ones, I’m sceptical of people of my age and generation. We’re often the generation that calls AI “A-One”, as a famous episode involving a US cabinet member – handling education of all things! – hilariously reveals.

I wouldn’t even trust myself, even if I’m actually AI personified! The only good thing I can design and develop would be maps on napkins about the aforementioned char kuey teow locations which are, if I’m honest, not that great, after all.

But I’ve thought about making my own digital contributions during these critical times because it seems any old fogey can do it. I plan to release TuDia, an app that points out where you need to go; TangTu and TangNi to tell you when you’ve arrived here or there, and TuPun and TuLah to argue or commiserate with you when you’re lost.

And why not? The needs are real and urgent. All I’m asking for is complete access to all Malaysians’ personal data with a promise not to sell it to Elon Musk or Israel under a 50-year exclusive agreement that’ll be classified as a national secret forever.
Ah, silly dreams. I think all that’ll happen to me is, as Penangites like to say, that I’ll Pi Mai Pi Mai Tang Tu Jugak.
Which may work out as the name of another app that describes life in Malaysia Bolehland.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
4e776a100c80e4cc: Sebenarnya saya malas nak tulis pasal bendera terbalik lagi sebab dah banyak kali tulis. Tetapi, apabila saya terbaca tentang bendera Malaysia yang ‘sengaja’ diterbalikkan, maka saya rasa terpanggil untuk menjelaskan beberapa perkara tentang sikap serta pandangan saya tentang Jalur Gemilang kita. Kemudian saya rasa terpanggil juga untuk mengingatkan orang muda kita supaya jangan galak sangat pasal freedom of speech and expression sampai tak kenal saudara, keluarga dan ibu bapa.

Tergempar kita membaca pasal satu kumpulan yang dikatakan orang Malaysia di Australia telah mempamerkan kepada awam bendera Malaysia yang terbalik dan ada kata tercarik-carik. Kumpulan ini dipercayai rakyat Malaysia dari Sabah dan Sarawak yang menggelarkan diri mereka Sabah dan Sarawak Keluar Malaysia (SSKM). Perbuatan ini saya anggap ‘agak berat’ dan perlu suatu komentar terhadapnya dengan cara baik dan beradab daripada bidasan dan cemuhan media sosial yang tidak terkawal.

Pertama sekali saya ingin mengucapkan terima kasih kepada menteri di Jabatan Perdana Menteri dari Sabah, Mustapha Sakmud. Beliau memberi teguran dan nasihat yang beradab dan bernas maka saya harap oang di Australia itu dengar baik-baik. Jangan terlajak kata nanti masa depan binasa. Sekarang mungkin gagah di Australia tetapi sepandai tupai melompat silap hari bulan kena balik negara sendiri semula. Siapa tahu nasib kita kecuali tuhan. Jadi, kalau kita dah ada rumah dan keluarga di sesuatu corner of the world, jangan cepat-cepat perlekeh, nanti kita juga yang terpaksa mencarinya di akhir hayat.

Isu bendera yang lalu bagi saya cukup jelas semuanya tidak disengajakan. Dari Editor Sin Chew kepada Kementerian Pendidikan, kesilapan Umno dan PAS Terengganu dan juga ‘Apek Tua’ di Pulau Pinang semuanya not on purpose. Ada yang tersilap dan ada yang cuai terlepas pandang sebab tidak pergi semak kerja suruhan kita sendiri. Saya telah mencadangkan supaya kita semua maaf-maafkan dan let it go tetapi jangan ulang lagi. Walaupun ada juga orang Umno yang suka mendabik dada sebagai paling patriotik mencemuh, menghina dan mengugut pihak yang tersilap pasang bendera, saya selalu menasihatkan individu tersebut supaya bertenang dan jangan cuba cari modal politik seperti ini.

Namun demikian, orang itu mendapat banyak political mileage dengan sandiwaranya. Saya tidak nampak pula beliau bising pasal bendera terbalik yang disengajakan orang Sabah dan Sarawak di Australia. Mungkin sebab Sabah dan Sarawak bakal sebagai king makers dalam PRU16. Kalau Onn Hafiz Ghazi gunakan istilah selective prosecution kini kita lihat ada parti yang buat selective criticism dalam isu bendera terbalik dengan sengaja.

Kembali kita kepada orang Sabah dan Sarawak di Australia ini, bagaimana kita nak nasihatkan mereka selain daripada apa yang dikatakan menteri di Jabatan Perdana Menteri itu? Biar saya guna analogi keluarga saya sebagai nasihat dan renungan untuk hidup berkeluarga. Sabah, Sarawak dan Semenanjung adalah sebuah keluarga dari aspek politik kenegaraan. Sabah dan Sarawak telah bersama Semenanjung Tanah Melayu selama 63 tahun. Umur saya sekarang 64 tahun. Saya mempunyai seorang isteri, lima orang anak, tiga orang menantu dan empat orang cucu. Ada tiga perkara penting dalam kita hidup berkeluarga.

Pertama, jangan sekali-kali guna perkataan cerai, nyah atau get out of the family. Kalau sebolehnya jangan langsung terkeluar kata-kata itu sehingga kita menghembus nafas terakhir di dunia ini. Walau apa perit sekali pun we do not say those words. Kata pepatah Melayu air yang dicincang tidak akan putus. Wise Malays. Melayu lama memang cerdik, tetapi Melayu baharu nampak terlalu gopoh-gapah. Tuhan telah menyatukan saya dan isteri. Selepas itu tuhan kurniakan kami tiga anak perempuan dan dua anak lelaki. Akhir sekali tuhan kurniakan kami semua empat orang cucu daripada perkahwinan anak-anak perempuan kami. Anak lelaki dua orang masih eligible kalau ada yang nak apply. Memang semua perkahwinan antara dua orang manusia berbeza akan ada isu, krisis dan macam-macam cabaran. Looking back semua cabaran itu 99% adalah dari diri kita sendiri dan bukan pun pasal orang lain buat. Sungguh. Blaming others for out own shortcoming is the easiest thing in the world. Jadi, kena refleksi dalaman dulu sebelum mengata salah orang ini dan orang itu. Apabila saya sakit jantung, sakit darah perut dan melalui severe panic disorder, isteri saya was by my side every time. Ada ketika yang kita tak berduit hingga kena pinjam abang sendiri atau minta anak buat loan. Itu semua lumrah hidup. We need family. Siapa lagi yang nak tolong.

Kedua, saya membina rumah di Kajang sebagai a refuge untuk semua anak saya. Saya dah siapkan konsep lima ‘studio apartmen’ yang lengkap dengan tandas, dapur, living room dan tempat tidur selesa serta aircond setiap bilik. Saya kata kalau kamu bergaduh dengan suami atau isteri you can come back and cool off di Kajang. Saya tahu berdasarkan pengalaman saya dan isteri, you cannot avoid conflicts jadi kita kena manage ia dengan menyediakan alternative refuge dan juga tempat untuk mereka mengadu. Saya dan isteri selalu mendengar keluhan anak-anak perempuan tentang suami mereka dan selalu kami mengajukan kesabaran dan pengalaman kami sendiri. Jangan cepat kita bercerai-berai atau mengadu domba sama ada dalam keluarga manusia atau keluarga negara. We can always manage whatever conflict kalau kita tidak burn the bridge dengan sesiapa.

Ketiga adalah tempat kami sediakan untuk cucu. Cucu adalah kurniaan tuhan yang amat penting bagi kehidupan kami semua. Saya sebagai ‘atuk’ dan isteri sebagai ‘nenek’ menjadikan rumah di Kajang sebagai resort bila hujung minggu dan di hari-hari cuti sekolah panjang di mana papa dan mama dua-dua bekerja di pejabat masing-masing. Saya tidak suka cucu saya ditinggalkan bertiga tanpa penyeliaan orang dewasa. Ada juga keadaan di mana bila krisis keluarga berlaku, mereka boleh menetap secara indefinitely di Kajang sehingga krisis berlalu. Seperti juga sesebuah negara, kalau kita mempunyai krisis di tempat tinggal di luar negara maka ke Malaysia jugalah kita pulang. Maka itu jangan senang-senang menolak negara atau menyisihkannya hanya kerana satu dua isu yang boleh diselesaikan dengan masa dan hikmah.

Sebagai mesej politik, kita semua ada negara dan ada keluarga dalam negara itu. Kita semua rakyat Malaysia di Semenanjung, Sabah dan Sarawak. Ia suatu gagasan penting bagi kita semua. Memang akan sentiasa ada konflik atau isu kaum, agama, politik dan sebeban lagi tetapi jika kita teguh dalam satu famili dan ada tempat untuk berlabuh maka kedua-duanya adalah important asset bagi kita. Menterbalikkan dan mencarik bendera negara dengan sengaja adalah suatu perkara yang cukup berat bagi saya. Ia sama dengan beberapa mahasiswa yang bakar gambar perdana menteri yang saban hari bekerja kuat. Itu mungkin budaya Barat atau Australia. Mungkin kumpulan tersebut hendak bakar, carik atau menterbalikkan bendera Australia pula di bawah freedom of expression di lain hari pula? Apa makna loyalty to family dan nation kalau begitu. Apa makna perbincangan dan bertolak ansur dalam hubungan antara manusia kalau jambatan dibakar terlebih dulu? Jambatan yang runtuh tidak boleh memanfaatkan sesiapa yang mungkin ada solusi baharu di masa hadapan.
Renung-renungkanlah pepatah Melayu agar tidak membakar kelambu sebab seekor nyamuk yang dimarahkan.

cfed78c7b30043db: President Donald Trump has declared the imports of foreign-made factory robots to be a national security threat—ordering new US negotiations with trading partners while holding out the possibility of imposing new tariffs on such robot imports in the future.

Issued on October 28, Trump’s presidential proclamation represents heightened government scrutiny of foreign-made industrial robots that could complicate the manufacturing operations of major US corporations that rely on such robots. Those companies include Detroit automakers General Motors and Ford, electric vehicle manufacturer Tesla, and aerospace and defense giants like Boeing and Lockheed Martin.

Trump’s proclamation describes industrial robots and machinery as being crucial for producing US military weapon systems along with representing a “driving force” behind all critical infrastructure sectors within the US economy. 028d5ff4b1d516d0: An Exile Hub fellow shares their personal experiences and reflections
Originally published on Global Voices
Image from Exile Hub. Used with permission.

Exile Hub is one of Global Voices’ partners in Southeast Asia, emerging in response to the 2021 coup in Myanmar, and focusing on empowering journalists and human rights defenders. This article by a fellow of Exile Hub was published on August 15, 2026, and an edited version is republished under a content partnership agreement.
“Can I keep doing this work?”
I have asked myself that question more times than I can count.
When I first entered journalism as a young person, I was full of energy, conviction, and dreams. I believed journalism was a way to uncover the truth and to make sure people’s voices were heard.
Four years later, I began to realize that somewhere along the way, I was slowly losing parts of myself.
When I was 19, I never imagined that the career I chose would become both my livelihood and one of the reasons the road home would feel so far away.

In the early days of the 2021 revolution in Myanmar, I took part in protests. As the security situation deteriorated, I had to leave home. Eventually, I found myself in Mae Sot, a small town along the Thai–Myanmar border. There, I was fortunate to have the opportunity to study journalism for free.

I had loved writing since I was young. I started with short news pieces, then moved on to feature stories and video reporting, and eventually became a news presenter. I was proud to call myself a journalist. I was so proud, in fact, that I never used a pen name. I reported under my real name.
One of the first lessons I learned in journalism was simple: don’t put your own emotions into the story. But over time, I learned something else. Journalists are human too.
When other people’s pain becomes part of you
Sometimes I would call a source for an interview and listen as they described what had happened to them. Their pain would stay with me.
My responsibility was to listen carefully and then find the words to make their experiences visible to others. But sometimes, carrying their stories felt like carrying the pain twice.
After some interviews, I would put down my phone, open my laptop, and stare at the screen. No words would come.
I remember once speaking with a source just before mealtime. My stomach told me I was hungry, but after hearing their story, there was a heaviness in my chest, and I could not eat.
As these experiences accumulated, something began to change.
Eventually, I stopped crying.
I could finish an interview and immediately continue with the next task. But it wasn’t because the stories no longer affected me.
I had simply become numb.

And that numbness slowly changed me without my realizing it. I became tired more easily. I became irritable. I overthought things. My mood sank, and even my relationships with other people began to suffer.
Yet there was something strange about all of this.
On the days when I picked up my camera bag, carried my tripod, and went out into the field, some of that exhaustion disappeared.
Walking along windy roads, meeting people and listening to their lives, I would suddenly remember:
I still love this work.
And that’s why I couldn’t quite let it go.
When passion is not enough
COVID-19 and Myanmar’s political upheaval interrupted my education. Journalism became my livelihood, and surviving from one day to the next left little space to think seriously about my own future.
Eventually, one question began following me almost every day: What will become of me?
I became afraid that nothing would.
At the same time, media organizations were losing funding. Programs were closing. Journalists were losing their jobs.
When one of the programs I worked for ended, I became unemployed for around seven months.
It was one of the hardest periods of my life.
I told myself that if I could not find another job in journalism within a little over a year, I would change careers completely.
Fortunately, I eventually found my way back, working again as both a reporter and news presenter.
I continue because I genuinely love this work.
But love alone does not make the realities of life in exile easier. The income is not always enough to build a stable life.
And perhaps the hardest part is this:
On the days when I desperately want to go home, I cannot.
Even if I cannot return myself, I wish I could bring my family to visit me. But financially, that is not always possible either.
I want to see the people I love. I want to eat my mother’s cooking. I miss the smell of home.
Most of all, I miss my mother.
She raised me by herself, and as she grows older, I want to be able to care for her in return. One of my deepest fears is that something will happen to her before I have the chance to see her again.
That distance makes an already exhausting life in exile even heavier.
When the mind begins to affect the body
At one point, I tried counseling.
But each session cost more than THB 800 (USD 24). I could not afford to continue for the long term, so eventually I stopped.
Over time, the emotional pressure began affecting my physical health as well. I was hospitalized twice, both times in serious conditions.
Being hospitalized in another country is difficult enough, even when you can afford it. When money is already tight, the anxiety becomes even greater.
After those experiences, I stopped trying to transform my life all at once.
Instead, I started small.
I learned to be grateful that I was alive today.
If the weather was beautiful, I appreciated it.
If I finished one task, I allowed myself to feel proud of it.
I would be lying if I said I no longer worry about where I will be in five or ten years — I still do.
But I am trying to spend less time living inside an uncertain future and more time doing the best I can with the day in front of me.
I still sometimes struggle in crowded places. There are moments when breathing becomes difficult, or my emotions change quickly.
And yet, strangely, when I am out reporting, I can become completely absorbed in the work and somehow manage.
The difference now is that I have learned to accept these parts of myself rather than constantly fight against them.
I have also learned something else:
We cannot carry everything alone.
Having someone who listens, someone who cares, someone who simply asks, “Are you okay?” can sometimes feel like medicine for the mind.
Still here, still trying
When I first entered journalism, I was simply a young person who wanted to write the truth.
Four years later, after witnessing so many painful stories, I have learned that telling other people’s stories also requires learning how to care for myself.
I still do not know what my future will look like.
I do not know when the road will take me home.
But there is one thing I have come to believe:
“As long as we are still alive, there is still something we can try.”
So I keep going with that belief.
I try to spend more time with the people who have cared for me and held me up when things became difficult. I try to appreciate them while they are still beside me.
And through all the days when I long to go home, I am still trying to survive in both of the identities I carry: as a journalist and as a human being.
Written by Exile Hub

b394caaea4801868: Google parent Alphabet reported its Q3 financial results on Wednesday afternoon, showing a healthy rise in revenue for the months of July to September. But the company's stock price has taken a beating, marking one of the largest post-earnings drops in its history. It comes down to several troubling aspects of the new report, including an admission by the company that AI search isn't earning as much as organic search, and despite that, Google expects to spend even more on AI next year.

The company took in almost $128 billion in Q3 2026, earning more than $26 billion in net income. These may sound like good numbers, but financial markets are not impressed. While revenue is up 25 percent versus last year, net income is almost $9 billion lower. As of this story's publication, the stock price is down almost 12 percent, and it was down about 13 percent earlier in the day.

While revenue was up 25 percent year over year, analysts expected more. Google reported earnings per share of $2.12, but the consensus projection ahead of Wednesday was $3.02. Google's Cloud products actually beat expectations, crossing $30 billion in revenue. That's about a billion more than analyst guesses.
8b3ed8665efbf0d7: Stenko Vlad/Shutterstock A few years ago, the singer Billie Eilish opened up on the Howard Stern Show about how she began watching porn around age 11. “I’m so angry that porn is so loved, and I’m so angry at myself for thinking that it was ok,” she said. Eilish became addicted to porn, and it led to problems. “The first few times I had sex, I was not saying no to things that were not good,” she said. She had nightmares because the content she was watching was so violent and abusive. Online porn is a multi-million dollar business, driven by algorithms designed to keep people clicking for more. These algorithms push more and more extreme content, often for free, to people who didn’t go searching for it. This can include strangulation, exploitation or incest porn, that’s often misogynistic and racist too. “If you take incest and strangulation, we can look at content studies from the 1980s, for example, when there was hardly any of that material,” Clare McGlynn, professor of law at Durham University in the UK, tells The Conversation Weekly podcast. “Today both incest and strangulation becomes mainstream.” In the UK, the government will ban the possession and publication of incest and strangulation porn from early November. McGlynn, who worked with civil society groups to push the regulation of extreme content, says it’s a “huge step” that sends a message about the harms of “normalising sexual violence”. McGlynn, who has written a recent book about the rise of extreme porn, says large online porn platforms are pushing people towards more and more extreme content. Their business model is to keep you engaged. They want us on the platform for as long as possible, and the way to do that is to feed you more content, not necessarily what you were looking for, but also, the more extreme, the more polarising, the more shocking content … unfortunately, that seems to be what our kind of base instincts go for and what does actually engage us to keep us searching. McGlynn says an abundance of extreme and violent porn is shaping the sex lives of young people, and it can lead to an increased risk of problematic behaviour. There’s a study that followed 16,000 young people, showing that high porn use, particularly at a young age, is a big risk factor in problematic sexual behaviour of young teenage boys. And there’s studies in Australia and the US … showing that the more porn they watch, the more strangulation they see, and then the more they identify that they act out the strangulation. 10696ec422baa2f8: The Hora 1 site is at the base of this peak of rock in northern Malawi. Chelsea Smith, CC BY-NDIn the ancient past, when human communities were small and the only way to travel was by walking, what were the chances of meeting a stranger? And what would happen next? We know that ancient people lived by foraging their food from wild plants and animals, but we know a lot less about their social lives. Would there be conflict as people defended territory? Or would they choose to share? Sometimes survival depends on choosing wisely between these options. Defending a territory has a cost, and it’s not always worth it. To understand how ancient people interacted with one another, we can start by looking at the food they ate. When food resources are densely clustered in predictable ways, it makes sense to establish and maintain a territory around them. When resources are sparsely distributed, they are harder to defend. One example of territoriality in modern foraging people comes from the Okiek in the mountains of Kenya. Here, families control the crucially important activity of honey-harvesting. In contrast, foraging groups that live in places where the next meal is less predictable also tend to be less territorial. For example, until recently !Kung foragers in the arid parts of the Kalahari Desert searched for animals to hunt across wide areas, and boundaries between groups were much more fluid. A smoky torch used to harvest honey. Jessica Thompson, CC BY-ND The strategies used by the Okiek and the !Kung are different solutions to the same problem: weighing the risk of going hungry against the risk of unfriendly social encounters. Applying this principle to archaeological finds can reveal clues about ancient human social organisation. The problem is how to find food remains from the ancient past. We are archaeologists who do research in Malawi, excavating fossil animal bones and stone tools from natural shelters of rock. Our aim is to understand how early humans lived from the end of the last ice age, between 19,000 and 10,000 years ago, until the start of farming and herd-keeping just a few thousand years ago. Although no glaciers were present in tropical Malawi during the last ice age, global environments were different from today. We wanted to know more about food availability then, and how this might have affected social interactions. We focused on a large shelter called Hora 1, located on a spectacular granite mountain that emerges like a tooth from the open woodlands in northern Malawi. Traces of ancient human activity are everywhere in this area: red coloured paintings on the rock walls, stone tools made of shiny quartz, hearths, human burials and, in the layers of earth carefully excavated over several visits, hundreds of thousands of bones. These are the remnants of uncountable meals for the communities who lived here. Hora Mountain rising from the landscape of northern Malawi. Chelsea Smith, CC BY-NC Of this formidable number of broken, cooked, cut, chewed and discarded animal parts we were able to identify almost 13,000 individual fragments, collectively spanning the last 21,000 years of human occupation. We have published a paper about these fragments and what they tell us about ancient cultural boundaries related to food availability. Our findings challenge the existing view that it was mostly coastal environments that promoted boundary formation in the past. Hunting close to home Large animals can provide a meal for a large group, so when hunters encounter them, they may prefer to chase them, even if that means ignoring smaller prey. But most of the bones we found belonged to small animals: tiny antelopes, hares, monkeys, and other creatures. That suggests that large prey with a lot of meat – like zebras, wildebeest and even rhinoceroses – were not very common in this valley in the past. Although the fragments were very small, we could see that they came from everywhere in the body: limbs, torsos and heads were all present. This suggests that these animals were hunted close to the site, and the whole carcass was brought back (not just the best parts of large animals). The bones indicate that foragers at Hora 1 hunted close to home throughout the thousands of years recorded in the archaeological deposits. We confirmed this by comparing the chemistry of the local geology to chemical traces in the animal teeth: we found that they matched. The fossil tooth of a wildebeest from HOR-1, an animal that has not been recorded in modern times in this part of Malawi. The lines in the tooth are where small samples were taken for chemical analysis. Ruoyang Tu, CC BY-NC But there is a twist to this story. The animal bones were extremely fragmented, on average only the size of a little finger. Then we looked at some of the smallest and most nutrient poor bones in the skeleton: the phalanges, or finger and toe bones. Most had been broken open to recover even the smallest amounts of fatty marrow from inside. Probably food was not so abundant in this valley if people spent their time on such meagre packages of nutrients. So why didn’t people just range further to find more food, and what kept them at that site for so long? We think the answer lies in their social worlds. In-group cooperation and out-group hostility We found that animals were of different ages when they died: youngsters, adults, and even animals so old their teeth were worn down. This suggests some form of indiscriminate mass hunting such as the use of nets or traps. It is also possible that fire was used to aid communal game drives of larger animals. All these practices would have required coordination of labour, as well as social norms on how to split the bounty. This in-group cooperation likely came with some sense of shared identity, like a cultural group. The next question is how far across the landscape this group would have roamed. Were they like the !Kung, who maintain strong social ties with neighbouring groups? Or were they more like the Okiek, focused on keeping resources within their families? A clue came from an unexpected source: ancient DNA. DNA preserved in some of the human burials found at these sites showed that relatedness became smaller very quickly as one moved further from the sites. Starting 19,000 years ago, at the end of the ice age, an invisible boundary was taking shape in tropical Africa, separating “us and them”. Ancient human DNA was recovered from ancient foragers buried at Hora 1 and at this cave, which is about 100km north of the Hora 1 site. Jacob Davis, CC BY-NC All this evidence together points to behaviour that was very “local” in nature. However, the focus on recovering every scrap of food suggests that prey were not abundant enough to justify active defence of this territory. We also do not see evidence for persistent violent encounters or large, stable settlements, as have been documented near rich sources of food such as lakes and oceans. It is possible that these boundaries were only symbolically defended, for instance through collective practices like the 9,500-year-old funerary pyre that we recently described from Hora 1. Read more: Oldest known cremation in Africa poses 9,500-year-old mystery about Stone Age hunter-gatherers Most “cultural groups” that are known from archaeology are inferred from durable artifacts that preserve well, such as ornaments made of animal teeth and shells, or pottery shaped in a specific way. But most foragers spent so much time on the move that they never made such heavy things. In tropical Africa, our research has unearthed evidence for ancient cultural boundaries even without these objects. We have also found that there can be a “home” territory and a strong sense of in-group cultural belonging without violence against other groups. Finally, we have shown that the vast interior of the continent, while less studied than its coasts, is a rich source of information on the evolution of human cooperation and competition. Alex Bertacchi received funding for this research from the US National Science Foundation. Jessica C. Thompson has received funding for excavations at the Hora 1 site from the National Geographic Society, Wenner-Gren Foundation, Emory University, and Yale University.
e6f6442f7057ac5e: When people view sexualised images of women, they tend to remember them less well than sexualised images of men; a quirk of memory that psychologists link to objectification. But in our new study, my colleagues and I found an unlikely “fix” – applying a mild electrical current to the forehead. Objectification means seeing someone as a body, or a set of body parts, rather than as a whole person. Our results, published in Social Neuroscience, suggest this bias in perception is not hard-wired and can be changed – at least for a while. Psychologists measure it with an upside-down test. People are much better at recognising faces and bodies the right way up – typically about 80% right, against 55% upside down – because we take in how all the parts fit together. With objects, such as houses, turning them over matters far less, because we recognise them by their parts. A 2012 study used this test on sexualised images. Volunteers briefly saw a photo, then had to pick it out from a pair: the photo itself and its mirror image. Men and women alike did far better with men in underwear when the photos were upright, but did about as well with women in similar poses either way – the pattern expected for objects. The finding has been debated, and some attempts to repeat it have failed. But a 2022 analysis pooling results from 41 papers found the “upright advantage” – how much better people recognise someone the right way up than upside down – is smaller for sexualised women than sexualised men. Sexually objectified women are seen as less competent and less fully human, and women who absorb this view of themselves tend to have poorer body image and worse mental, physical and sexual health. Exposure to sexualised media is also linked to greater tolerance of sexual violence against women. The bias also shifts with circumstances. In a 2015 study, blurring out women’s chests and groins, or describing them as medical graduates raising money for cancer research, made people recognise their bodies more like men’s. Power plays a part. In earlier research in Canada, a colleague and I asked people to spend ten minutes writing about a time they had power over someone, or when someone had power over them. An established way to make people feel powerful or powerless. Women who felt powerful showed the object-like pattern for sexualised men, and powerful men showed it for sexualised women. People who felt powerless showed the upright advantage for both. Power, rather than gender itself, may be central to objectification. Where the brain stimulation idea came from The idea of trying brain stimulation came from my lab’s work on a famous illusion. In the Thatcher illusion, first shown with a photo of the former British prime minister, a face with its eyes and mouth turned upside down looks grotesque the right way up but almost normal upside down. Turning “Thatcherised” faces upside down also hurts recognition much less than it does with ordinary faces – just as with sexualised women. We had found that the same weak current made Thatcherised faces easier to recognise the right way up, bringing back the usual difference. Would it do the same for sexualised women? The Thatcher illusion. In our new study, 76 university students tried to memorise photos of male and female models posing in underwear – half of them upside down. They then saw the same photos again, each the same way up as before and mixed with 32 new ones, and said whether they had seen each one before. Half the students received a weak current for ten minutes, using a technique called transcranial direct current stimulation. The others received a placebo that switched off after 30 seconds – a standard way of mimicking the tingle of the real thing. Neither the students nor the researchers testing them knew who got which. The placebo group showed the familiar pattern. They remembered men far better when the photos were upright than when upside down. For women, the difference was much smaller, mainly because they remembered upright women less well than upright men. In the stimulated group, recognition of upright images of women improved, and the gap between images of men and women disappeared. The current did not change the upright advantage for images of men. Why? Our best explanation comes from a theory of how people learn to see. With experience, the brain learns to play down features that all faces share and to pick out the details that tell one person from another. But some shared features grab attention instead, such as the flipped eyes and mouth of a Thatcherised face – or, we suspect, the body parts on display in sexualised images. They crowd out the details that tell one person from another. The current may weaken that pull. Our study was a single lab session with university students, and we only measured its immediate effects, not attitudes or behaviour. Because every image was sexualised, we also cannot say how much of the gap comes from sexualisation itself rather than other differences between the photos. Brain stimulation is no cure for sexism. But if ten minutes of a weak current – or ten minutes spent writing about feeling powerful or powerless – can shift how people see a body, objectification looks less like a fixed feature of human vision and more like a habit. And habits, unlike hard-wiring, can change. Ciro Civile receives funding from the Economic and Social Research Council and previously from the European Union Horizon
05e64d90fcbc7502: Their petition to the authorities has already gathered over 500 signatures
Originally published on Global Voices
DigiAction picnic held in Lozhan village, Albania. Photo by Qendra KAZUS. Used with permission.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

In rural parts of Albania, youth are seldom mobilized to help solve local environmental and other problems in their communities, although they, too, are affected by them. This has been the case in the eastern Korce region as well, which was hit by heavy rainfall and subsequent devastating floods in November 2025.

In the Maliq municipality, one of the affected areas, the situation was worsened by improper disposal of waste that blocked drainage channels, including the Devoll River, which flows through the area. Illegal waste disposal has obstructed the river’s infrastructure and contributed to widespread flooding. Despite efforts by the authorities to improve waste management and clean up the river, the situation has remained dire.
Waste accumulated at the Devoll River Bridge in Maliq, Albania. Photo from November 21, 2025 by Qendra KAZUS. Used with permission.

In 2026, a local non-governmental organization (NGO), Qendra KAZUS, recruited and trained local youth to help solve this long-standing issue by turning them into environmental advocates. Global Voices conducted an email interview with Dhorjela Cela, the group’s executive director, to learn about how Qendra KAZUS implemented a project that brought together youth, digital democracy, environmental challenges, and advocacy. The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.

Dhorjela Cule (DC): Qendra KAZUS was founded in 2024 and focuses on young people’s activism and engagement. Our team brings together journalists, photojournalists, and education specialists with years of experience in media, law, and mentoring.

Our mission is to strengthen democracy and the rule of law through youth advocacy and to raise awareness around preserving cultural heritage, protecting the environment, and building capacity in ICT and media. As a young organization, our work relied mainly on small activities and projects.

Digital Sparks gave us the opportunity to prioritize digital advocacy. We saw a chance to give young people in rural areas and cities tools they use every day — their phones and social media — and turn them into instruments of civic participation and accountability.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

DC: The Devoll River in the eastern Korça region is facing a serious environmental situation. Plastic pollution, inert waste, agricultural waste, and other debris accumulate along the riverbanks. During winter floods, high river flows expose and spread this waste, blocking drainage canals, and water overflows from the riverbed into agricultural land and residential areas, damaging soil health, livelihoods, and the local ecosystem.
In the villages of Lozhan and Pojan, the waste is considerable, and local authorities seem to have their hands tied in finding a solution.

What worried us most was that young people from rural areas, whose families depend on agriculture and are directly affected, were excluded from the search for solutions. They had phones and strong opinions, but no channel to turn them into public pressure.
We wanted to show that the right to a clean environment is something young people can demand with evidence and a collective voice.
Waste on the banks of the Devoll River in Pojan from May 2026. Photo by Qendra KAZUS. Used with permission.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?

DC: We implemented three phases of the project. First, we recruited and trained 44 young people from Maliq municipality in MoJo, aiming to turn mobile storytelling, video editing for reels, and graphic design in Canva into a powerful advocacy tool.

Second, we organized two Digital Picnics along the Devoll River and the affected farmland, piloting two locations in the villages of Pojan and Lozhan, where participants filmed and photographed the accumulation of waste, creating a “visual pollution map”. Thirty materials produced by the young people were published on social media to raise public awareness.

Finally, we launched an online petition, through which we will ask the Maliq municipality to step up cleaning actions, with the joint commitment of the municipality and the community, as well as community education and awareness.
The petition was hosted on Change.org to reach a wider audience and has collected 506 signatures so far, exceeding our target.
Participants of the DigiAction Picnic in Pojan, Albania. Photo by Qendra KAZUS. Used with permission.
GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.

DC: For the young participants, the project turned social media from an entertainment tool into a tool for action. Forty-four young people learned to document environmental problems and communicate them publicly.

“I had never seen the use of social media from this perspective. Now, I have a different approach to the posts I can make,” said Igli, one of the young people who joined the training and field activity.

For the community, the Digital Picnics made the pollution visible: everyone had the chance to see the waste accumulated along the river in videos and posts, and hundreds of people engaged with our content online.

The petition gave residents and supporters a simple way to take a stand, and 506 people signed it online. The materials now form a public archive of evidence that the community can use in future discussions with local authorities.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?
DC: Through Digital Sparks, we came to understand digital democracy more broadly: using technology to document facts, mobilize people, and demand accountability from institutions.
We learned how evidence, whether a video, a poster, or a signature, gives citizens credibility when they address public authorities.

We also gained practical experience in campaign planning, content strategy, moderating online comments, using Instagram and TikTok analytics, and digital safety and ethics, including the protection of young participants and personal data.
As a team, this project taught us how to turn this knowledge into youth-led digital civic action.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

DC: One of the most valuable lessons is that in the digital era, young people need little technical equipment, but much more mentoring and guidance to lead them towards becoming responsible citizens who make demands and engage in concrete action to be part of decision-making. Their phones and creativity are enough when they have a clear purpose and guidance.
Second, an informal and enjoyable format like the Digital Picnic lowers barriers to participation and attracts young people, including girls and those from marginalized groups or low-income families.

Images and facts are more persuasive to institutions than complaints, but this experience taught us that flexibility is essential. Choosing Change.org instead of Google Forms for the petition taught us to adapt tools to the audience.
Finally, institutional change and engagement take time, and follow-up is as important as mobilization.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

DC: Qendra KAZUS has started implementing another project in which part of the knowledge gained is being applied. The use of social media by young people as a powerful mechanism to raise their voice and demand more engagement and responsibility from institutions is this time focused on cultural heritage.

What remains essential for us is identifying a completely different approach to young people, through the channels and platforms where they spend a considerable part of their time and focus their communication.

It is worth stressing that finding a meeting point with young people, through a method that is interesting to them, is of particular importance. We have managed to involve them by showing that social media can also be used as a healthy mechanism that achieves results for their demands.

95da20d12b9a0c2b: Like the Strait of Hormuz, the Suez Canal is a vital waterway for global trade. Viktor Hladchenko/ShutterstockMonths after the US and Israel launched Operation Epic Fury against Iran, the Strait of Hormuz remains largely closed. The UK chose not to get directly involved in the conflict. Nonetheless, it has been exposed to the crisis through record-high diesel prices as well as a spike in inflation. This echoes an earlier crisis in the Middle East, as my recent research illustrates. Seventy years ago, the Egyptian government nationalised the Suez canal, sparking the Suez crisis. The canal, which passes through Egypt from the Red Sea to the Mediterranean, was a vital link for ships travelling between Europe and Asia. After its completion in 1869 by a French-led company, the Egyptian government held a 44% stake in it. However, financial difficulties forced Egypt to sell its shares to the British government in 1875, leaving Britain and France with substantial financial interests in the canal. Following the Egyptian nationalisation of the canal, France and Britain – together with Israel – invaded Egypt in an attempt to regain control of the vital waterway. But the invasion was a spectacular failure that was condemned by the international community. The crisis came to symbolise Britain’s loss of superpower status. Today, the US midterm elections are increasing the pressure on the Trump administration over the current conflict. Elections in Israel have also had some bearing on the conflict, with recent reports that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pushed for renewed strikes ahead of the election. Other reports suggest that the US and Israel have drawn up plans to resume strikes after the elections. In 1956, US presidential elections were also an important part of the calculus. But back then, Britain and France had assumed that the elections would distract the US from their actions. This was a miscalculation. In communication with UK Prime Minister Anthony Eden the day after the vote, US President Dwight D. Eisenhower was clear that his administration would not tolerate the UK, France and Israel’s continued actions. He demanded a negotiated settlement through the UN. The parallels between Suez and Hormuz go beyond the closure of two vital waterways. Both crises raise the same question: how far can geopolitical power outrun economic power? Superpowers in decline In 1944, the American foreign policy professor William T.R. Fox coined the term “super-power”. He defined it as the consequence of “great wealth, great population, and favourable geographic position”. This is similar to how the historian Phillips O’Brien defines great power today. Fox saw three superpowers at that time: the US, Britain, and the Soviet Union. He later acknowledged that including Britain had been a mistake, primarily because of its relative decline against the US and later the rest of Europe. Arguably a similar shift is taking place today. There are arguments over what is the best measure of an economy, but on the basis of purchasing power the shift is striking. China has moved from being a fraction of the size of the US economy in 1990 to being well ahead today. In the 19th century, Britain was the dominant global power and benefited from what economists call “exorbitant privilege”. This was the ability to easily finance debt at favourable interest rates because sterling played a central role in the international monetary system. London was also the world’s leading financial centre. But as Britain declined, this privilege gradually shifted towards the US. Its loss became particularly pressing during the Suez crisis as the pound came under intense pressure. Similarly today, there are signs of strain in the financial system that underpins American power. During the Suez crisis, Britain’s currency weakness and dependence on American financial support constrained its ability to act independently, despite its considerable military power. The crisis was also part of wider cold war geopolitics. An arms deal signed in 1955 between Egypt and the Soviet Union had upset the regional balance of power and contributed to Israel’s decision to get involved in a preventative war. In response to the arms deal, the US withdrew financing for the Aswan Dam, a major infrastructure project on the River Nile. Then, in 1956, Egypt nationalised the Suez canal, sparking the crisis. British leaders sought to portray Egyptian president Gamal Abdel Nasser as a 1930s dictator, intent on regional dominance. Egyptian president Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal in 1956. Wikimedia Commons The US intervention in Iran has similar connotations. US secretary of war Pete Hegseth has presented the assassination of the Iranian leadership as necessary to prevent an existential threat from “America’s mortal enemy”. Geoeconomics, the relationship between economics and geopolitics, also played a central role in the Suez crisis. The canal was a major conduit for Middle Eastern oil and there were fears that the nationalisation of the canal would disrupt UK oil supplies. But ironically, it was the decision to invade Egypt that led to a shortage of oil and fuel rationing in the UK. The wider cold war was a key factor in the US stance on events. The US did not want to be seen to be condoning imperial actions in Egypt while condemning Russian imperialism in Hungary. Just as the Suez crisis needs to be understood in the context of the cold war, the current conflict should also be seen through the lens of “cold war II” geopolitics. Relations between the US and China have not thawed, while proxy wars bear similarities to the first cold war. Today, the US is increasingly stretched, most clearly seen in the depletion of its munitions. These were already under pressure (in part because of its support for Ukraine) and have been further reduced by the war with Iran. The Suez crisis illustrates how political leaders can be slow to appreciate the economic constraints on their geopolitical ambitions. The US today is not Britain in 1956, yet the conflict in Iran has prompted questions about the limits of American power. As its relative economic dominance is challenged, will the US also have to reconsider the extent of its global military commitments?
